items.title: Circular Ecosystem‐Orchestrating Leadership: Microfoundations of Ecosystem‐Related Dynamic Capabilities for a Circular Economy Transition
items.abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) increasingly depends on circular ecosystems: networks of autonomous yet interdependent actors that must coordinate material, information, and value flows to narrow, slow, and close resource loops. This creates a governance problem: Circularity requires orchestration, yet no single actor can impose coordination hierarchically. Combining an integrative review of peer‐reviewed articles at the intersection of CE, dynamic capabilities (DCs), and leadership research with theory synthesis, we introduce Circular Ecosystem‐Orchestrating Leadership (CEOL): an actor‐level, boundary‐spanning leadership capability that helps convert coordination barriers into governance outputs. We theorize three mechanisms: (1) narrative bridging translates divergent circularity meanings into shared interpretive frames; (2) platform convening creates credible multilateral commitments for coordinated investment; and (3) institutional entrepreneurship produces legitimate rule adaptation across public and private arenas. Each mechanism has a primary pathway to collective sensing, seizing, or reconfiguring respectively, but the mechanisms interact laterally and are recursively reshaped by the collective capabilities they support. Through these governance outputs, CEOL microfounds ecosystem‐level DCs. The framework advances CE leadership research beyond firm‐level adoption, extends DC theory by specifying governance‐mediated microfoundations of collective capabilities, and reframes circular ecosystem governance as a contested, territorially conditioned achievement vulnerable to narrative capture, platform capture or exclusion, and regulatory capture.

items.title: Spatializing the Circular Economy: Firm-Level Evidence and Socio-Demographic Factors within a National Post-Consumer Sneaker Network
items.abstract: Post-consumer footwear constitutes a highly heterogeneous and minimally circular segment of the consumer goods economy. Although the sector has a substantial environmental footprint, empirical research on post-consumer footwear collection and reverse logistics remains limited. This study contributes to circular economy scholarship by showing that post-consumer sneaker collection depends largely on intermediary capacity, territorial coordination, and robust reverse-logistics infrastructure. Using a novel, spatially granular shipment dataset (2024-2025) covering hundreds of U.S. ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs), the analysis examines the spatial organization, temporal dynamics, and persistence of a national post-consumer sneaker collection network managed by Sneaker Impact. By integrating shipment records with American Community Survey data, the research identifies the socio-demographic factors associated with participation in reverse logistics systems. The findings indicate spatial heterogeneity and significant variation in participation frequency, alongside a modest core of recurrently active locations. Aggregate throughput growth mainly coincided with an increase in the number of active ZCTAs, while average shipment activity per active ZCTA changed little, though these patterns remain confounded by unobserved organizational outreach. Community circular participation exhibits modest socio-demographic stratification. Among the variables examined, educational attainment is the strongest and most consistent correlate of shipment activity, while income shows a slight negative association when controlling for educational attainment. However, socio-demographic characteristics explain only a limited share of the variation in shipment activity, suggesting that organizational and infrastructural factors also play an important role in shaping collection performance. items.title: Researching Business Models for Building Sustainable Agriculture
items.abstract: Business models are increasingly recognized as key architectures that may help coordinate technological, organizational, social, and territorial innovations in sustainable agriculture. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 325 publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (2002–2026) to map the epistemic, conceptual, and intellectual structure of research on business models for building sustainable agriculture. Using Price’s, Lotka’s, Bradford’s, and Zipf’s laws, along with co-citation analysis, the study examines temporal growth, author productivity, journal concentration, thematic clusters, and foundational literature. Results suggest exponential growth in scientific production, strong alignment with SDGs related to food security, circular economy, climate action, and biodiversity, and a highly concentrated intellectual core centered on business model design, sustainability transitions, and digital transformation. Four thematic clusters emerge: innovation and agricultural systems; management, governance, and business models; sustainability and climate-energy dynamics; and challenges, assessment, and ecosystem services. Co-citation analysis reveals three major axes shaping the field: strategic business model design, circular and sustainable value creation, and digital and territorial transformation of agri-food systems. Overall, the findings suggest that sustainable agriculture may benefit from hybrid business models integrating technological innovation, circularity, governance, and multi-actor collaboration.

items.title: Material Circularity and Waste-Management GHG Emissions of Construction and Demolition Waste in Bangkok: A Dynamic Material Flow Analysis
items.abstract: Construction and demolition waste (CDW) is a major urban material flow whose long-term generation depends on the age structure of the building stock. This study develops an inflow-driven, cohort-based dynamic material flow analysis (dMFA) for Bangkok that integrates reconstructed pre-2004 building cohorts, CDW generation, a system-level Material Circularity Indicator (MCIsys), and waste-management greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting. Six scenarios, representing a business-as-usual baseline and single and combined applications of waste prevention, recycling, and lifetime extension, were evaluated through 2100. Demolition waste dominated the modeled CDW stream, with concrete as the largest urban-mining stream. Total CDW reached a mid-century maximum of 13.8 Mt/yr around 2062, ranging from 12.1 to 14.6 Mt/yr in 2055–2066 across the reconstruction and inflow sensitivity cases. MCIsys increased from 0.128 under the baseline to 0.290 under Circular Routing and 0.313 under Ambitious Circular Economy by 2100. Within the direct waste-management boundary, which excludes avoided virgin-material production, higher recycling increased cumulative GHG emissions by 3–30% over 2025–2100 across all tested inflow cases because of recycling processing and longer transport, whereas lifetime extension lowered them by 9–22% within the horizon by delaying demolition. The MCIsys contrast remained robust under parameter uncertainty, and the GHG increase under circular routing occurred in all paired simulations.

items.title: Economic succession: an ecology-informed diagnostic framework for sustainable urban transformation
items.abstract: Cities around the world face the difficult task of transforming their economies to decarbonize, use resources more efficiently, strengthen resilience, and broaden access to opportunity. Yet a transition that progresses in one city may stall in another, and urban economics offers limited practical guidance for explaining why. To address this gap, this Conceptual Analysis develops urban economic succession as a middle-range framework for ordered but non-deterministic change in an urban economy's portfolio of activities. It translates the causal architecture of ecological succession into six economically observable components: opportunity availability, access to potential activities, local capability fit, interactions among activities, historical legacies and feedback, and extra-local connectivity. The framework brings together insights from sectoral transition, urban scaling, relatedness, economic complexity, production networks, and urban metabolism, while distinguishing changes in economic composition from judgments about what counts as sustainable. Five falsifiable propositions and a seven-step diagnostic workflow show how it can identify different barriers to green industrial diversification, circular production, low-carbon buildings, resilience, and other sustainable transformations. The framework does not treat cities as biological ecosystems, assume that urban economies follow a universal sequence, or equate greater internal cycling with greater sustainability. Instead, it offers a comparative research program for identifying recurrent transition pathways, explaining why cities depart from them, and matching interventions to the specific constraints operating in particular city-regions.

items.title: Survivalist circularity: theorising fragility and displacement within necessity-driven circular economies
items.abstract: The scholarship on circular economy (CE) is increasingly recognising that in low income contexts, repair, reuse, repurposing, second-hand exchange and material recovery may be driven by economic necessity rather than environmental intention. This paper builds on the established necessity-driven circular economy and develops a narrower, mechanism-level construct of survivalist circularity. Survivalist circularity is defined as circular material practices that can only be sustained under a binding material or livelihood constraint. The construct and its boundaries are defined by a purposive conceptual synthesis of CE, informal recovery, sustainable-livelihoods, frugal-innovation, value-retention, measurement and just-transition literatures. Five testable propositions and a two-axis model relate material constraint to institutional support for value retention. The main prediction is conditional displacement, whereby relaxing a binding constraint decreases the necessity-attributable component of circular practice, while total circularity decreases only where designed, institutional, market or value-based drivers do not substitute. Our paper makes four contributions. It theoretically detects a constraint-contingent mechanism and a temporal displacement risk in necessity-driven CE. It distinguishes survivalist circularity from informality, frugal innovation and geographic or poverty labels in terms of construction. Methodologically, it prioritises the distinction between formal CE institutionalisation and directly observed material practice. In policy, it defines institutional substitution as the sequencing of repair access, secondary markets, safe recovery systems and worker protections before or as necessity weakens. Thus the construct is not a label for Global South or low-income circularity generally, but a testable causal regime, whose value for empirical work depends on demonstrating counterfactual dependence on constraint.

items.title: LOCALIZATION OF INDUSTRIAL LUBRICANTS AND PETROLEUM PRODUCT SUPPLY CHAINS IN SAUDI ARABIAS OIL AND GAS SECTOR UNDER VISION 2030
items.abstract: The Saudi initiative to localise its industry is now moving the procurement of oil and gas away from simple import substitution and towards the development of domestic capabilities. Industrial lubricants and other petroleum products serve as a good example since they involve regular demand alongside complex formulations, depend on imported additives, have to meet equipment approval requirements, and also have potential in the area of the circular economy. This study draws on peer-reviewed evidence published between 2020 and 2025 to look at where localisation can generate defensible value throughout the supply chain for lubricants and petroleum products and to identify the capabilities needed to ensure reliability, quality, and cost control. A structured integrative review of thirty studies verified by the DOI was carried out and the studies were coded according to feasibility of localisation, supplier capability, resilience, digitalisation, sustainability, and governance. The findings show that localisation should advance at an uneven rate along the value chain. Activities such as blending, packaging, laboratory testing, warehousing, providing field technical services, collecting used oil, and certain re-refining operations present relatively short-term opportunities, while advanced additive chemistry and special formulations need a much longer period for building up capabilities.

items.title: BIM and digital twin integration in circular construction: addressing lifecycle fragmentation
items.venue: Journal of Engineering Design and Technology
items.abstract: Purpose The construction sector faces increasing pressure to transition toward circular economy (CE) practices to reduce material waste, embodied carbon, and lifecycle environmental impacts. Digital construction technologies from construction 4.0, particularly building information modeling (BIM) and digital twins (DTs), are widely promoted as key enablers of this transition. However, the current body of knowledge remains fragmented, with limited clarity on how BIM and DT collectively support circular strategies across the building lifecycle. This study aims to systematically synthesize and clarify how digital technologies enable CE implementation across lifecycle stages and identify where integration remains weak. Design/methodology/approach A PRISMA-guided review was conducted using Scopus as the primary database. The search strategy was structured around three dimensions: WHAT (digital technologies), TO WHAT (lifecycle phases), and FOR WHAT (circular objectives). A total of 266 peer-reviewed studies were included following screening and eligibility assessment. The review synthesizes frameworks, tools, and application patterns that link BIM, DTs, and complementary construction 4.0 technologies to CE outcomes. Findings The results reveal three insights. First, digital-enabled circular construction remains design-centric, with limited continuity into operation, maintenance, and end-of-life stages. Second, advanced capabilities such as artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and IoT-enabled feedback are underused for lifecycle-wide circular optimization. Third, interoperable and empirically validated BIM–DT ecosystems are scarce, and context-sensitive implementation frameworks remain underdeveloped. Research limitations/implications This review relies on Scopus as the sole database, and although justified on its coverage basis, this introduces potential source-selection bias; future syntheses should triangulate with WoS and other databases like Google Scholar.

items.title: Circular economy-driven bio-digital building adaptation: integrating biodegradable materials with AI-enabled lifecycle tracking
items.venue: International Journal of Building Pathology and Adaptation
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how circular economy principles in the built environment can be advanced by integrating biodegradable construction materials with digital lifecycle intelligence. It addresses the persistent challenges of embodied carbon reduction, waste minimisation and material recovery in building adaptation and retrofitting, aiming to develop and validate a bio-digital framework that enables regenerative material cycles. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory mixed-method research design was adopted, combining a systematic literature review with the development of a circular economy-driven bio-digital adaptation framework. Two illustrative case scenarios modular partition systems using mycelium composites and ceiling insulation retrofits using hempcrete were analysed using life cycle assessment material circularity indicators, and AI-supported decision simulations. Framework validation was undertaken through a Delphi-lite expert workshop involving academic and industry stakeholders, providing quantitative ratings and qualitative feedback on feasibility, scalability and innovation. Findings The results indicate that bio-digital systems can achieve substantial embodied carbon reductions (up to 58%) and high circularity performance (Material Circularity Indicator >0.8) compared with conventional alternatives. The scenarios demonstrate that biodegradable materials, when supported by digital tracking, material passports, and AI-enabled decision support, can extend service life, enable controlled biodegradation, and support reuse pathways. Expert feedback confirmed the framework's innovation and practical relevance, while identifying durability, certification, and cost as key adoption challenges. Originality/value This study presents the first integrated bio-digital adaptation framework that explicitly links biodegradable materials with digital lifecycle intelligence. items.title: Material Flow Analysis of Electronic Waste Management for Sustainable Urban Resource Management in Gazipur City Bangladesh
items.abstract: Electronic waste (e-waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste streams worldwide, posing significant environmental and public health challenges, particularly in developing countries where recycling is dominated by the informal sector. This study quantifies e-waste generation, material flows, and management practices in Gazipur City Corporation, Bangladesh, using Material Flow Analysis (MFA) integrated with household surveys (n = 375), stakeholder interviews, field observations, and secondary data. Approximately 6,245.21 tonnes of e-waste were generated in 2024, equivalent to 2.43 kg capita⁻¹ year⁻¹. Large household appliances accounted for the largest share of the waste stream, with refrigerators (42.05%), televisions (19.44%), and microwave ovens (9.26%) being the major contributors. Nearly 47% of e-waste was managed through informal collection and recycling networks or disposed of with municipal solid waste, increasing environmental and health risks. Key barriers included inadequate collection infrastructure, weak regulatory enforcement, limited public awareness, and the absence of effective Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). The study recommends strengthening formal collection systems, integrating informal recyclers into regulated recycling networks, and implementing EPR within a circular economy framework to improve resource recovery. These findings provide quantitative evidence to support sustainable urban resource management and e-waste policy development in rapidly urbanizing low- and middle-income countries.

items.title: Industrial symbiosis for sustainable manufacturing: An application to steel and cement industries in Kuwait
items.abstract: Industrial symbiosis offers a practical way to reduce industrial waste and virgin material use by exchanging by-products between nearby industries. This study exhibits the industrial symbiosis between steel and cement industries in Kuwait that can provide more effective industrial waste management to compensate the negative environmental impact of the conventional ‘take-make-dispose’ method. The purpose of this research is to investigate industrial symbiosis as a way to increase the sustainability of the manufacturing sector in Kuwait and to create a circular economy. The main objectives are to evaluate the feasibility of establishing a by-product exchange between steel and cement companies, to assess resource efficiency, to develop a closed-loop system framework, to quantify environmental benefits, and to evaluate the economic consequences. Data on waste streams and resource requirements were collected from steel and cement manufacturing companies in a specific industrial area. Input-output matching was used to identify symbiotic relationships in which one company’s waste could serve as another’s input material. Material flow analysis, a simplified life cycle assessment, and cost-benefit analysis were used to estimate the material, environmental, and economic effects of the proposed exchange. Using KCC’s reported current consumption of 756 tons/day of steel slag as the baseline, the study evaluates a hypothetical incremental exchange in which an additional 658 tons/day generated by KWT Steel is introduced into KCC’s cement-production system. The resulting environmental and economic effects are estimated as screening-level outcomes based on company data and literature-derived assumptions. At full modeled utilization, KCC’s clinker requirement decreases by 658 tons/day, while the estimated gross CO 2 reduction has a central value of 546.1 tons/day and ranges from 427.7 to 605.4 tons/day. items.title: Circular Bioenergy Production from Heavy-Metal-Contaminated Biomass: An Integrated Biorefinery Optimization Approach
items.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CHEMISTRY AND CHEMICAL PROCESSES
items.abstract: The increasing prevalence of heavy-metal-contaminated biomass in industrial, agricultural, and remediation processes poses challenges for the environment and the bioenergy sector. This paper elaborates and analyzes a risk-conscious integrated bio-refinery optimization model for circular bioenergy generation from contaminated biomass, enabling the production of both biodiesel and biogas while accounting for heavy-metal fate and associated environmental risks. System performance was evaluated based on low, moderate, and high levels of contamination (10–1,000 mg·kg⁻¹) using deterministic multi-objective optimization, global sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo propagation of uncertainty, and multivariate regime classification. Findings indicate that total energy recovery decreased from 13,610 to 6,665 MJ·t⁻¹ biomass with increasing contamination; nevertheless, anaerobic digestion gradually replaced energy production, with a maximum contribution of 75.2 percent to total output at high contamination. Biodiesel production went down to 172.4 to 44.6 kg·t⁻¹, and still, the amount of metals in biodiesel was at a quarter of the previous range, 0.5 mg·kg⁻¹. The fraction of incoming heavy metals immobilized in the digestate exceeded96 percent, and it met regulatory limits for land application in all situations, with compliance rates over 90 percent under stochastic uncertainty. Pareto-optimal solutions have shown obvious trade offs in terms of energy recovery, metal risk index (0.07-0.18), and circularity performance (0.79 0.92). In contrast, principal component and cluster analysis revealed operation regimes influenced by contamination. The investigation introduces a system-level approach and reinvigorates the concept of heavy-metal contamination as a manageable design constraint, offering a significant pathway to sustainable bioenergy recovery from polluted landscapes within the circular bioeconomy.

items.title: Public Sector Analytics for Territorial Healthcare Planning: Federated Learning Under the European Health Data Space
items.venue: International Journal of Clinical Research and Medical Sciences
items.abstract: This paper applies public sector analytics to the challenges of demographic decline, population ageing, and progressive desertification of healthcare and social care services in many European territories. These trends threaten territorial cohesion and equitable access to care. The European Health Data Space (EHDS) establishes a new regulatory and infrastructural framework for primary and secondary use of health data across Member States, opening opportunities for advanced analytics under strict data protection safeguards. This paper argues that federated learning (FL), embedded within the EHDS governance framework, has the potential to serve as a policy data infrastructure to support territorial healthcare planning in ageing and shrinking regions. Public sector analytics components include long-term care demand forecasting, healthcare service availability indices, territorial inequality measurement, cross-regional benchmark comparisons, and policy intervention readiness scoring. Rather than focusing on algorithmic performance, we develop a conceptual model linking FL-enabled distributed analytics to concrete policy questions on care demand, service availability, and territorial inequalities in access. We first map the information needs of policy-makers dealing with demographic change and territorial cohesion, then analyse how EHDS provisions on secondary use, Health Data Access Bodies, and privacy-enhancing technologies can underpin multi-territorial FL projects. Building on this analysis, we propose a policy-oriented framework describing actors, processes, and outputs of EHDS-compliant FL initiatives aimed at informing regional and national health and social care strategies. We discuss implications for territorial cohesion, sustainability of health systems, and future research on governance of federated learning in European health data spaces.

items.title: A method for monitoring aircraft height above ground across diverse landforms using GNSS reflected signals: a field study
items.abstract: Altitude above Ground Level (AGL) is an important parameter in aircraft flight operations and safety. Conventional aircraft altitude measurement techniques are largely constrained by their dependence on active signal transmission, sensitivity to environmental conditions, limited operational coverage, and inherently localized single-point measurement geometry. This paper presents a method that leverages Global Navigation Satellite System-Reflectometry (GNSS-R) to acquire AGL height, providing a complementary solution to current measurement systems. The proposed system employs an upward-Right-Hand Circular Polarization (RHCP) antenna and a downward-Left-Hand Circular Polarization (LHCP) antenna together with an Intermediate Frequency (IF) collector for raw data collection. The collected data are subsequently processed offline using a Software Defined Receiver (SDR). This paper proposes the Short‑Time Shortest‑Path (STSP) method to retrieve high‑accuracy GNSS‑R AGL, which uses only 25 incoherent accumulations and selects the shortest path delay when the reflected waveform exhibits multiple peaks. For a feasibility assessment, we installed the system on an Aurora SA60L aircraft and conducted an approximately 288-km flight from Dongying City to Tai’an City of Shandong Province, China. Dual-frequency Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) IF data on the shared frequency bands were collected during the flight over diverse terrains, including rural, urban, suburban, and mountainous areas. BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) B1C/B2a, Global Positioning System (GPS)/Quasi-Zenith Satellite System (QZSS) L1 C/A/L5, and Galileo E1C/E5a signals were leveraged to compute the code- level path -delay differences between direct and reflected signals. The measurements were used to retrieve the aircraft's heights above multiple distinct specular reflection points. items.title: Measuring effective surface energy in non-equilibrium granular fluids using an innovative orbital tensiometer apparatus
items.abstract: Dense granular media lack a well-established analog of classical liquid tensiometry, although localized interfacial barriers can strongly influence segregation, buoyancy, and intruder stability. Using a calibrated dual-mode orbital calorimeter-rheometer, we show that a partially submerged intruder can serve as an in situ mechanical probe of the grain-mediated restoring response in an orbitally driven dense bed. In the rigid-body core-rotation regime at low peak acceleration, Γ=2.5, and low granular temperature, Tg≈10-7m2s-2, the intruder follows a stable circular orbit with negligible radial drift and intrinsic spin. This kinematic state indicates that the inward centripetal force required in the laboratory frame is balanced predominantly by a localized restoring interaction associated with the air-grain-intruder contact configuration. By combining the measured density-contrast centrifugal demand with the specific interfacial area of the ternary bead mixture and a geometry-calibrated effective radial transmission area, we obtain an effective granular interfacial-stress scale of γgm≈2.38×10-2Jm-2. The inferred value agrees within 1.2% with an independently obtained thermomechanical reference at the corresponding low granular temperature. The result provides a mechanical explanation for the granular Archimedean anomaly, in which the intruder remains stably surface supported while the displaced granular volume supplies less than half of its static weight under a conventional hydrostatic estimate. At the fluidization threshold, Γ=6.02, kinetic thermalization raises the granular temperature to Tg≈10-4m2s-2; the localized restoring configuration is then destabilized, and the intruder exhibits orientation instability, rapid inward migration, intrinsic rotation, and deep convective submersion. items.venue: Socio-economic relations in the digital society
items.abstract: The relevance of this study stems from the continuing conceptual ambiguity surrounding the meaning of circularity in economic activity and the need to distinguish clearly between its conceptual essence, implementation mechanisms, levels of manifestation, and outcomes. The aim of the study is to advance the conceptual foundations of the circularity of economic activity by clarifying the relationships between the key concepts, substantiating its internal structure, identifying its interconnected dimensions, and systematizing its defining characteristics. The study is conceptual in nature and is based on an integrative analysis of the scientific literature, using qualitative content analysis, comparison, grouping, systematization, theoretical synthesis, and structural and logical generalization.The study systematizes the main approaches to interpreting the circular economy and clarifies the relationships between the concepts of the “circular economy”, the “circular approach”, and the “circularity of economic activity”. The circularity of economic activity is proposed to be understood as the degree to which resources, materials, components, and products are actually reused and kept in productive use over an extended period, while preserving their utility and the value already created, substituting primary resources, and maintaining organized recurring flows. The study substantiates the integration of the resource-and-product and value-and-chain approaches and, on this basis, identifies three interconnected dimensions of circularity: the resource-and-product dimension, the economic-and-value dimension, and the production-and-chain dimension. Six defining characteristics of circularity are identified: repeated use, duration of use, substitution of primary resources, value retention, return and exchange, and systemic coherence. items.title: Policy Instruments Fostering Site Level Application of Circular Practices in Construction
items.abstract: One of the most pursued predicaments in the recent past is the slowness in transmuting circular practices. In the hope of many apparent advantages, construction firms have been attempting to embrace circularity-oriented functions, thus controlling their negativities to the extent possible. However, many of these are futile attempts that have been made ad hoc without having validated policy instruments intact. Only a few studies have taken an overarching approach to address this matter and effectively inculcate circularity at construction sites. This article aims to fill this knowledge gap by introducing a structured outline resulting in 9 policy categories and over 100 policy instruments. Developed from a review of 90 studies selected from the Google Scholar platform and 16 policy documents essentially contributed by eminent research groups, these policy instruments were subsequently validated in a series of 18 semi-structured interviews with experts and industry personnel having international exposure in large-scale construction projects. This study provides over 150 practical examples of scaffolding circularity as a noble cause. Of a practical insight, a fundamental reconfiguration of site operations is deemed indispensable.

items.title: Envisioning transition pathways for a sustainable meat and protein supply system in Japan: A Research through Design approach
items.abstract: The transition toward sustainable protein supply is constrained by consumer, supply-side, and policy barriers that are often studied separately, leaving unclear how a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis can inform multilevel intervention pathways. In Japan, small, dispersed farmland and imported-feed dependence intersect with established expectations of price and convenience. This exploratory case study examined Japan’s meat and protein supply system through a Research through Design approach integrating the multi-level perspective and Transition Design. Interviews with 21 participants and a co-creation workshop were used to structure current problems, envision desirable futures, and backcast potential interventions. The diagnosis showed how regulative, normative, and cognitive rules mutually reinforce these structural and cultural constraints. The research team synthesized participant outputs into three contrasting scenarios: pasture-raised lean beef, localized circular communities, and food-printer technology. Cross-scenario comparison yielded two provisional design principles: creating experiential proximity, which makes unfamiliar transition options tangible through situated experience, and culturally situated value translation, which connects sustainability values with meanings embedded in existing food cultures. The principles were instantiated differently and combined with pathway-specific system and governance components, including grading standards and sales channels, interorganizational coordination, and food law, labeling, and safety standards. The contribution lies in translating fragmented actor perspectives and a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis into a future-oriented intervention portfolio while making the interpretive steps traceable. The resulting principles and configurations provide testable propositions for comparative research and future pilot studies.

items.title: Strategic Transformation of Enterprise Management in the Context of the Transition to a Circular Economy
items.abstract: The article examines the specifics of the impact of the circular economy conception on the development of small and medium-sized businesses in Ukraine. The main focus is on analyzing the challenges that arise in the process of implementing circular business models, as well as on determining their potential for increasing resource efficiency and ensuring long-term competitiveness of enterprises. Despite the significant number of works on the circular economy, practical mechanisms for adapting the strategic management system of small and medium-sized businesses to the conditions of martial law and postwar reconstruction in Ukraine remain insufficiently covered. The issue of integrating circular tools with digital transformation and the development of territorial communities requires systematic development. The aim of the study is to develop theoretical provisions and scientific and methodological approaches to the strategic transformation of enterprise management in the context of the transition to a circular economy by substantiating modern mechanisms for integrating circular principles into the strategic management system and developing practical recommendations for increasing resource efficiency and competitiveness of enterprises. In studying the dynamics of small and medium-sized enterprises and employment, the authors used methods of scientific generalization, comparative and statistical analysis. To assess the regulatory framework and form strategic directions, methods of institutional and system analysis were used. The key principles of the circular economy are revealed, in particular, preserving the economic value of products, materials and resources throughout the entire life cycle, and the feasibility of their integration into the management system of small and medium-sized enterprises is substantiated. items.title: Transición agroecológica en agroecosistemas de Estelí, Nicaragua: aportes a la sostenibilidad territorial
items.abstract: La transición hacia sistemas agroecológicos sostenibles constituye un proceso clave para fortalecer la sostenibilidad de los territorios rurales frente a desafíos ambientales, productivos y sociales. El presente estudio tuvo como objetivo caracterizar el nivel de transición agroecológica y la relación entre los elementos de la agroecología en 20 agroecosistemas del departamento de Estelí, Nicaragua. La investigación se desarrolló bajo un diseño no experimental, con enfoque mixto, alcance descriptivo, correlacional y corte transversal, mediante encuestas, entrevistas semiestructuradas, observación directa y revisión documental. Los resultados evidenciaron un valor promedio del Índice de Transición Agroecológica (CAET) de 60.11%, lo que ubica a la mayoría de los agroecosistemas en una fase de transición inicial. Los elementos con mayor desarrollo fueron cultura y tradición alimentaria, resiliencia y diversidad, mientras que gobernanza responsable y valores humanos y sociales presentaron los niveles más bajos. El análisis de correlación mostró que la economía circular y solidaria, la gobernanza y la eficiencia productiva presentan mayor asociación con el nivel de transición agroecológica. Asimismo, los sistemas que no utilizan pesticidas químicos alcanzaron mayores valores de CAET, evidenciando un mejor desempeño agroecológico. Se concluye que la transición agroecológica en los agroecosistemas constituye un proceso multidimensional y heterogéneo, condicionado por la integración de factores ecológicos, sociales y económicos. Por tanto, se requiere fortalecer el acompañamiento técnico, la organización territorial, el intercambio de conocimientos, y la reducción progresiva de insumos externos para avanzar hacia sistemas sostenibles y resilientes.

items.title: Recovery of Critical Raw Materials from extractive waste supported by AI algorithms within a geodata framework
items.abstract: The European Union’s dependence on extra-EU imports for Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) poses significant risks to strategic industries. Secondary resources, particularly extractive waste from abandoned mining sites, represent an underexploited opportunity to enhance supply security and circular economy objectives. This paper presents the URBES (Urban Mining and Extractive Waste Information System) project, an intelligent platform designed to integrate mineralogical, geochemical, and urban-resource datasets within a geodata framework for the systematic inventory, organisation, and preliminary screening of CRM-bearing secondary deposits in Italy. The datasets are developed in accordance with INSPIRE and M4EU standards and their extension within the mineral resources domain. This framework enables the application of artificial intelligence and machine-learning techniques to support data integration, information retrieval, and the prioritisation of secondary resources for further investigation, in line with the objectives of the Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252), thereby providing a unified information framework for scientific research, environmental management, and policy implementation.

items.title: Digital and Intelligent Technologies for Construction and Demolition Waste Sorting: A Systematic Mapping Review of Research Maturity, Circularity Outcomes, and Industry Gaps
items.abstract: Construction and demolition waste (CDW) sorting is increasingly supported by digital and intelligent technologies, yet their functional coverage, maturity, circular economy (CE) contribution and alignment with industrial practice remain fragmented. This review systematically mapped the field using a PRISMA-based search, with 396 publications forming the broader bibliometric corpus. Within this corpus, 204 publications were retained for the scoped review, comprising 185 primary technical studies and 19 review articles. An illustrative ZenRobotics/Kuljetusrinki case was examined separately within a case-bounded academic-industry comparison. Artificial intelligence, computer vision, and sensing dominated the technical literature, particularly for identification, classification, localisation, and segmentation, while fewer studies progressed to robotic handling, physical separation, and integrated system functions. Among the 185 primary technical studies, validation remained concentrated at lower maturity levels, with 54.1% at laboratory maturity, 6.5% testing fully realistic CDW conditions, 18.9% reporting external or independent validation, and 3.2% reporting industrial deployment. Although 94.1% of these studies had a direct CE link, specific CE and sustainability outcome-related evidence such as recovered material quality, reuse, and landfill diversion was reported less consistently than technical performance. The case-bounded comparison showed that several capabilities investigated separately across the academic literature were integrated within the selected operational case, while independently verified operational and CE outcomes remained limited. These findings highlight the need for robust, integrated and operationally validated CDW sorting systems that connect emerging technologies with measurable recovery, material quality and circular outcomes under practical operating conditions.

items.title: Brane space localization and genus-0 T-duality with $H$-flux
items.abstract: We construct a geometric theory on the brane space $S^2M=C^\infty(S^2,M)$ associated to a gerbe with connection on $M$. Normalized logarithmic holonomy around the latitude circles defines an average holonomy line bundle on the brane space, whose connection and averaged flux give an equivariantly flat superconnection. We prove that the completed periodic exotic twisted cohomology defined by this superconnection localizes to the twisted cohomology of $M$. This {\bf brane space localization} happens in two stages: circle localization lands on the free path space of $M$, and contracting the paths, after a correction of the twisting form, brings us back to $M$. Parallel transport along the meridians lets us average gerbe module connections, after which the circular iterated-integral construction applies. The resulting {\bf twisted brane Bismut-Chern forms} restrict to the twisted Chern forms on $M$; their variation is described by {\bf twisted brane Bismut-Chern-Simons forms.} For a T-dual pair, transporting the classical Hori morphisms through localization yields {\bf graded genus-0 T-duality} on brane cohomology. The composite of each morphism with its dual is minus the Euler operator in the level variable, so these morphisms are isomorphisms at every nonzero level. At level one these morphisms are compatible with the brane character and twisted $K$-theory T-duality.

Digital Twins in AEC: Gemini Principles, ISO 19650 Information Management, Lifecycle Decisions, Cybersecurity, Interoperability, and Circular Economy
items.abstract: This chapter examines the rapidly evolving role of Digital Twins in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction industry, emphasizing their integration with Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence, ISO 19650 information management, and Industry 5.0 principles. Digital Twins, continuously updated through Building Information Management, IoT sensing, and AI analytics enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and lifecycle optimization. The chapter highlights foundational frameworks such as the Gemini Principles, ISO 23247, and human-in-the-loop approaches that ensure transparency, trust, and explainability in Digital Twin-driven decisions. Critical challengesincluding cybersecurity vulnerabilities, semantic interoperability, and ethical governanceare addressed through zero-trust architectures, ontology-based data models, explainable Artificial Intelligence, and blockchain-enabled auditability. The chapter further explores how Digital Twins support sustainability and the circular economy via material passports, carbon tracking, and resource-efficient lifecycle strategies. Case studies demonstrate measurable benefits in safety, energy performance, and predictive analytics, positioning Digital Twins as central to human-centric, resilient, and sustainable Construction 6.0 ecosystems.

items.title: SolarEV Cities for deep urban decarbonization: A critical review of integration gaps and transition pathways
items.abstract: Urban decarbonization is essential for meeting global climate goals; however, progress toward integrated low-carbon urban energy systems remains inadequately slow. The SolarEV City Concept integrates rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation with electric vehicles (EVs) as city-scale distributed mobile energy storage, using EV batteries to increase the value and flexibility of urban rooftop PV. Modeling studies suggest that high-penetration PV+EV systems could supply 60–95% of municipal electricity demand under scenarios aligned with future sustainable-city development, but real-world integration remains limited. Despite rapid worldwide growth of both PV and EV markets, bidirectional Vehicle-to-Home/Building (V2H/V2B) and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) applications have advanced unevenly, revealing a persistent PV-EV integration gap. This critical integrative review analyzes this gap using a socio-techno-economic framework encompassing six interdependent dimensions: climate, urban structure, technology, economics, policy, and society, across nine countries: Australia, China, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, and the United States. Cross-national comparison shows that implementation is constrained by fragmented bidirectional-charging standards, immature value-stacking and compensation models, distribution-grid and market-access constraints, regulatory separation between energy and transport sectors, and equity barriers that disproportionately limit access for renters, apartment residents, and lower-income households. Five transition-pathway archetypes, ranging from Japan’s resilience-driven V2H pathway to regulation-enabled commercial V2G pathways in France and the Netherlands, demonstrate that SolarEV Cities require a transition from parallel PV and EV promotion toward shared urban-energy visions, interoperable digital infrastructure, feeder-aware planning, inclusive market designs, and multi-stakeholder implementation platforms that convert rapid PV

items.title: Transition vers une économie circulaire : une étude de cas longitudinale de gouvernance régionale
items.abstract: Cet article étudie le positionnement dans le processus de transition sociétale d’une Région française chargée de la gouvernance de transition de son territoire vers une économie circulaire (TVEC). Elle fait face à trois paradoxes relevés dans la littérature pluridisciplinaire : imbrication dans un régime qui résiste, pilotage d’une transition imprévisible, et promotion de réseaux auto-organisés émergents. L’étude longitudinale de l’élaboration, avec 150 participants, et du lancement de la mise en œuvre d’un cas de plan Régional de TVEC montre des contournements plutôt que des résolutions de ces paradoxes. Des pistes de recherche sont ouvertes autour de deux spécificités françaises identifiées dans cette gouvernance : la TVEC envisagée comme moteur de développement territorial et l’incompatible conjugaison entre les rôles de décideur-financeur et d’acteur intermédiaire. Il en résulte une invitation aux acteurs de TVEC à se rassembler, dans des arènes distinctes du régime, pour expérimenter en recherche-action une méta-gouvernance de TVEC.

items.title: The Productive Palimpsest: Quasi-Industrial Zoning and Industrial Recomposition in Seongsu-dong, Seoul
items.abstract: Quasi-industrial zoning is often described either as a mechanism for protecting manufacturing or as a flexible platform for mixed-use redevelopment. Seongsu-dong, Seoul, suggests that the two functions can coexist while also pulling in different directions. This study combines a historical and institutional reconstruction with establishment and workplace-employment statistics for 2015–2024, building use-approval data for 2016–2025, and a limited secondary analysis of IRB-approved interviews collected in 2024 for ground-level validation. Because the national establishment survey changed its enumeration framework in 2020, business trends are read through two internally comparable intervals. Manufacturing contracted in both intervals, while information, communications, professional services, design, research, and other knowledge-intensive activities expanded. Knowledge industry centers (KICs) remained a major industrial development type during the same period, and several expanding knowledge-intensive sectors fall within their statutory eligibility categories. These parallel patterns are institutionally compatible, but the business statistics do not identify actual KIC tenants and therefore do not show that sectoral growth occurred within KICs. New-construction approvals also shifted sharply toward office and consumer-oriented development in 2021–2025; this development-flow evidence is interpreted separately from existing building stock and triangulated with recent registry-based research on Seongsu’s physical transformation. A selective re-analysis of four previously collected interviews provides mechanism-level evidence of short lease horizons, relocation pressure, productive-space requirements, KIC operational mismatch, and thinning supplier networks, without treating these cases as representative of the district. items.title: From barriers to bundles: a risk-policy appraisal of alternative marine fuels
items.abstract: The transition to alternative marine fuels is often framed through fuel choice decisions, technical feasibility, or specific policy measures such as pricing, subsidies, standards, and training. Less attention has been given to governance at the port-shipping interface, where fuel availability, bunkering infrastructure, vessel deployment, safety readiness, investment timing, and sufficient demand must align under uncertainty. A comparative governance appraisal is therefore needed to identify which systemic risks warrant priority and which policy responses remain robust across stakeholder perspectives and transition horizons. This study addresses this need through an integrated risk-policy appraisal of the alternative-fuel transition. The analysis combines single-round structured fuzzy expert elicitation, descriptive rating-dispersion analysis, stakeholder-survey triangulation, and selected contextual indicators. Systemic risks are assessed to the year 2040, while policy instruments and 63 functionally feasible policy portfolios are evaluated for 2030 and 2040 under port-oriented and shipowner-oriented conditions. The findings suggest that transition fragility does not stem from a single hurdle but from interacting fuel supply constraints, fuel price volatility, policy instability, safety disruption, stranded asset exposure, and port–fleet misalignment. Under the salience dispersion screening rule, safety disruption and port-fleet misalignment emerge as the clearest relative fragility hotspots. A carbon levy shows the strongest robustness profile among the evaluated individual instruments, but the results do not support a pricing-only approach. Within the evaluated set, the preferred portfolio combines a carbon levy, CAPEX subsidy, standardisation/codes, and training/competence schemes. The study contributes a transparent comparative governance screening framework, linking risk salience, rating dispersion, instrument robustness, and portfolio risk coverage under uncer

items.title: Syntropic infrastructure for regenerative urban metabolic reorganization in an Atlantic island city
items.abstract: Urban climate vulnerability is increasingly associated with ecological fragmentation, thermal amplification, hydrological disruption, and declining ecosystem functionality across densely urbanized territories. This study proposes syntropic infrastructure as a regenerative urban framework capable of reorganizing ecological, hydrological, and thermal regulation processes through multiscalar spatial connectivity. Using Santa Cruz de Tenerife as a case study, the research integrates ecological connectivity metrics, land surface temperature (LST), soil organic carbon (SOC), hydrological runoff modeling, and socioecological accessibility indicators within a GIS-based spatial assessment framework standardized at 250 m grid resolution. Results revealed severe ecological fragmentation across the consolidated metropolitan matrix, with Probability of Connectivity values below 0.15 and Integral Index of Connectivity values below 0.10 throughout most coastal urban sectors. Thermal analyses identified persistent surface temperature anomalies ranging between +3 °C and +5 °C relative to peri-urban vegetated reference areas. Pearson correlation analyses demonstrated significant inverse relationships between SOC and LST ( r = −0.64, p < 0.01), while imperviousness intensity showed a strong positive association with thermal amplification ( r = 0.71, p < 0.01). Spatial autocorrelation analyses additionally confirmed significant clustering of thermal hotspots and degraded soils. The findings suggest that syntropic infrastructure may operate as a regenerative planning framework capable of increasing ecological connectivity, evapotranspirative cooling, hydrological retention, and socioecological resilience through integrated adaptive interventions in vulnerable coastal and island metropolitan systems.

items.title: Metric Selection Framework: A Method for Optimizing Multidimensional Value Assessment of Resource Recovery Systems
items.venue: Annual Review of Environment and Resources
items.abstract: This article introduces the metric selection framework (MSF), developed as part of the CVORR+ methodology. CVORR+ is a systems-based evaluation toolkit designed to support complex sustainability assessment and decision-making. Within CVORR+, the MSF translates system analysis into decision-oriented, multidimensional metrics for monitoring, assessment, and evaluation of progress toward sustainability targets. Grounded in a value-focused decision-making approach, the framework combines expert elicitation with stakeholder engagement to ensure that metrics are system grounded, context specific, and practically relevant. Applied to England's plastic packaging system, the MSF reveals systemic inefficiencies, identifies leverage points for intervention, and informs policy design to support systemic value recovery. The case study demonstrates the heuristic and practical value of the MSF in capturing interdependencies across environmental, economic, social, and technical domains. Future developments will streamline the translation from system conceptualization to metric development, ensuring that metrics are responsive to long-term monitoring and policy-making, remain aligned with technological and regulatory shifts, and enhance the robustness and transferability of CVORR+.

items.title: Circular Economy Financial Performance: Sustainability (ESGUI), and Tourism Uncertainty (TUI)
items.abstract: Although circular economy investments are seen as an important tool for achieving the SDGs, studies that examine the different sources of uncertainty affecting these investments within a nonlinear framework remain limited. The current literature largely focuses only on traditional uncertainty indices such as EPU, GPR, and pandemic‐related uncertainty. This study fills this gap in literature by including, for the first time in the circular economy literature, two newly developed uncertainty indices, the ESG‐related sustainability uncertainty indices (ESGUI) and the Tourism Uncertainty Index (TUI), alongside traditional uncertainty indicators, and examining their associations with circular economy financial performance. In this study, wavelet power spectrum (WPS), wavelet quantile regression (WQR), wavelet quantile‐on‐quantile regression (WQQR), and Baruník–Křehlík frequency‐domain connectedness (BKFSC) methods were used. The findings show that the relationships between uncertainty and circular economy financial performance differ across investment horizons and market regimes. WQQR results show that the relationships between ESGUI and TUI and circular economy financial performance are nonlinear and vary by market regime. Similarly, the relationships between EPU, GPR, PNDMC, the S&P 500, and circular economy financial performance also differ by market conditions. These findings highlight the importance of considering different sources of uncertainty and general market conditions together when evaluating circular economy financial performance.

items.title: Exploring public actors’ beliefs about behavioural change for the mobility transition and their expectations for transdisciplinary collaborations
items.venue: GAIA - Ecological Perspectives for Science and Society
items.abstract: Politics and public administration are key actors when it comes to the implementation of behaviour change policies for sustainable mobility. We explore their beliefs on the matter and their expectations for transdisciplinary cooperations with scientific actors.Policy measures are central to shaping individual mobility behaviour, and a coherent policy approach is essential to advance sustainable transport transitions. While research provides extensive insights into the malleability of mobility behaviour, little is known about what policymakers and administrators know about behaviour change. This study addresses the gap through qualitative interviews with 13 political and administrative actors in Berlin and Brandenburg, combining Sabatier's Advocacy Coalition Framework from 1988 and Michie and colleagues' Behaviour Change Wheel. We explore who public actors view as their allies for the transition, and their expectations for collaboration with scientific actors. Our findings indicate that public actors possess substantial knowledge of behavioural change measures, many of which align with the Behaviour Change Wheel. Yet, their beliefs about mobility behaviour change vary in sophistication, and systematic links between assumptions and interventions are lacking. Public actors tend to view civil society as a key ally. Understanding their specific expectations for cooperation with scientific actors strengthens transdisciplinary research processes.

items.title: The sense and sensibility of the circular material use rate: a case study of EU's key circularity indicator
items.abstract: The Circular Material Use Rate (CMUR) has become a flagship indicator for monitoring progress towards a circular economy in the European Union. Promising in its conceptual simplicity, CMUR is widely employed in policy evaluations, international comparisons, and national target-setting. Yet despite its prominence, the indicator has been subject to limited empirical scrutiny. This paper examines the performance and interpretive validity of CMUR through a case study of Iceland, an economy characterized by high levels of imported materials, large-scale aluminum production, high percentage of renewable energy, significant biomass flows, and substantial domestic extraction of rock, sand and gravel. Based on a calculation of Iceland’s CMUR for 2024 and six policy-relevant scenarios—those being transport-related fossil fuel phase-out, increased recycling of household waste, food-waste reduction, material-efficiency measures in cement use, sufficiency scenarios for electronics and textiles, and all measures combined—the analysis shows that CMUR exhibits limited responsiveness to core circular economy interventions in this particular case. In some scenarios, such as food-waste prevention, CMUR decreases when environmental performance improves. The paper identifies one main structural reason for this behavior: the overwhelming dominance of a few inert and/or structurally non-circular materials in domestic consumption. To address this, the paper explores a contextualization of CMUR by modifying the boundary conditions for those materials. The findings highlight the importance of contextual interpretation when CMUR is used to evaluate circular performance and to inform policy. The analysis further suggests that similar interpretive challenges may arise in other European economies with comparable material-flow structures.

items.title: Circular Economy in the Built Environment: A Systematic Literature Review 2005–2025
items.abstract: The circular economy (CE) offers a viable pathway for advancing sustainable development in the built environment (BE) due to its potential to reduce waste, resource extraction, and environmental impacts. This study conducts a systematic literature review (2005–2025) to examine CE research through a unifying analytical perspective across the micro, meso, and macro levels of the BE and their integration with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It applies a sequential two‐stage design combining science mapping and critical content analysis. Findings show that existing research in the field remains conceptually fragmented across the three levels. CE‐SDG linkages remain generic and rarely operationalised within the BE. Seven cross‐level enabling mechanisms including life‐cycle analysis, circular design strategies, circular business models, circularity assessment, digital technologies, stakeholders collaboration, and integration with the SDGs, emerge as the connective tissue linking levels together. Building on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual framework that operationalises cross‐level linkages to support CE implementation in the BE. The framework offers a diagnostic tool that practitioners and policymakers can use to identify level‐specific characteristics, cross‐level relationships, enabling mechanisms, and remaining gaps. The study contributes to the existing knowledge by providing an integrative approach and recommendations for future CE research, policy, and implementation in the BE.

items.title: Circularity for Whom? Selective Social Sustainability in the Just Circular Economy
items.abstract: Circularity is often framed as a bridge paradigm supporting sustainability transitions — but a bridge to where, and for whom? Drawing on qualitative analysis of twelve circular bioeconomy business models in Argentina, this Perspective examines their social practices against the five justice dimensions of the just circular economy (JCE). The analysis shows that social sustainability was neither completely absent nor comprehensively incorporated. Concrete achievements in employment, livelihoods, and formal protection coexisted with weaker integration of shared decision-making, territorial knowledge, long-term organisational autonomy, and the distribution of burdens within circular systems. We conceptualise this recurrent but non-uniform pattern as selective social sustainability. The concept explains how organisational, evaluative, and governance arrangements make certain social concerns more visible, actionable, and enduring than others, without presuming deliberate exclusion or a single organisational cause. Its central contribution is to complement the JCE’s normative benchmark with a diagnostic lens for identifying why genuine social advances do not necessarily develop into integrated just circular transitions.

items.title: Eurodelta 2050+: Spatial Strategies for a Circular Built Environment
items.abstract: How can the transition to circular construction be organized at the territorial scale? Focusing on the Eurodelta region, which spans parts of the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany, the book examines how cities, regions, and infrastructure systems can collaborate to support the circular transformation of the built environment. Based on the findings of the ASSET project, it demonstrates how spatial planning, policy, and infrastructure can reduce waste, reuse materials, and rethink urban development. Addressing both opportunities and limitations, the volume provides insights into real-world challenges such as housing demand, resource scarcity, and fragmented governance. Rather than offering one-sizefits-all solutions, it promotes practical, place-based approaches to circularity. By fostering more coordinated regional strategies, it offers valuable insights for planners, policymakers, and researchers engaged in circular transition processes. items.title: THE CIRCULAR ECONOMY, A FACTOR OF TERRITORIAL DEVELOPMENT: AN ANALYSIS OF WASTE RECOVERY VALUE CHAINS IN KOUDOUGOU (BURKINA FASO)
items.venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
items.abstract: The circular economy model stands in contrast to the traditional linear model, which is based in part on the systematic disposal of waste in landfill, with its associated environmental impacts. Against a backdrop of dwindling natural resources and environmental crises, the circular economy paradigm is emerging as a catalyst for fostering and driving innovative practices that are environmentally friendly and promote sustainable development. This article aims to analyse the socio-economic opportunities arising from waste recovery in the medium-sized town of Koudougou. The methodology is based on a qualitative approach, combining literature review, direct observations and field surveys. The surveys enabled qualitative data to be collected from 39 stakeholders in the waste value chain between September 2023 and February 2024. The results reveal the emergence of informal waste recovery sectors through salvage, reuse, recycling and composting. Although these circular economy activities generate jobs and contribute to regional development, their potential remains hampered by a lack of regulation and support. Effective involvement by local authorities, through the structuring of these sectors and the training of stakeholders, is essential to ensure the long-term sustainability of this local circular economy.

items.title: Circular economy approaches for textile industry wastewater and sludge: Sustainable valorization and resource recovery
Modelling the circular economy–renewable integration nexus: a cross-national empirical analysis of smart-technology adoption, territorial CO₂ emissions, and the material footprint
items.abstract: Climate neutrality relies on two levers usually examined separately: circular-economy (CE) practices and renewable integration. Drawing on ecological modernization theory and the environmental Kuznets curve (EKC), we regress per-capita carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions in 20 European Union member states over 2014–2023 (N = 200) on the circular material use (CMU) rate and the renewable energy (REN) share, with smart-technology adoption [ST; internet penetration and research and development (R&D) intensity] as a moderator. The pooled ordinary least squares (OLS), two-way fixed-effects (FE), and random-effects models use cluster-robust standard errors and a wild cluster bootstrap. A 1-percentage-point rise in the renewable energy share is associated with approximately 0.9% lower per-capita emissions in the baseline FE model (p = 0.095) and 0.95% in the moderated model (p = 0.030; bootstrap p = 0.048). CMU has no significant unconditional association with emissions in the levels models, and income exhibits concave curvature, although the implied EKC turning point lies above the sample maximum. The CMU × ST interaction is positive and significant (β = 0.0065, p = 0.009; bootstrap p = 0.033) and is robust across all 20 leave-one-country-out subsamples: the circularity–emissions slope becomes less favourable as adoption rises, with the estimated interaction coefficient larger for internet diffusion than for R&D intensity, although the two estimates cannot be statistically distinguished. Because no conditional slope is individually significant, this association is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, a digital-rebound mechanism. For the material footprint outcome, the CMU coefficient is negative, and the interaction changes sign, but neither is significant, so the pattern is specific to production-based CO₂ accounting.

items.title: A Multi-Dimensional Approach to Orange Peel Waste Management in the Circular Economy Perspective
items.abstract: This study develops an integrated circular economy assessment framework for valorizing orange peel waste (OPW), applied to a biocomposite production process for additive manufacturing and comparatively evaluated against anaerobic digestion, incineration, and animal feed pathways. The methodology combines three sequential steps: (i) a Holistic Diagnosis (HD), supported by Systemic Design and META-SWOT/C-DE analyses, to map material and energy flows, stakeholder relations, and territorial dynamics; (ii) a cradle-to-gate Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) to quantify environmental impacts of pelletized biocomposite production; and (iii) a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) integrated with circular economy indicators based on the 9R framework to compare alternative OPW valorization options. Results demonstrate that agricultural waste valorization requires a systemic and multidisciplinary approach, where technological efficiency is integrated with environmental and contextual dimensions. The analysis highlights key leverage points—such as multi-stream waste valorization and renewable energy integration—while identifying structural constraints related to seasonality, biopolymer costs, and scalability. Environmental findings confirm that substituting virgin materials with agri-food residues reduces impacts, particularly by avoiding disposal and lowering resource depletion. Sensitivity analyses further underline the importance of low-carbon electricity mixes and increased OPW incorporation to support decarbonization and long-term circular transition pathways in agro-industrial systems.

items.title: Development of a Mechanism for the Transition of the Regional Economic System to a Circular Economy
items.abstract: Purpose. To provide a statistical justification for differentiated circular economy transition strategies across Russian regions and to develop a mechanism linking the territorial profile of a region to the selection of a management strategy, priority measures, and project selection criteria. Materials and methods. The empirical dataset covers 85 regions of the Russian Federation and includes comparable data for 2021 2023. The study draws on official statistics from the Federal State Statistics Service and the Unified Interdepartmental Information and Statistical System. The A–G typology was constructed before the environmental and energy characteristics were calculated and was used as an external stratification framework. Medians and structural shares were calculated, together with Spearman’s rank and Pearson’s correlation coefficients. Differences in energy-related indexes were tested using the Kruskal–Wallis test and effect-size measures. The methodological framework of the mechanism comprises four components: the integral readiness R, the weakest mandatory block B, the potential effect P, and the data quality D. Unavailable direct indexes of the final use of secondary resources were not replaced with assumed values. Results. The median environmental stress index across the seven types of regional economic systems ranges from 0.365 to 0.562, while median air pollutant emissions from stationary sources ranges from 17.9 to 374.1 kg per capita. Types B and D, comprising 26 of the 85 regions, account for 66.2% of the emissions recorded in the sample and 60.4% of environmental protection expenditure. The correlation of emissions and expenditure is ρ = 0.854 according to Spearman’s coefficient and r = 0.844 according to Pearson’s coefficient; for the specific values ρ = 0.851 (p < 0.001). items.title: Campos territoriales en transición: investigación situada, gobernanza territorial y construcción colectiva del conocimiento
items.abstract: Problem statement: Territorial scholarship analyzes power relations, multiple territorialities, materialities, governance, and transformations; however, an analytical space remains for understanding configurations in which these dimensions are reconfigured interdependently and disputes extend to the conditions through which territory is produced and governed. Objective: To formulate and delimit the concept of territorial fields in transition and examine its implications for territorial governance and collective knowledge-building. Methodology: The article develops a reflexive systematization of a situated research trajectory, organized around six fields of problematization and analyzed through the reconstruction of research problems, findings, conceptual frictions, and processes of situated translation. Results: The comparison identifies reconfigurations of positions, rules, scales, forms of knowledge, materialities, and authority, with different intensities across the fields examined. Conclusions: Territorial fields in transition are proposed as relational, materially situated, multiscalar, and temporally open configurations. Transition is understood as contingent and non-teleological; governance participates in the production of territorial order, while collective knowledge-building constitutes an epistemological and political dimension of that process.

items.title: SUSTAINABILITY, TERRITORY, AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY IN THE GREEN HYDROGEN VALUE CHAIN: CHALLENGES AND PROSPECTS FOR THE ENERGY TRANSITION IN BRAZIL
authors: Ana Verucia Leitão da Silva Vasconcelos
items.abstract: A transição energética contemporânea tem impulsionado a busca por alternativas capazes de reduzir a dependência de fontes fósseis e ampliar a participação de recursos renováveis nos sistemas energéticos. Nesse contexto, o hidrogênio verde destaca-se como uma alternativa associada à descarbonização, à diversificação energética e à integração de diferentes atividades produtivas, embora sua consolidação no Brasil esteja relacionada a aspectos de sustentabilidade, organização territorial, infraestrutura e economia circular. Este estudo teve como objetivo analisar os desafios e as perspectivas da cadeia do hidrogênio verde e suas contribuições para a transição energética no Brasil. A pesquisa caracteriza-se como qualitativa, desenvolvida por meio de revisão bibliográfica, com base em dissertações, artigos científicos publicados em periódicos e livros, obtidos em repositórios acadêmicos e institucionais, periódicos científicos e plataformas editoriais. A abordagem adotada permitiu articular e interpretar as dimensões da sustentabilidade, do território e da economia circular no contexto da cadeia do hidrogênio verde. Os resultados evidenciaram que a cadeia do hidrogênio verde no Brasil apresenta desafios relacionados à sustentabilidade, à infraestrutura, à organização territorial e à integração circular dos recursos. Constatou-se que sua expansão depende da articulação entre fontes renováveis, infraestrutura energética e logística, planejamento territorial e estratégias de reaproveitamento de recursos. Conclui-se que a integração dessas dimensões pode contribuir para a diversificação dos sistemas energéticos e para o avanço da transição energética brasileira.

items.title: Enabling a Circular Economy through a Digital Product Passport in the Automotive Industry: Essential Data Points for Enhancing R-Strategies
items.abstract: The transition towards a circular economy in the manufacturing industry requires transparent and interoperable data flows across product lifecycles. Digital product passports have emerged as a key instrument to enable such transparency by providing standardized information on product composition, use, and end-of-life management. However, there is limited understanding of which specific data points are essential to operationalize such a new system and enable circular strategies within the automotive sector. This study examines how digital product passports can facilitate circular economy practices, with a focus on the car body as a representative component group. The research aims to identify and validate essential data points needed by suppliers, OEMs, and end-of-life actors to successfully use the passport and implement R-strategies effectively. A semi-systematic literature review was conducted to develop an initial data point framework, which was subsequently validated through expert interviews with stakeholders across the automotive value chain to identify potential gaps between theory and practice. The findings suggest that data points on material composition are most critical for enhancing traceability and closing material loops. At the same time, information regarding maintenance and performance is less important in the context of a car body. Moreover, the study emphasizes that pragmatic, stepwise implementation approaches are essential to ensure acceptance and feasibility across actor groups. By integrating perspectives from circular economy theory and current digital product initiatives, the study contributes an analytical framework for prioritizing data categories relevant to digital product passport development. The results can support policymakers and industry actors in aligning data requirements with circularity objectives, providing a foundation for future empirical validation.
