items.title: Automation readiness of material passports in construction: Passport-centred systematic review of lifecycle information infrastructures
Integrating BIM and material passports to foster circularity in offsite construction: a five-layer digital framework
items.venue: International Journal of Building Pathology and Adaptation
items.abstract: Purpose Circular economy (CE) integration in offsite construction (OSC) is increasingly recognised as a pathway to reduce waste, carbon emissions and inefficient material practices. However, the digital mechanisms required to operationalise circularity across design, construction and reuse phases in OSC remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Design/methodology/approach This study develops a five-layer digital integration framework that aligns building information modelling (BIM) with material passports (MPs) to support circular workflows. Drawing on a systematic literature review (SLR) of 40 peer-reviewed studies, the framework comprises: (1) Data Input Layer, (2) BIM Platform Layer, (3) Integration Layer, (4) Lifecycle Feedback Layer and (5) Circular Decision Support Layer. Findings The synthesis layer identifies key digital bottlenecks across the five layers, including missing CE metadata, poor interoperability and a lack of lifecycle feedback loops. By embedding circular material intelligence within BIM environments, the framework offers a scalable roadmap for traceability, reuse planning and CE-driven decision-making in OSC. Practical implications The framework provides industry stakeholders with a scalable roadmap to enable material traceability, reuse planning and circular decision-making across the OSC lifecycle. It supports practical alignment with emerging CE policies and market incentives. Originality/value This study contributes a theoretically grounded framework and practical recommendations for advancing digital circular construction. It lays the groundwork for future digital tool development and policy alignment to supports CE adoption in the built environment.
cites_core: Barriers to the Circular Economy: Evidence From the European Union (EU)

items.title: Material passports for circular built environments: a systematic review of information requirements, digital tools and implementation barriers
items.abstract: Purpose Material passports are increasingly presented as instruments for circular construction, yet the specific information requirements, digital infrastructures and implementation barriers that shape their use across building lifecycle stages remain fragmented. This study aims to synthesise the material passport literature and develop an information-centred framework for circular built environments. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted using a structured search, screening and eligibility protocol. The final corpus consists of 51 journal-based studies published between 2018 and 2026. Descriptive analysis, thematic co-word analysis and thematic coding were used to classify information requirements, digital tools, lifecycle stages, circularity functions and implementation barriers. Automated pre-screening was used only to reduce the initial metadata pool; the final corpus was determined through eligibility screening and structured thematic coding. Findings Material passports connect material data with BIM-enabled systems, databases, digital platforms, digital twins, blockchain-based traceability, lifecycle assessment and decision-support tools across the building lifecycle. The dominant implementation barriers concern interoperability, standardisation, platform integration, economic feasibility, stakeholder coordination and regulatory alignment. Originality/value The study contributes by reframing material passports as an information ecosystem for circular built environments. It provides a lifecycle-based mapping of information requirements, digital tools, circularity functions and barriers, and proposes a conceptual framework to support future passport-enabled circular construction research and practice. Unlike studies that examine material passports primarily as building information modelling extensions, circular economy tools or digital product passport templates, this review explains how data requirements, digital processing an

items.title: Preparing for Dynamic Material Passports (DMPs) and Digital Product Passports (DPPs): Industry Guidance for the Irish Construction Sector
items.abstract: This guidance supports the Irish construction sector in preparing for the adoption of Dynamic Material Passports (DMPs) and Digital Product Passports (DPPs). It explains how structured digital information can improve material traceability, support circular economy principles and enable better management of construction products and materials throughout their lifecycle. The guidance considers emerging European regulatory requirements and relevant international standards, including ISO 19650, and provides practical recommendations for organisations seeking to develop passport-related information management processes. It is intended for public clients, designers, contractors, manufacturers, suppliers and asset managers.

items.title: RASTREABILIDADE INFORMACIONAL E DESMONTE DE SISTEMAS CONSTRUTIVOS INOVADORES: UMA PROPOSTA DE PASSAPORTE DIGITAL DE MATERIAIS PARA OS DOCUMENTOS DE AVALIAÇÃO TÉCNICA
authors: Adla Kellen Dionisio Sousa de Oliveira
items.abstract: A transição para uma economia circular na construção depende da possibilidade de desmontagem e da disponibilidade de informações sobre materiais, componentes, conexões e alternativas de fim de vida. Este estudo avaliou se os Documentos de Avaliação Técnica (DATecs), emitidos no âmbito do PBQP-H, fornecem informações para o desmonte, a rastreabilidade e a estruturação de passaportes digitais de materiais. Para isso, foi realizada uma pesquisa documental em uma seleção de 14 DATecs. Os documentos foram analisados por meio de uma lista de critérios organizada em três categorias: sistema construtivo, materiais e componentes e rastreabilidade e informação. Os resultados indicam que nenhum documento apresenta de forma completa os pontos e a sequência de desmonte. Além disso, nenhum dos documentos fornece informações suficientes para avaliar a toxicidade dos materiais. Adicionalmente, foram identificadas limitações na identificação de conexões, composição dos componentes, custos, tempo de desmontagem e possibilidades de reuso. Com base nos resultados observados, propõe-se a implantação do Passaporte Digital de Materiais para os DATecs. A proposta prevê que, quando o DATec for submetido ou renovado, contenha um modelo digital com dados completos de: rastreabilidade e identificação digital; composição química, toxicidade e saúde; reversibilidade, conexões e manual de desmonte; e desempenho de ciclo de vida e circularidade. Essa proposta pode contribuir para uma futura integração dos DATecs com modelos BIM e o Passaporte Digital de Materiais, com potencial para aumentar a rastreabilidade e a circularidade dos sistemas construtivos inovadores, e, assim, favorecer o atendimento aos princípios da Economia Circular e do Design for Disassembly.

items.title: Circular Economy Principles in Architecture
items.abstract: This paper examines circular economy principles in architecture through a multidisciplinary architectural lens. It considers reuse, repair, disassembly, material passports, and resource efficiency, while linking design choices to user experience, environmental performance, material responsibility and project delivery. The discussion synthesises established architectural literature, design guidance and recognised standards rather than presenting a new empirical survey. It argues that context-sensitive analysis, inclusive design, coordinated technical decisions and post-occupancy evaluation are essential to credible architectural outcomes. The paper concludes with practical directions for design teams and identifies the need for project-specific evidence before generalising strategies across climates, building types or communities.

items.title: Communities, Collaboration, and Trust
"Semiconductor-X" - Abschlussbericht zum Teilvorhaben Merck Electronics KGaA
items.abstract: Merck Electronics KGaA hat die im Teilvorhaben vorgesehenen Beiträge im Wesentlichen erreicht und damit seinen Beitrag zu den Zielen von Semiconductor-X geleistet. Im Mittelpunkt standen die Entwicklung semantischer Datenmodelle sowie Konzepte für den souveränen und standardisierten Austausch von Material-, Prozess- und Nachhaltigkeitsdaten an der Schnittstelle zwischen Halbleitermaterialzulieferern und Halbleiterherstellern. In AP3.2 wurden existierende Modelle auf ihre Anwendbarkeit im Kontext von Semiconductor-X untersucht, digitale Zwillinge und Halbleitermaterialien semantisch beschrieben sowie Material-, Prozess- und Ergebnisdaten interoperabel miteinander verknüpft. Die entwickelten Konzepte wurden in die Digital Reference für Halbleiterfabriken integriert und für EDC-basierte Datenräume sowie erste Datenanalyseszenarien prototypisch umgesetzt. Dabei wurden insbesondere Anforderungen an Datenqualität, Datensouveränität und Datenschutz berücksichtigt. In AP3.3 wurden die Datenstrukturen um Product-Carbon-Footprint- und weitere Materialpassdaten erweitert. Der integrierte Demonstrator zeigte, wie Daten eines Zulieferers über einen Digital Material Passport übernommen, bei Merck um Prozessdaten ergänzt und über Semiconductor-X an nachgelagerte Partner weitergegeben werden können. Mit der Präsentation auf der Hannover Messe 2026 wurde die technische und fachliche Machbarkeit eines standardisierten, souveränen und branchenübergreifenden Datenaustauschs zwischen Chem-X, Semiconductor-X und Decide4ECO erfolgreich validiert. Das Reaktorkonzept ergänzte die Arbeiten als konkrete Quelle für strukturierte Prozessdaten und wurde durch die Inbetriebnahme eines ersten Reaktors erfolgreich verwertet. Insgesamt wurden wichtige Grundlagen geschaffen, um Material-, Prozess- und Nachhaltigkeitsinformationen semantisch interoperabel zu verknüpfen und für Traceability, Ursachenanalysen, KI-gestützte Auswertungen sowie die Verbesserung von Qualität, Yield, Resilienz und Nachhaltig

items.title: Technical Brief: Hydroengineering and Geologic Intelligence Modules
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The Hydroengineering and Geologic Intelligence Modules extend Classified Earthworks from material separation and transformation into a governed landscape-intervention architecture. The hydroengineering module asks how classified mineral, organic, ceramic, compost, biochar, and aggregate fractions might participate in site-specific water management. The geologic intelligence module treats sampling, testing, transformation, deployment, and monitoring as linked data events. The central object is not "improved dirt" but a bounded suitability relation among a material batch, intended use, site, design, evidence, authority, and time. A material passport records provenance, tests, uncertainty, restrictions, decisions, and later observations. It does not itself certify safety or authorize deployment. Likewise, general patterns such as slowing runoff or increasing infiltration are design possibilities, not universal prescriptions: infiltration can mobilize contaminants, destabilize slopes, damage structures, alter groundwater, or displace flooding. This brief defines the two modules, their shared ontology, decision gates, passport lifecycle, hydrologic and data-governance constraints, monitoring loop, realization funnel, and evaluation program. It remains a system proposal pending qualified site, laboratory, engineering, legal, community, and environmental review.

items.title: Classified Earthworks
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Classified Earthworks is a proposed field-scale architecture for turning heterogeneous soil, excavation spoil, sediments, mineral fines, and biomass into source-traceable material classes whose possible uses are bounded by sampling, testing, transformation, engineering review, and continuing evidence. It joins materials recovery to landscape water design and makes each excavation both a custody event and a potential observation of soil, geology, and hydrology. The system is not a claim that local material is safe, that firing preserves its chemistry, that infiltration is desirable at every site, or that a passport certifies performance. Source material can be heterogeneous, contaminated, unstable, saline, reactive, culturally sensitive, legally restricted, or unsuitable for reuse. Screening and separation can concentrate hazards and create wastewater, dust, emissions, or residuals. Hydrologic interventions can mobilize contamination, destabilize slopes, damage habitat, or affect downstream rights. This paper defines a batch and use-class contract, custody chain, decision outcomes, transformation boundaries, material passport, safety and professional-authority gates, data-governance model, pilot evidence ladder, and realization funnel. Its central contribution is a governed routing architecture: material is characterized and assigned only to uses supported by the evidence and jurisdiction of a declared project profile.

items.title: BIM for Circular Built Environments: Data, Indicators, and Implementation Frameworks
items.venue: SpringerBriefs in applied sciences and technology
items.abstract: This study explores how Circular Economy (CE) indicators can be effectively integrated into Building Information Modelling (BIM) to support sustainability in the built environment. Given the construction sector’s significant contribution to resource use and carbon emissions, there is an urgent need for improved lifecycle data and circularity assessment methods. While BIM offers strong potential for managing building data across all lifecycle stages, its use for CE purposes remains limited due to fragmented data structures and lack of standardised indicators. The research is based on a multi-language survey of stakeholders across the architecture, engineering, construction, and operations (AECO) sector in several European countries. The findings show that although awareness of BIM-CE integration is high, its practical implementation is still low and mostly restricted to early design phases. Many organisations rely on manual data handling, and BIM systems are often not prepared to support structured circularity data. Key barriers include lack of standardised metrics, insufficient regulatory frameworks, limited product-level data, and low digital maturity. The study highlights the importance of tools such as material passports and digital logbooks to improve data traceability. A policy framework is proposed focusing on interoperability, standardisation, capacity building, and regulatory support to enable scalable BIM-CE integration.

items.title: What should AI agents know? Explicit knowledge for trustworthy, sustainable materials research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can propose materials, interpret measurements and increasingly coordinate experiments. Yet reliable scientific autonomy requires more than capable models: research systems must preserve what is known, where evidence came from and which actions are justified. We argue that machine-actionable scientific knowledge is essential for trustworthy autonomous research, and that ontologygrounded knowledge graphs are a particularly powerful way of achieving it when scientific meaning must be shared across disciplines, systems and scales. Using The World Avatar (TWA) as a case study, we examine how ontologies, dynamic knowledge graphs and software agents connect models, literature, experiments and laboratory assets, and how ontology-derived tools can constrain large language model (LLM) actions. A reported design-to-synthesis study of a new metal–organic polyhedron demonstrates the integration of previously separate tasks, but not yet an environmental benefit or fully autonomous discovery. A material-passport example further shows how shared semantics can support industrial circularity assessment. We distinguish structural validation from scientific verification, and circularity indicators from demonstrated environmental benefits. The priority is not to create a universal platform but to build evidence-preserving research infrastructure whose scientific and sustainability benefits can be tested.

items.title: A Multi-Level Digital Passport Architecture for Emerging Regional Value Chains: Batch-Level Passports for Agro-Waste-Based Construction Products
items.abstract: Under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, the Digital Product Passport (DPP) is set at model, batch or item level in line with the traceability practice of each value chain. Emerging value chains, such as those of agro-waste-based construction products, connect actors from different sectors and require upstream data to be checked and transferred to the product passport. This study proposes a multi-level passport architecture in which a Digital Material Passport (DMP), associated with each residue batch, records origin, legal status, handling and measured properties, and is linked to the product DPP. The architecture was applied in Emilia-Romagna, Italy, to six agricultural residues, three of which feed five lime-based product models at Technology Readiness Level 3–4: a screed, two blocks and two panels. Screening identified seven batch parameters to verify before production. For the three residues used, producers documented 15 of 42 attributes, the laboratory 11, and 16 remain to be supplied; legal status was documented for one batch, as biomass fuel. Half of the DMP data remained within factory production control as acceptance checks; the other half were transmitted to the batch-level DPP as composition, bio-based content, origin and legal status of inputs, and embodied carbon.

items.title: Machine Recognition of Elastoplastic Materials in Material Genetics
items.venue: Journal of Civil Engineering and Architecture
items.abstract: The studies [12, 13] separated two levels of material identification: Geometry Builder determines the morphology and the localC0/C1/C2 class structure of the deformation curve, whereas Material Builder solves the first physical inverse problem for a fixed architecture. The present work combines these levels into a machine-recognition problem in which the architecture and the observable physical passport are mutually dependent variables. The main theoretical result is a finite-dimensional reduction of the physically generalized Reinsch principle for an irreversible material. After the solution is represented in the genetic basis, the reversible integrals and antisymmetric Pfaffian channels are analytically integrated with respect to strain and condensed into segment matrices. The resulting target form is analogous to the Ritz method in its finite-dimensional reduction mechanism, but differs in the underlying principle: stationarity of a nonintegrable variational Pfaffian form is required instead of stationarity of potential energy. At each step of the deterministic genealogy, the point of maximum absolute defect specifies the reproduction location, while the profiled Ritz-Reinsch form selects the physically preferable admissible pair of offspring classes after closure of the observable Material Passport. For a prescribed experimental resolutionδ, the recognition result is the first genealogical state satisfyingERMS ≤δ andE∞ ≤δ. The resulting model is therefore not claimed to be the global minimum among all conceivable partitions; it is the least-complex experimentally admissible state of the deterministic Recognition genealogy.

items.title: A Scoping Review and Reference Model for Circularity of Engineered Wood Products
items.abstract: Timber reuse is increasingly positioned as a strategy to meet rising demand for timber in construction while reducing environmental impacts. Engineered wood products (EWPs) offer considerable potential because of their structural performance and dimensional stability. However, uncertainty regarding in-service degradation, particularly exposure to moisture, limits confidence in their suitability for high-value reuse at end of life. Although circular timber research widely emphasises design for disassembly, condition verification during the use phase remains insufficiently integrated into reuse frameworks. This scoping review analyses 35 publications to examine how moisture-related risks are addressed in circular timber construction. Moisture is widely acknowledged as a durability risk, but it is not routinely monitored in a way that supports reuse decision-making. Digital tools such as BIM, Digital Product Passports, material passports, and sensors are often proposed but remain weakly connected to condition-based decision-making. To synthesise these insights, this review develops a reference model structured around four domains: Digitalisation and Traceability, Disassembly Potential, Material Integrity, and Systemic Enablers. The model explicitly integrates in-situ moisture performance into circular timber frameworks by linking documented material condition to reuse confidence. The findings highlight the need to integrate long-term monitoring and data continuity into timber reuse workflows, providing a structured basis for reuse decisions informed by verified performance data.

items.title: THE EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE ON THE INTERNATIONAL LEGAL GOVERNANCE OF FUTURE META-MATERIALS Legislative Foresight for the Post-Lithium and Post-Silicon Age A Comprehensive Framework for Sovereign Licensing, Transnational Liability, and Global Resource Justice in the Era of Advanced Materials
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The El-Rakhawi Doctrine on the International Legal Governance of Future Meta-Materials presents the first comprehensive legal framework for governing emerging advanced materials technologies. Grounded in a Declaration of Scientific Honesty, the doctrine acknowledges that meta-materials remain largely theoretical while establishing governance frameworks for their potential realization. It introduces twelve groundbreaking innovations: (1) Precise Meta-Materials Definition Framework with Positive List mechanism; (2) TRIPS Compatibility Protocol invoking Articles 8 and 31 and the Doha Declaration; (3) El-Rakhawi Sovereign Licensing Model with enhanced proof mechanisms including digital watermarking, blockchain timestamping, and punitive damages; (4) Conditional Open Patent Framework with tiered royalties; (5) Super-Metals Freedom Treaty with Narrow National Security Exception Protocol; (6) Sustainable Financing Mechanism with 0.5% global levy; (7) Raw Materials Justice Principle allocating 15% to resource-rich nations; (8) Three-Phase Implementation Roadmap (2026-2040+); (9) Graduated Sanctions Framework; (10) Digital Material Passport System on blockchain; (11) Doctrine of Distributed Liability for self-healing materials; (12) Sovereign Recycling Rights and Extended Producer Responsibility. This doctrine extends the El-Rakhawi legal architecture into materials governance, providing actionable frameworks for equitable technology transfer, environmental protection, and global resource justice. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23106589

items.title: The Application of BIM and Digital Twins in Sustainable Supply Chain Management: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The construction industry faces persistent challenges in achieving sustainable and circular supply chain management due to fragmented material flows, limited information continuity, and weak coordination among stakeholders. Building Information Modelling (BIM) and Digital Twins offer complementary capabilities for addressing these challenges, yet their roles in sustainable and circular supply chains remain insufficiently integrated. This study critically reviews the literature on BIM and Digital Twins in Sustainable Supply Chain Management (SSCM) and the Circular Economy (CE) in construction. A structured literature review was conducted to identify major research trends, knowledge structures, thematic developments, implementation mechanisms, and research gaps. The analysis synthesizes the literature around key thematic areas, including material passports, reverse logistics (RL), off-site construction (OSC), artificial intelligence (AI), technology integration, construction and demolition waste (CDW), and decision-making. The findings indicate that BIM primarily supports structured lifecycle information, material traceability, and information continuity, while Digital Twins extend these capabilities through dynamic data integration, monitoring, and decision support. However, fragmented technological applications, interoperability limitations, insufficient data, organisational barriers, and limited integration across supply chain processes continue to constrain implementation. Based on these findings, a Digital–Circular Supply Chain Framework is proposed to conceptualize how BIM and Digital Twins can connect information, material flows, and decision-making to support SSCM and CE throughout the construction life cycle.
cites_core: Conceptualizing the circular economy: An analysis of 114 definitions

items.title: The Living Building Challenge: Examining Practical Barriers to Circular and Regenerative Design
items.abstract: Since its inception in 2006, the Living Building Challenge (LBC) has become a leading framework for sustainable building design. However, uptake remains limited, with only 35 projects achieving full certification globally as of 2026. These rare examples offer insights into the systemic constraints to circular and regenerative construction. This study examines Australian LBC projects to identify potential support mechanisms that could facilitate wider adoption of circular construction practices. A mixed-methods approach combined a review of previous LBC projects with thematic analysis of 12 semi-structured interviews involving members of the National Circularity Centre Building (NCCB) delivery team, as well as external professionals with LBC experience. Located in Bega, New South Wales, the NCCB is the third Australian project to pursue full LBC certification. Although the LBC’s stringent requirements are frequently associated with increased project time and cost, the findings indicate that these impacts may be symptoms of broader industry constraints and project management complexity. Key barriers include inadequate team composition at initiation, delayed integration of LBC in the design process, and difficulties meeting strict material procurement criteria. Procurement challenges are further exacerbated by limited support and transparency in the manufacturing sector. These findings suggest that stronger early-project support, earlier integration of LBC requirements, and increased uptake of material passport (MP) databases (e.g., Declare Label and Product Aware), could improve the feasibility and scalability of high-performance circular and regenerative building outcomes.

items.title: BIM-Enabled Circular Construction and Material Lifecycle Management: A Critical Review of Digital Strategies for Resource-Efficient and Low-Carbon Building Delivery
items.venue: International Journal of Frontline Research in Engineering and Technology
items.abstract: The integration of Building Information Modelling (BIM) with circular construction presents an opportunity to improve material efficiency and support low-carbon building delivery across the building lifecycle. This review examines how BIM-enabled digital strategies are being applied to circular construction and material lifecycle management, the resource-efficiency and environmental outcomes associated with these applications, the barriers limiting their implementation, and the research gaps that remain. The findings indicate that BIM is increasingly being integrated with lifecycle assessment, material passports, circularity assessment tools, material databases, traceability systems, and design-for-deconstruction approaches. These applications support material quantification, environmental assessment, reuse planning, recovery, and more informed design decision-making, with the strongest evidence concentrated in the design and construction phases. However, the review identifies persistent limitations in maintaining reliable material information across the full building lifecycle. Fragmented and incomplete data, inconsistent standards, implementation costs, skills gaps, organisational resistance, and interoperability challenges continue to constrain wider adoption. The review further finds that BIM-enabled digital capability does not automatically translate into measurable environmental benefits; outcomes depend on information quality, system integration, and the extent to which digital information informs project decisions. A conceptual framework is proposed positioning BIM as a lifecycle-oriented decision-support environment that connects material information, circular strategies, and measurable resource and environmental outcomes. The review highlights the need for interoperable, dynamic, and empirically validated digital workflows to support the transition towards circular and low-carbon construction.

items.title: Advanced Wood Modification in the Circular Economy: A Critical Review of Performance, Machinability, and Recycling Pathways
items.abstract: Wood modification has been developed as a non-biocidal concept to overcome inherent material limitations such as dimensional instability and biological durability. But sustainability assessment must extend beyond initial functional performance to include machinability, interface compatibility, repairability and end-of-life (EoL) cascade potential. This critical narrative review integrates the mechanisms, processing dynamics and circular economy implications of 4 major modification routes: thermal treatment, acetylation, furfurylation and thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) densification. The review uses a purposively selected core evidence set of 40 peer-reviewed articles, complemented by contextual references, standards, and foundational sources; coverage emphasizes seminal studies and recent literature. The synthesis shows that thermal modification and acetylation can enhance hygroscopic and dimensional stability through different mechanisms, but with different trade-offs in mechanical toughness and secondary processing. Furfurylation can improve hardness and decay resistance, but also increase brittleness and recycling difficulties. THM densification improves the local load-bearing capacity, but moisture-induced set-recovery is a major limitation. Cross-contamination in heterogeneous waste streams, residual chemical matrices, changed surface–energy interactions with adhesives, and limited standardization of sorting protocols are important barriers to circular material loops across the modification routes. Ultimately, this critical narrative review provides an integrated decision framework connecting cell wall modification chemistry, secondary processing dynamics (machinability and adhesive bonding), digital material passports for traceability, and cascading end-of-life (EoL) decision pathways. Future work should consider design for disassembly, digital material traceability and multi-criteria sustainability assessment.

items.title: Built Heritage Passport (BHP): A multi-scale digital framework for urban heritage management and circularity
items.abstract: The building industry’s consumption of finite resources has a significant environmental impact, which the Circular Economy (CE) seeks to mitigate through reuse and recycling. Within this context, urban heritage rehabilitation plays a crucial role in CE by extending the lifespan of existing structures, but its integration requires structured documentation and efficient data management. Despite growing research on building passports, material passports, and digital inventories, a key research problem remains: the lack of a comprehensive built heritage management system that integrates multiple scales while accounting for conservation, circularity, and sustainability. This study develops a conceptual and methodological framework, demonstrated through a preliminary application. The main objective is to develop Built Heritage Passport (BHP) as an integrated, multi-scale framework for circularity and heritage management across sites, buildings, elements, and materials. This is developed using an inductive reasoning approach, combining a structured review of existing frameworks, indicators, and case studies. The method integrates Historic Building Information Modeling (HBIM) with a web-based inventory system to support structured data entry, visualization, participation, and access across scales. BHP frameworks are developed using four passport models, including site, building, element, and material. The case of Massawa, Eritrea, serves as a proof-of-concept illustrating how the framework can be populated under real-world constraints despite its preliminary and incomplete state. Overall, the results demonstrate that the BHP framework effectively structures multi-scale heritage information into interconnected layers, sub-layers, and indicators/descriptors, enabling improved data organization, accessibility, cross-scale integration, and interoperability with HBIM and web-based inventory systems.
cites_core: Circular Economy Strategies in Eight Historic Port Cities: Criteria and Indicators Towards a Circular City Assessment Framework

items.title: Smart Infrastructure, Circular Construction, and Sustainable Event Urbanism: A Scenario-Based Assessment of Dallas–Arlington for the FIFA World Cup 2026
items.abstract: Mega-events compress demands on mobility, energy, accommodation, waste and digital coordination into a few weeks, yet infrastructure decisions made for them can shape urban systems for decades. This paper develops a scenario-based assessment of how smart infrastructure and circular construction can support sustainable and resilient urban development, using the Dallas–Arlington hosting zone of the FIFA World Cup 2026 as a case. It introduces the Smart Circular Event Model (SCEM), which couples five subsystems—mobility, accommodation, energy, waste and digital coordination—and evaluates interventions for technical efficacy, structural substitution risk, governance consequences and legacy value. An author-derived Interdependency Stress Index (β) compares configurations; it is explicitly a scenario-comparison measure, not a physical failure threshold. Under the modelled baseline β is approximately 0.65, rising to approximately 0.78 when the full set of demand-distribution and circular interventions is assumed. Limited post-event operator reports are used only as directional operational evidence and do not validate β or establish intervention causality. The analysis indicates that smart infrastructure can provide compensatory capacity by distributing demand, reducing waste and accelerating low-carbon legacy assets, but it cannot replace fixed mass-transit capacity. Circular construction measures—particularly design for deconstruction, material passports and conversion of temporary public-realm elements into permanent assets—can strengthen legacy value when embedded in procurement and delivery requirements. The framework is offered as a transparent planning aid pending empirical validation against match-day telemetry and post-event infrastructure data.

items.title: From circular strategies to life-cycle impacts: a systematic review of strategies, indicators and digital enablers in sustainable buildings
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how circular economy (CE) strategies can be integrated with life-cycle thinking (LCT) methods in buildings and construction. It addresses the separation between circular goals, such as reuse, recycling, waste prevention and resource retention, and whole-life impacts, such as embodied carbon, operational energy, cost and recovery yield. This separation can conceal impact shifting across project phases. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review guided by the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation checks and targeted journal searches. The 153 analytically coded CE-LCT studies, published between 2020 and 2025, were each assigned a predominant analytical scope and appraised for research design, boundaries, assumptions, outcome verification and transferability. Findings Life-cycle assessment, life-cycle costing, material-flow analysis and building-level circularity indicators (CIs) provide complementary but non-equivalent evidence and are rarely combined. Building information modelling, material passports, digital twins, artificial intelligence, blockchain and digital marketplaces can improve information continuity, although most studies demonstrate technical potential rather than verified circular outcomes. A phase-resolved CE-LCT framework is proposed to connect circular strategies, assessment methods, digital data flows and measurable indicators throughout the building life cycle. Originality/value The study bridges CE objectives and LCT impact categories and consolidates the coding of strategies, methods, tools and indicators. It offers an evidence-derived conceptual framework that helps researchers, practitioners and policymakers identify gaps, compare interventions and structure the translation of circularity goals into measurable whole-life outcomes.

items.title: Recycled Materials and Sustainable Construction Chemicals for Low-Carbon Industrial Development in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Saudi Arabia’s industrial growth offers two key materials challenges: reducing the embodied carbon of construction and diverting mineral, glass, polymeric, metallurgical, and construction-and-demolition waste from disposal. This review analyzes how recycled materials and sustainable construction chemicals can be integrated as a unified low-carbon strategy, rather than as separate innovations. It synthesizes 2020–2025 literature on recycled aggregates, recycled powders and glass, supplementary cementitious materials, alkali-activated binders, limestone-calcined-clay systems, and performance-enhancing chemicals such as polycarboxylate superplasticizers and corrosion inhibitors. The review focuses on the Saudi context, where high temperatures, chloride-rich coastal environments, long transport distances, rapid project schedules, and evolving circular-economy goals influence the balance between the laboratory results and real-world implementation. Results show that carbon reduction is greatest when high-volume mineral substitution is combined with admixtures that maintain workability, reduce water demand, manage durability risks, and extend service life. While recycled aggregate reduces demand for natural resources, it can increase porosity and binder requirements; therefore, effective treatment, grading, and use of low-clinker binders are essential. Waste glass and finely processed demolition powders can serve as aggregates or reactive components, but particle size, alkali-silica reaction control, and source consistency are critical. Alkali-activated and limestone-calcined-clay binders enable further clinker reduction, making chemical compatibility increasingly important as binder chemistry differs from ordinary Portland cement. A successful Saudi transition ought to prioritize performance-based specifications, regional material passports, verified life-cycle assessments, local beneficiation infrastructure, and procurement policies that reward whole-life carbon reducti

items.title: Integrating BIM and Lean Principles for Sustainable Deconstruction Planning: A Case Study on a Prefabricated Student Residence Building in Romania
items.abstract: The construction sector is a major contributor to global energy consumption and carbon emissions, with building demolition generating significant waste and environmental impact. This research investigates the synergistic application of Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Lean Construction principles to optimize the end - of - life phase of prefabricated buildings, which are prevalent across Eastern Europe. Through an in - depth case study of the C7 student residence in Bucharest, Romania - a typical prefabricated building constructed in 1967 - the study demonstrates a methodology for transitioning from conventional demolition to systematic, value - driven deconstruction. An experimental campaign assessed in - situ material properties and structural integrity of concrete and steel reinforcement after approximately 55 years of service. Results showed that concrete compressive strengths (26.5 - 29.3 MPa) exceeded original design specifications (C24/25), and steel reinforcement exhibited no significant degradation, confirming the potential for direct reuse. These findings were integrated into a detailed BIM model (LOD 350) to create a comprehensive digital material inventory and component - specific material passports documenting location, dimensions, properties, condition, and recommended end - of - life pathways. Lean principles - including value stream mapping, flow optimization, and pull planning - were applied to design an optimized deconstruction sequence prioritizing material recovery. The integrated BIM - Lean framework enables recovery of approximately 65% of building materials by weight for direct reuse or high - value recycling, compared to 30 - 40% in conventional demolition. Reusing 4,800 m² of concrete panels avoids approximately 720 t CO₂ - eq, with additional emissions savings from steel reuse. This research demonstrates that combining in - situ testing, BIM - based digital documentation, and Lean planning significantly enhances deconstruction outcom

items.title: Circular Economy and Construction Waste Management in Saudi Mega-Projects: Pathways Towards Vision 2030 Sustainability Targets
items.venue: Global Academic Journal of Economics and Business
items.abstract: Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 is accelerating the delivery of large-scale urban, tourism, transport, industrial and infrastructure projects while simultaneously strengthening national ambitions for environmental protection, resource efficiency and waste diversion. The scale of this development creates a strategic challenge: construction and demolition waste cannot be managed only as an end-of-pipe disposal problem. It must be addressed through a circular economy model that prevents waste, preserves material value, enables reuse and high-value recycling, and creates dependable markets for secondary construction materials. This paper develops a Saudi-contextualised pathway for integrating circular economy principles with construction waste management in mega-projects. A structured narrative review was undertaken using recent peer-reviewed literature, Saudi policy and regulatory sources, international circular-economy standards, and contemporary research on digital construction and material passports. The review identifies persistent barriers including fragmented responsibilities, limited lifecycle awareness, insufficient source segregation, inconsistent quality assurance for recovered materials, weak secondary-material demand, data gaps, and inadequate contractual incentives. In response, the paper proposes an integrated Circular Construction and Waste Management Framework organised around six linked stages: prevention and demand reduction; circular design; circular procurement; construction-stage segregation and control; recovery and quality assurance; and reintegration of secondary materials into new projects. Digital traceability, governance, market development and performance measurement operate across all stages. The framework introduces practical indicators for material efficiency, waste intensity, source segregation, diversion, reuse, recycled content and traceable recovery. items.title: The global waste recovery and context meter: from global waste management assessment to construction material reuse optimization
items.abstract: Although progress has been made in reducing waste generation, achievements vary widely across countries. Global waste indices are strongly influenced by economic, social, logistic, and other contextual factors, and detailed, cost-effective, and real-time data remain limited. This study investigates how big data, online public and professional perspectives, and statistical indicators can be integrated to assess and compare waste-management performance across countries, how this methodology can be applied to construction waste management, and how construction waste management can be improved through a construction material reuse platform. This research developed the Global Waste Recovery and Context Meter (WaRC meter ), an integrated tool combining waste-related Google information with macro-environmental indicators to assess waste-management patterns and their national context. WaRC meter examines 84 countries by analyzing 988 waste-management keywords alongside 71 macro-environment indicators. The mean absolute relationship |r| was 0.568 and the R 2 median for Ridge regression models, post Nested LOOCV, reached 0.571 (mean = 0.490), while the in-sample median was 0.879. WaRC meter ranking has been validated by priority correlations against the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) Waste Management Score/Rank r Score = –0.67 and r Rank = 0.627, OECD total primary waste generated per person 2022 (r = –0.576), and OECD Material footprint intensity 2024 (r = –0.541) and other indexes. To address construction waste management, the developed WaRC meter was applied to analyze the density of 215 construction waste-management-related keywords across 91 countries. These data were subsequently integrated with 71 macro-context indicators to assess and rank countries according to their construction waste-management performance. That foundational record identified three strategic imperatives—(1) circular resource valorization in orbit, (2) in-space part procurement eliminating Earth-to-orbit launch penalties, and (3) autonomous orbital infrastructure construction (space stations and lunar/orbital depots)—alongside three mandatory physical-engineering hurdles: (i) multi-material compositional analysis of heterogeneous debris, (ii) zero-gravity debris refining and additive feedstock processing, and (iii) extreme-environment 3D printer durability under vacuum, atomic oxygen, thermal cycling, and ionizing radiation. This monograph provides the complete mathematical, thermodynamic, spintronic, and statutory formalization of the March 28, 2025 architecture. Second, we derive the microgravity (Bo -> 0) Navier-Stokes and Marangoni thermocapillary melt-pool Hamiltonian for Coaxial Laser-Wire Directed Energy Deposition (LW-DED), regulated in closed loop by Real-Time Optimization (RTO P2.0). Third, we establish printer survivability via SiO2/SiC self-healing printheads, radiation-immune Voltage-Gated Spin-Orbit Torque Magnetic Tunnel Junction (VGSOT-MTJ) control memory, and Human-in-Command (HIC) with "The Hammer" sub-100-ns physical-layer interlock (tau_cutoff = 85 ns) under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, SEC Rule 15c3-5, and Delaware Carema

items.title: AI-Based Generative Structural Design for Reuse: Integrating Material Banks and LCA
items.abstract: The transition of the construction industry towards a circular economy demands Structural Design for Reuse (StDfR) from end-of-life assets. However, designing with finite stock constraints imposes a complex combinatorial problem. Traditional approaches aiming for single optimal solutions limit diversity, presenting high computational costs and poor generalization. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a generative StDfR framework integrating Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), employing Reinforcement Learning and Graph Neural Networks parameterized by material banks. The model generated hundreds of diverse and viable structural designs in approximately five minutes, covering three truss topologies and various scenarios ranging from entirely new steel to full reuse. Notably, LCA revealed that full reuse does not guarantee the lowest environmental impact due to oversizing with reused elements, the transport of this additional weight, distances from deconstruction sites, and the reconditioning process, highlighting the efficiency of hybrid designs. By automating the information workflow between structural and sustainability teams, this AI approach provides agile StDfR support. Ultimately, the framework generates the final Building Information Modeling (BIM) model in the open Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), consolidating geometric, structural, and logistical project information. This tool empowers decision-making in conceptual phases, promoting the circularity of end-of-life assets.

items.title: Ubuntu-Informed Knowledge Governance for Assistive Technology and Accessibility in Ghanaian Basic Schools
items.venue: Regional journal of information and knowledge management.
items.abstract: Rationale of Study – Ubuntu is often cited in inclusive education and information and knowledge management (IKM) as a cultural context, but rarely treated as an operational logic for governing access, participation, and equity in schooling. Methodology – This paper uses conceptual synthesis and theoretical integration, drawing purposively on Ubuntu scholarship, knowledge governance, Ghanaian inclusive education policy, Universal Design for Learning, differentiated instruction, and assistive technology literature. Findings – The paper proposes the Ubuntu-Informed Inclusive Knowledge Ecosystem (UIIKE) model, reframing assistive technology (AT) and accessibility as institutional knowledge stewardship organised through four governance functions: recognition, provisioning, translation, and accountability. The model explains why device-only interventions underperform where accessible-content workflows, pedagogical mediation, maintenance routines, and monitoring are weak. Implications – UIIKE offers feasible, Ubuntu-aligned actions for basic schools and districts, including clear roles, modest resource planning, structured peer mediation, shared material banks, and simple access-and-participation tracking tools. Originality – By positioning Ubuntu as an implementable governance epistemology rather than a metaphor, the paper connects indigenous African thought to practical mechanisms for disability-inclusive education in Ghanaian basic schools.

items.title: A critical analysis of challenges in tangible cultural heritage conservation in Lalitpur Metropolitan city, Nepal
items.venue: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Lalitpur Metropolitan City (LMC) possesses a high concentration of tangible cultural heritage, including the Patan Durbar Square UNESCO World Heritage site. Post-2015 Gorkha Earthquake restoration efforts face multifaceted technical, institutional, financial, and socio-economic challenges. This study quantifies and ranks these constraints using a mixed-method approach comprising field surveys (n = 145), Relative Importance Index (RII) analysis, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions. Results reveal that the erosion of traditional craftsmanship and skilled labor (RII = 0.92), scarcity of authentic building materials like dachi apa bricks (RII = 0.91), and structural seismic vulnerability (RII = 0.89) are the primary technical bottlenecks. Financially, the absence of a dedicated municipal heritage fund (RII = 0.92) and rigid public procurement frameworks constrain execution quality. Empirical field observations across 213 municipal projects revealed widespread usage of non-authentic substitutes (39 projects utilized machine-made bricks and 39 used cement mortar). To ensure sustainable conservation, the paper advocates for a single-window inter-agency coordination mechanism (RII = 0.92), a municipal heritage material bank, specialized procurement norms under Nepalese law, and community-led Guthi revival.

items.title: Brewing knowledge: Fostering interdisciplinary learning through beer science
items.abstract: The brewing industry in Brazil has significantly expanded, reaching 1,729 breweries in 2022. This growth has increased the demand for specialized professionals, although the academic training of undergraduates (biologists, chemists, biotechnologists, etc.) rarely delves deeply into this topic. This abstract aims to present an initiative that brings together teaching, research, and extension activities centered on beer science, working in an interdisciplinary manner, with a focus on promoting scientific knowledge related to brewing production. This initiative is contextualized at the Federal University of Alfenas, where the "Beer Science" course (since 2017), the "Beer with Science" extension project (since 2019), and related academic research on brewing production have been developed. The extension project's activities formed the central axis of the initiative, to which other activities were linked, including: 1. production of didactic materials (ebooks, production sheets, bulletins, infographics, videos, a dynamic brewery map, and a website); 2. virtual and in-person brewery visits, YouTube live streams, in-person workshops; 3. research on yeast hydration, increasing the antioxidant potential of beer by incorporating marolo, development of new fermentation protocols; 4. teaching activities in the course that connected with material developments. The management of activities was carried out using agile methodologies and digital technologies (Google Drive and Kanbanflow), integrating seven institutions and twelve collaborators. The workshops and visits were evaluated through forms. Various communication channels were used, highlighting social networks (Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, ResearchGate). A total of 22,186 access to materials were made to posts (1,848 per month), emphasizing the positive impact on the community. items.title: Exploring the Strategies of Secondary English Teachers in Enhancing Students' Literacy Skills: A Case Study
items.venue: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
items.abstract: Background and Aim: Literacy underachievement remains a persistent problem in Philippine basic education, with Filipino learners ranking among the lowest in the 2018 PISA reading comprehension results (Librea et al., 2023). While much existing research quantifies the effectiveness of individual literacy strategies through experimental designs, comparatively few qualitative studies explore how secondary English teachers themselves experience, select, and adapt these strategies within their own classrooms. This case study addresses that gap by exploring the strategies secondary English teachers employ to enhance their students' literacy skills, and the reasoning behind these strategies, within a single Philippine public secondary school. Materials and Methods: A single bounded qualitative case study design was employed, with the case defined as the group of eight English teachers at Tambulig National High School, Tambulig District, treated as one bounded unit of analysis. Participants were purposively selected based on current English teaching assignment, active engagement in literacy instruction, and at least three years of teaching experience. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in Cebuanong Binisaya using a guide validated by three experts, then transcribed, translated into English, and validated through member checking. Data were analyzed following Merriam and Tisdell's (2016) case study procedures, involving familiarization, coding, thematic categorization, and interpretation. Results: Five interrelated themes emerged, corresponding to the study's Input-Process-Output conceptual framework: (1) input factors, including students' persistent literacy needs and teachers' varied professional backgrounds; (2) strategies employed, converging around structured reading, writing, and vocabulary approaches; (3) the influence of pedagogical content knowledge, ranging from theory-articulated to experience-derived adaptation; (4) challenges encountered, including mixed-a

Institutional lock-in and circular procurement in the Nigerian construction industry: an interpretive structural analysis
items.abstract: Circular procurement is increasingly promoted as a mechanism for operationalizing circular economy (CE) principles in construction; however, adoption remains limited in many developing economies. Existing studies largely identify and rank barriers without explaining how such constraints interact structurally or shape the sequencing of interventions. This study examines the structural relationships among barriers to circular procurement in the Nigerian construction industry using a combination of interpretive structural modelling (ISM) and MICMAC analyses informed by expert judgement. Five barrier categories were validated through a focus group discussion session with 11 purposively selected construction professionals. ISM was applied to derive a hierarchical model, while MICMAC classified barriers according to driving and dependence power. The findings reveal a tightly coupled system in which all barriers exhibit strong mutual influence and fall within the linkage cluster. The inadequacy of government policies and initiatives emerges as the foundational constraint shaping organizational culture, procurement routines, stakeholder capabilities, and financial conditions. These reinforcing relationships indicate institutional lock-in around linear procurement practices. The study advances circular procurement scholarship by shifting from variable-centered barrier ranking to systems-based explanation and offers evidence-based guidance for sequencing institutional, organisational, and market-level interventions in developing economy construction contexts.

items.title: Uncovering Trends and Thematic Domains of Green Procurement in Construction: A Global Bibliometric Perspective
items.abstract: Escalating environmental pressures, resource constraints, and increasing regulatory expectations are intensifying the need for more sustainable approaches within the construction sector, which remains a major contributor to global waste generation, resource consumption, and carbon emissions . In this context, green procurement (GP) has emerged as a critical mechanism shaping material selection, supply chain configurations, and markets for sustainable products and practices. By influencing supply and demand dynamics, it plays a central role in steering the sector toward more sustainable outcomes. Despite its recognized role in advancing sustainability transitions through approaches such as green public procurement (GPP), sustainable procurement (SP), and environmentally responsible sourcing, the literature remains fragmented across disciplines and thematic orientations, resulting in conceptual ambiguity and a limited understanding of how green procurement is structured and evolving within construction. To address this gap, this study employs a bibliometric approach to systematically examine the intellectual structure and development trajectory of green procurement research in construction. By examining global publication patterns, the study identifies prominent scholars, leading journals, influential countries, and emerging research themes and keyword trends within GP research in the construction sector. Drawing on the Web of Science database, a total of 284 studies published from 2000 to 2026 were evaluated using VOSviewer through co-occurrence and overlay analyses to identify thematic clusters, knowledge domains, and emerging research trends. The findings reveal five major thematic domains: (1) Foundational Procurement and Management Themes; (2) Institutional Frameworks and Environmental Governance Perspectives; (3) Circular Economy and Resource Flow Strategies; (4) Adoption Barriers and Implementation Challenges; and (5) Operational Practices and Construction Appl

items.title: Integrating Resilience, Circular Economy, and Nature-Based Solutions in Urban Regeneration: Pathways Toward Low-Carbon and Climate-Adaptive European Cities
items.abstract: Urban regeneration offers an opportunity to address climate risks, resource-intensive development and socio-spatial inequalities, yet resilience, circular economy and nature-based solutions (NBS) are frequently considered in separate planning and policy domains. This paper develops an integrated conceptual framework for low-carbon and climate-adaptive European urban regeneration through a critical synthesis of literature on urban resilience, circular built environments, NBS, governance and spatial planning. The framework identifies shared decision points and proposes a sequence linking place-based diagnosis, joint objectives, comparative appraisal, coordinated de-livery and adaptive monitoring, with equity and lifecycle assessment embedded throughout. It identifies spatial, temporal and institutional coordination as potential integration mechanisms and examines tensions involving building retention, ecological maintenance, land values and displacement. A comparative European case-study protocol is specified to support subsequent empirical evaluation. The findings reported are conceptual propositions rather than measured project outcomes, and their effectiveness requires validation using transparent case selection, coded evidence and comparable indicators. The paper contributes a decision-orientated structure for evaluating trade-offs across carbon, climate risk, resource use, ecological function and social inclusion.

items.title: Evolution of innovative strategies in the revitalization of post-industrial sites: A case study of the military aviation plant (WZL-4)
items.abstract: This article explores the transformation of demolition and revitalization practices over the past two decades, using the 2008 redevelopment of the Military Aviation Plant No. 4 (WZL-4) in Warsaw, Poland, as a pivotal case study. At the time, the project stood out for its forward-thinking approaches to stakeholder governance, waste management, and infrastructural integration, setting benchmarks for post-industrial redevelopment in Central Europe. This paper analyzes the WZL-4 revitalization in the context of its era – highlighting practices that were considered innovative at the time and remain relevant today – while contrasting them with contemporary strategies employed up to 2025. Drawing upon a comparative methodology and current scientific literature, the study identifies trends, innovations, and persistent challenges in the field of demolition and brownfield regeneration. It highlights key technological, procedural, and managerial advancements including BIM-based project coordination, risk-informed planning, smart monitoring, and circular economy integration. The paper contributes a dual-perspective evaluation: both retrospective and forward looking, offering insight into how best practices have evolved and providing a roadmap for future sustainable urban redevelopment projects grounded in systemic innovation.

The 3rd Southern Africa Regional Science Association 2025 Conference Proceedings: Rethinking the Regional Development Opportunities and Challenges in Southern Africa
items.abstract: The 3rd Southern Africa Regional Science Association (SARSA) 2025 Conference Proceedings, published under the theme “Rethinking the Regional Development Opportunities and Challenges in Southern Africa,” brings together research examining the spatial dimensions of development across Southern Africa and other parts of the Global South. The volume presents empirical and conceptual contributions on urban infrastructure and service delivery; informal settlements and housing; energy access and climate adaptation; urban sustainability and resilience; urban policy and governance; rural economies; and the circular economy in construction. Drawing on diverse geographical contexts and interdisciplinary perspectives, the papers explore the complex relationships between urbanisation, spatial inequality, infrastructure provision, environmental sustainability, and regional development. Collectively, they demonstrate the importance of context-sensitive research and integrated planning approaches in understanding development challenges and identifying opportunities for more inclusive and sustainable futures. The proceedings offer a valuable resource for academics, researchers, students, policymakers, planners, and development practitioners interested in regional science, spatial planning, and sustainable development in Southern Africa and beyond.

items.title: Knowledge and competency framework for quantity surveyors to perform circular economy practices successfully in the construction industry
items.abstract: Purpose The construction industry significantly contributes to resource depletion and waste generation, necessitating the adoption of circular economy (CE) practices. The successful implementation of CE practices depends on the knowledge and competencies of construction professionals, particularly quantity surveyors (QSs), whose cost, procurement and contractual decisions strongly influence CE adoption. Therefore, this study aims to develop a knowledge and competency framework for QSs to perform CE practices successfully in the construction industry. Design/methodology/approach An interpretive research philosophy with a qualitative approach was adopted using the Delphi technique. A two-round Delphi study was conducted involving 20 experts in Round 1 and 17 experts in Round 2, resulting in a total of 37 interviews. The data were analysed through code-based content analysis using NVivo14. Findings The findings highlight QS involvement across design, construction and end-of-life stages, identifying 14 significant CE practices. The study further identifies 17 common knowledge areas and 60 competencies, along with 11 QS-specific knowledge areas and 21 competencies required for each CE practice. Originality/value This study contributes to academic discourse by developing and empirically validating a comprehensive framework encompassing QS-specific knowledge areas, QS-specific competencies, common competencies and common knowledge areas. The core contribution of this study is in identifying QS-specific knowledge areas and competencies and systematically mapping them to the specific CE practices that QSs can perform across the project life cycle. For industry professionals, the framework assists in identifying, assessing and enhancing the specific knowledge areas and competencies required to effectively engage with CE practices to successfully embed CE into the construction industry.

items.title: Circular economy planning in higher education institutions: Between policy ambitions and regulatory constraints
items.abstract: Circular practices have the potential to support urban sustainability transitions and Higher Education Institutions have emerged as strategic actors because of their operational scale, knowledge production, and interaction with urban systems. This study explores the Circular Economy Plan, developed by the Lisbon School of Economics and Management, University of Lisbon, as an institutional initiative embedded in a broader urban circular transition agenda. A multi-method approach combines document and policy analysis, a review of European and Portuguese legislation, semi-structured interviews with staff, and on-site observation of campus operations. The findings show that planning the implementation of circular initiatives in Higher Education Institutions is strongly influenced by regulatory constraints, market conditions, organizational practices, and behavioral dynamics. The plan responds to these conditions via incremental adaptations to existing institutional structures. Applying a multi-level perspective, the study shows that these institutions operate as constrained boundary organizations, mediating between policy frameworks, institutional practices, and urban systems by engaging with supplier, municipal infrastructure and stakeholders. The study contributes to understanding how circular economy strategies are prepared for implementation in Higher Education Institutions and how institutional practices connect with urban systems under multi-level governance constraints.

items.title: FROM CIRCULAR ECONOMY INITIATIVES TO CONSERVATION OUTCOMES: A CRITICAL REVIEW AND MULTILEVEL GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK FOR RESOURCE, WASTE, AND BIODIVERSITY TRANSITIONS
items.venue: Bulletin of Engineering Science Technology and Industry
items.abstract: Circular-economy policy has expanded rapidly, yet its practical success is still commonly judged through recycling, investment, or project counts rather than verified reductions in resource pressure and ecological harm. This critical review updates the governance-oriented analysis of circular-economy initiatives in Andalusia with 32 recent Scopus-indexed records spanning regional policy, manufacturing, consumption, tourism, agri-food systems, infrastructure, finance, social enterprise, and waste management. A structured narrative synthesis was used to compare problem definitions, causal mechanisms, methods, outcomes, and transferability. The evidence shows that circular transition is strongest when five functions operate together: binding direction, coordinated delivery, demand-side participation, finance and infrastructure, and transparent outcome monitoring. Policy fragmentation, weak targets, limited data comparability, and the marginal treatment of biodiversity remain persistent constraints. Firm-level studies identify management commitment, reverse logistics, skills, technology, and customer demand as important enablers, but frequently stop at organizational performance. Regional studies reveal that normative pressure, absorptive capacity, and public-private investment shape adoption, although ecological additionality is rarely tested. We therefore propose a multilevel conservation-governance framework that connects circular inputs and practices to intermediate changes in material flows and then to climate, pollution, habitat, and distributional outcomes. The framework distinguishes process indicators from outcome and safeguard indicators, preventing recycling gains from being mistaken for absolute sustainability. It also embeds spatial differentiation, social inclusion, rebound-risk assessment, and adaptive monitoring. The review concludes that circular economy can support conservation only when it reduces primary extraction and residual waste in absolute term

items.title: The material flow analysis model REMIND-MFA: Global demand scenarios and circular flows for plastics, steel, and cement
items.abstract: Plastics, steel, and cement production are responsible for roughly one-fifth of global greenhouse gas emissions, and demand for these materials is rising rapidly. Low-emission production technologies remain costly, resource-constrained, and slow to scale. Circular economy measures are needed to reduce virgin material production. Robust demand modeling is a prerequisite for assessing both supply-side mitigation and demand-side circular economy strategies. We present REMIND-MFA, a global, top-down, economy-wide, stock-driven, prospective material flow analysis model for plastics, steel, and cement. We publish it here as a fourfold contribution of methods, open-source code, results, and a comprehensive data set of prospective stocks and flows. To our knowledge, it is the first material flow analysis which combines all of these characteristics while covering all three materials at country-level resolution. The main methodological innovations and distinguishing contributions are: a three-step stock extrapolation algorithm that derives consistent regional demand scenarios directly from gross domestic product and population trajectories of the shared socioeconomic pathways with minimal regional assumptions; a trade extrapolation method accounting for shifting patterns; recent historical data through at least 2022, capturing the globally significant peaks in China’s steel and cement demand and the onset of their decline; and a modular, automated codebase built for coupling with models like the integrated assessment model REMIND. We show baseline and illustrative circular economy scenario results, displaying strong demand growth under current policies and the potential for circularity to reduce virgin production.

items.title: A policy readiness evaluation framework for circular timber reuse: reframing timber construction
items.abstract: Purpose This paper develops and demonstrates the framework for circular timber construction (FCTC) to assess how well Australian policy settings support timber deconstruction and reuse. It addresses the gap between broad circular-economy commitments and the specific regulatory, economic, technical and market conditions needed to make reclaimed timber reuse practical in residential construction. Design/methodology/approach This original framework-development study combines systematic literature and policy review methods. Bibliometric mapping, thematic coding, comparative policy analysis and cognitive mapping were used to derive a 34-domain framework. Five experts then assessed each domain against centrality, clarity, coverage, operationalisability and applicability to the Australian policy context using a rapid modified Delphi-informed expert validation process. The FCTC was subsequently demonstrated through an illustrative documentary scoring exercise applied to selected Australian policies. Findings The reviewed Australian instruments address circular economy, waste, procurement and timber-related functions unevenly. In the illustrative scoring matrix, monitoring, policy review and procurement appear across the largest numbers of documents, while grading and defect-acceptance provisions are concentrated in a specialised timber standard. The assessment identifies uneven documentary coverage of the framework domains; it does not establish policy effectiveness or provide a comprehensive national readiness assessment. Research limitations/implications The study relies on published academic and grey literature, so emerging local initiatives or unpublished policy practices may not be fully captured. The scoring exercise is illustrative, not a validated national audit. Future research should extend validation through inter-rater calibration, sensitivity analysis, pilot use by policy and industry users and broader assessment across federal, state, territory and local polic

items.title: Road material stock and circularity potential in growing cities: the case of Singapore
items.abstract: In dense and land-constrained cities, road infrastructure systems may transition from expansion-led growth towards a greater reliance on maintenance, with implications for material demand and circularity. Using Singapore as an illustrative case, this study applies a bottom-up material flow analysis to quantify material stocks and flows in the urban road network from 1990 to 2022. Total road material stock increased from approximately 37.2 Mt in 1990 to 50.6 Mt in 2022. Granite aggregate accounted for the largest share of this stock, with smaller contributions from bitumen and steel slag aggregate. Although net stock growth was primarily associated with recorded road-network expansion, maintenance generated a persistent annual material demand through wearing course renewal. The cohort-based maintenance model estimates that 615 lane-km required resurfacing in 2022, generating 0.214 Mt of removed asphalt. Under the baseline assumption, 98% of this material was recovered as reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP). However, the use of RAP was constrained by the maximum incorporation limits applied to wearing- and base-course asphalt demand, indicating that high recovery does not necessarily result in high internal reuse. Road material stock per capita is approximately 9 t/cap in 2022, reflecting Singapore’s compact urban form and intensive use of shared infrastructure. Material efficiency declined from approximately 460 to 423 vehicle-kilometres per tonne between 2012 and 2022. The findings offer transferable insights for other high-density cities facing limited scope for network expansion, underscoring the need to shift policy attention from supporting infrastructure growth towards extending asset lifetimes, optimising renewal cycles, and improving material circularity in existing road networks.

items.title: A Systems-Based Framework For Evaluating Circular Resource Flows In Sustainable Urban Infrastructure Development
items.venue: Journal of Smart Infrastructure and Environmental Sustainability
items.abstract: The pace of urbanisation has brought with it an increased demand for resources, waste production and environmental degradation, and its issues call for circular resource management of urban infrastructure. This study introduces a systems-based conceptual framework for assessing circular resource flows using Material Flow Analysis (MFA), systems thinking, sustainability assessment and resource efficiency evaluation. It integrates a comprehensive material, water, energy and waste stream analysis to measure the circularity of a product and to pinpoint opportunities for recovery and reuse. A composite sustainability assessment is used to determine resource efficiency, the circularity rate, environmental performance and infrastructure resilience. This proposed framework had a resource efficiency of 84.6%, circularity rate of 71.8%, water reuse efficiency of 66.4%, carbon emission reduction of 29.7%, and an overall Composite Sustainability Index of 0.87, which were significantly better than that of conventional linear infrastructure systems. The results of the study suggest that Circular Resource Management (CRRM) based on a systems approach can increase the environmental performance and long-term infrastructure function. The proposed framework offers a work-in-progress decision support tool for planners and policy makers to encourage resilient, resource efficient and sustainable urban infrastructure development.
