Material stocks and flows of the road network in the Philippines: Implications for resource productivity and circular infrastructure planning
items.abstract: Road infrastructure is a major driver of construction mineral demand, yet its long-term material implications remain underexamined in the Philippines. This study applies a bottom-up dynamic material flow analysis to estimate material inflows, outflows, and in-use road material stocks (MS) from 1982 to 2024. Results show that the road network expanded by 45,285 km (29%) over the study period, along with a shift from unpaved to more material intensive paved surfaces. During the last decade, road construction, upgrading, and maintenance required an average annual material inflow of 32 Mt, of which 56% was associated with road maintenance works. In-use road MS increased from 380 Mt in 1982 to 792 Mt in 2024. The 2024 regional stock productivity, defined as gross regional domestic product (GRDP) per unit of road MS, was evaluated to compare regional economic output relative to the embedded road materials, together with other complementary indicators, namely GRDP per capita, road MS per capita, and road stock density. Results further showed considerable variation in regional stock productivity, indicating that larger road MS does not necessarily correspond to higher economic output per unit of road MS. Overall, the findings show that road infrastructure should be viewed not only as a transport asset, but also as a long-term material system requiring continued maintenance and eventual material management. The study highlights the need for more stock-aware infrastructure planning, stronger recovery and reuse of road materials, and better regionally differentiated strategies to improve resource circularity and productivity in the Philippines’ road infrastructure.

Advancing nutrient circularity in agriculture: Critical perspectives on recycling-derived bio-based fertilisers, production, and adoption challenges
Construction Logistics Optimization for Complex Urban Development and Infrastructure Projects Under Saudi Vision 2030
items.abstract: The importance of construction logistics in the delivery of dense urban developments, linear infrastructure, and the range of giga-projects outlined in Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 has been growing, since in these cases compressed timeframes, limited site areas, the need to import materials, the extreme climate conditions, and the fact that several projects are going on at the same time result in a number of closely linked logistics risks. This review gathers together evidence from peer-reviewed sources on urban construction logistics, construction supply-chain management, consolidation centres, Building Information Modelling (BIM), digital twins, off-site construction, resilience, transport decarbonisation and circular flows. The present paper employs an integrative review approach in order to compare different mechanisms, rather than combining incompatible effect sizes. The evidence shows that logistics performance improves as we move upstream from site expediting to coordinated demand planning, time-slot control, consolidation, visualised 4D logistics and data-led exception management. However, no single technology overcomes the problem of fragmented incentives: consolidation may shift costs between the various parties involved, internet platforms require a high degree of data discipline and interoperability, and just-in-time strategies may reduce storage but at the same time raise vulnerability to unreliable transport. The most credible optimisation model for achieving the objectives of Saudi Vision 2030 is therefore a multi-level system which includes common performance indicators covering strategic network design, tactical procurement and consolidation, and operational dispatch. The paper suggests a framework that is sensitive to the particular context and which focuses on logistics governance, digital visibility, resilient sourcing, low-emission transport, and reverse logistics. The areas that demand further research include freight data specific to Saudi Arabi

items.title: From agricultural residues to tradeable bio-assets in Africa: a policy and practice framework for circular agro-industrial value chains
items.abstract: Agricultural residues in Sub-Saharan Africa are often described as an underused resource, but their conversion into marketable products is constrained by feedstock variability, competing uses, logistics, product standards, environmental risks, and uncertain demand. Utilizing a critical narrative policy synthesis, this paper develops a policy and practice framework for assessing when selected agricultural residues can become credible circular bio-assets for local use and, where conditions permit, regional trade. The framework connects four decision layers: (1) technically and economically recoverable feedstock, ownership, and explicit smallholder and land-use safeguards; (2) technology and product selection; (3) environmental, technical, and economic evidence; and (4) quality assurance, finance, MSME AfCFTA compliance costs, and trade infrastructure. It examines cassava processing effluents, cocoa pod husks, palm oil mill effluents and other palm residues, sugarcane bagasse, and livestock manure across biochemical, thermochemical, bioconversion, and physicochemical pathways. Material Flow Analysis, Life Cycle Assessment, and Techno-Economic Analysis are treated as complementary evidence rather than as stand-alone proof of viability. The paper also examines the conditions under which AfCFTA trade facilitation, quality-assurance infrastructure, payment systems, and development finance can support commercialization. A critical comparison with existing African circular-bioeconomy reviews shows that prior work has largely focused on the potential and challenges of circular bioeconomy, the status of circular practices in selected food systems, or specific technology portfolios. This paper extends that literature by linking resource security, technology choice, evidence thresholds, product quality, market validation, and cross-border transaction requirements within one staged decision architecture governed by conditional decision gates. items.title: Circularity, Capacity Breaches, and Import-Anchored EPR for Solar PV and Battery Waste: A Probabilistic MFA-LCA Framework Applied to Zimbabwe
items.abstract: Remarkably, rapid rollout of solar photovoltaic (PV) and lithium-ion battery energy storage systems (BESS) across import-dependent emerging economies, often accelerated by climate-induced hydropower shortfalls and ageing thermal fleets, generates any major delayed end-of-life (EoL) waste liability in jurisdictions lacking domestic manufacturing or recycling infrastructure, in many respects. To gauge capacity timing and energetic circularity, we formalize the regularized Deferred Waste Liability Index (DWLI t) and the thermodynami-cally coherent Circularity-Weighted Energy Return (CWER), proving required and enough conditions for infrastructure lead times, net circular energy gains, and regional hub-and-spoke optimality, broadly speaking. A second general-izable estimation and policy-design framework is developed that integrates minimum-variance trade-and-survey triangulation, probabilistic dynamic material flow analysis (MFA), ISO 14040/14044 life cycle assessment (LCA), and regional scale-economy optimization, and verify it employing empirical data and three local operational case studies from Zimbabwe through 2060. In this 1 broader context, given zero existing formal PV or lithium-ion recycling capacity (DWLI t → +∞), even one capped 5,000 t yr −1 pilot trajectory is breaching the critical capacity threshold (DWLI t > 1) by 2042–2043 and peaks at 3.40 in 2050. Under the Accelerated Transition portfolio (13,415 MW PV and 7,813 MW/31,252 MWh BESS by 2040), cumulative EoL waste in Zimbabwe reaches 42,300 tonnes of PV and 28,400 tonnes of BESS by 2050, rising to 95,800 tonnes (95% prediction interval [PI]: 76,400–118,200) and 52,100 tonnes (95% PI: 41,200–64,900) by 2060; across all scenarios, combined cumulative waste spans 57,400–147,900 tonnes, with 76–81% of Accelerated Transition flows emerging between 2045 and 2060. items.title: Drivers, Barriers and Sustainability Outcomes of Green Innovation Adoption in Municipal Solid Waste Management in Southeast Asia: A Structured Integrative Review
items.venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
items.abstract: Southeast Asian cities are generating rapidly increasing volumes of municipal solid waste (MSW). Yet the green innovations that could divert waste from landfills have diffused slowly, and evidence on why they are adopted remains fragmented. This study conducts a structured integrative review of empirical research on the adoption of green innovation in MSW management in Southeast Asia. Twenty-six structured queries across a web search engine, scholarly platforms, and institutional repositories returned 242 records; 30 were assessed in detail, and 16 empirical journal articles published between 2015 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesized using the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, informed by diffusion of innovations and circular economy theory. Seven groups of green innovation were identified: source separation and household recycling; community waste banks; composting and biodigesters; smart and digital systems; municipal systems and materials recovery facilities; waste-to-energy; and producer responsibility. Environmental context factors were the most frequently reported, appearing in 14 of the 16 studies: regulation, enforcement, incentives, information, and social norms acted as drivers when strong and as barriers when weak. Organizational factors, notably financial support, partnerships, and local leadership, determined whether schemes could be sustained, while technological factors, chiefly infrastructure and cost, shaped implementation. Social and economic benefits were reported, but no study measured landfill diversion or emission reductions over time, and most studies lacked an explicit theory. The review proposes a sequential TOE-based framework, expressed as four propositions, that links institutional conditions, organizational capacity, and infrastructure to sustained adoption. items.title: Sectoral Coordination to Maximize China’s National and Provincial Building Carbon Emissions Mitigation
items.abstract: The building sector is central to achieving China’s carbon peak and neutrality targets, yet existing assessments seldom integrate full life cycle emissions into subnational policy design. Here we develop a building material–energy–emission (BMEE) model to quantify direct, indirect, and embodied CO 2 emissions from all building types across 31 Chinese mainland provinces from 2000 to 2060 and to evaluate 50 policy scenarios that combine five strategies: urban renewal, green buildings, low-carbon construction, circular economy, and energy transition. The model links dynamic material flow analysis with energy balance sheet splitting, supported by newly compiled national databases on building material and operational energy intensities, and incorporates a renovation module that prioritizes renovation over demolition. We find that China’s building emissions have peaked around 2017 and can decline to between 0.69 and 2.48 Gt (10 9 tonnes) CO 2 by 2060. Under the lowest-emission pathway, cumulative emissions are reduced by 39.5% relative to business-as-usual, with urban renewal providing the largest contribution to total mitigation, followed by green buildings and energy transition. Public buildings, the material sector, and northern provinces exhibit the largest mitigation potentials, while provincial results highlight distinct strategy priorities. Monte Carlo analysis confirms that these conclusions are robust despite widening parametric uncertainty. Our findings underscore the importance of sectoral coordination and regionally tailored policy packages to maximize building decarbonization in China and provide a scalable framework for other large countries facing concurrent new construction and stock-renewal challenges.

items.title: Regional end-of-life embodied carbon emissions of wood-frame housing: A hybrid-parametric assessment of single-family houses in Canada
items.abstract: The aging wood-frame single-family housing stock in North America represents a major future source of demolition waste and a substantial supply of recoverable wood materials. However, the embodied carbon implications of alternative end-of-life (EoL) strategies remain poorly understood at the regional scale due to limitations in temporal resolution, empirical validation, and carbon pathway characterization. This study develops a hybrid-parametric modelling framework that integrates historical construction eras, material flow analysis, the 9R circular economy hierarchy, and life cycle module-based carbon accounting (C1 D) to assess 81,598 single-family houses in Vancouver, Canada. The framework incorporates uncertainty through Monte Carlo simulations and is validated against four real-world deconstruction projects, demonstrating its capability to represent both material flows and carbon outcomes. The modelled wood generation (155.9 kg/m 2 ) and diversion rate (90%) fall within the observed ranges (120.8–179.0 kg/m 2 and 84–99%). Results show that EoL scenario selection has a substantially greater influence on embodied carbon performance than building age. Conventional demolition generates average net emissions of 9.39 kgCO₂e/m 2 . Moderate deconstruction (75% diversion) reduces this to 3.12 kgCO₂e/m 2 (−67%), whereas high-diversion pathways achieve net savings of 1.23 and 6.92 kgCO₂e/m 2 at 90% and 95% diversion. Structural lumber represents the largest recoverable material fraction and the primary source of mitigation potential. Sensitivity analysis identifies labour intensity, recovery efficiency, and allocation among reuse, repurposing, and recycling pathways as the dominant determinants of carbon outcomes. Biogenic carbon assessment further demonstrates that circular strategies primarily alter the timing and distribution of carbon flows through material substitution and emission deferral rather than permanent carbon sequestration. items.title: Urban Governance and the Choreography of Intermediary Roles in a Waste Cooking Oil-to-Biodiesel Loop in Shiga Prefecture, Japan
items.venue: The International Journal of Sustainability Policy and Practice
items.abstract: Local circular-economy initiatives often stall not because conversion technologies are unavailable but because material flows, operational routines, and responsibilities must be aligned across heterogeneous actors. This article traces a four-decade waste cooking oil (WCO) to biodiesel fuel (BDF) loop in Shiga Prefecture, Japan, and explains how intermediary roles overlapped and migrated among civic groups, municipalities, and a local fuel distributor as the loop moved from experimentation to routine service provision. Based on interviews (n = 10), municipal and organizational documents, and process tracing, the analysis applies a four-mode intermediation lens—facilitating, brokering, configuring, and structuring—to map how actors addressed three recurring coordination challenges: mobilizing dispersed household feedstock, stabilizing quality and compliance in conversion and logistics, and securing reliable offtake through procurement and fleet routines. The findings show that durable circular loops rely on redundant intermediation: rather than a clean handover between actors, multiple intermediaries simultaneously perform different modes, creating fallback capacity when political priorities, markets for used oils, or operational constraints shift. The article distills transferable design principles—early offtake commitments, visible and convenient collection infrastructure, shared quality gates, and hybrid municipal–private operating models—for cities building local circular ecosystems.

items.title: Assessment of Electronic Waste Management Environmental Pollution and Associated Health Risks in Gazipur City Bangladesh
items.abstract: Electronic waste (E-waste) is a rapidly growing environmental challenge in developing countries. This study assessed E-waste generation, management practices, environmental and occupational health risks, and institutional challenges in Gazipur City Corporation, Bangladesh. Using an integrated mixed-methods approach, including Material Flow Analysis (MFA), surveys, stakeholder interviews, and institutional assessment, data were collected from 375 respondents. The city generated 6,245.21 tons of E-waste in 2024 (2.43 kg person⁻¹ year⁻¹), with refrigerators, televisions, and microwave ovens as the major sources. Informal recycling dominated E-waste management, while unsafe handling practices increased environmental and occupational risks. Key barriers included inadequate recycling infrastructure, weak policy implementation, and limited institutional capacity. This study provides an integrated framework to support sustainable E-waste management, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), and circular economy implementation in Bangladesh and other developing countries.

items.title: Who pays for urban cleanliness? Governance cost, behavioral nudge design, and informal recycling in Bangkok's waste regime
items.abstract: Cities in the Global South increasingly consider market-based instruments such as Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) to encourage source separation, improve municipal cost recovery, and support circular-economy transitions. However, the fiscal promise of PAYT depends not only on fee design but also on operational awareness, institutional trust, behavioral readiness, and the inclusion of actors already embedded in recycling systems. This study assesses municipal fiscal exposure under constrained implementation conditions rather than conducting an ex-post causal evaluation or predicting long-term household compliance. Using Bangkok's 2025 waste-fee reform as a case study, the paper develops an exploratory, scenario-based diagnostic framework that combines Material Flow Analysis (MFA), municipal cost data, and publicly released NIDA Poll evidence from 1310 Bangkok residents. The evidence reveals a substantial acceptance–readiness gap: while 73.97% of respondents supported behavior-differentiated waste fees in principle, 80.76% reported no awareness of the registration requirement for the reduced 20 THB/month fee, and 60.46% anticipated low or no local cooperation with the program. Under the model assumptions, a higher-separation pathway (S = 30%; BMA, 2026) is associated with approximately 2.13 billion THB in annual municipal cost savings. Under lower-compliance conditions, represented by a conservative 5–10% effective separation range, scenario-calculated savings are substantially lower, with potential burdens shifting toward municipal budgets, households, informal recyclers, and peri-urban environments. The study operationalizes this divergence as the scenario-calculated fiscal component of governance cost: the opportunity cost of unrealized efficiency potential under weak implementation readiness. The Bangkok case suggests that urban governance capacity functions as an economic input shaping the financial and environmental viability of price-based urban reforms.

items.title: Regional SYMBIO Business models - Material flow and multi-criteria overview
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This record contains the presentations from the multi-stakeholder focus groups between March and June 2026, where SYMBIO brought together regional stakeholders in all six pilot countries: Croatia, Belgium, Slovenia, Austria, Spain and Italy. The SYMBIO project supports selected pilot regions in developing circular, bio-based business models enabled by industrial symbiosis. Earlier project work identified and assessed 6 promising regional value chains, using Material Flow Analysis and a Multi-Criteria overview of economic, environmental, regulatory and social aspects. Each focus group presented the regional value chain, its material flow, the ecosystem and a multi-criteria overview followed by a co-creation session to (1) validate the value chains, (2) identify barriers and enablers and (3) validate the regional ecosystem, necessary to implement industrial symbiosis. The following table shows all regional focus groups: Country Value chain(s) Date Location Croatia Forestry residues PHA 11th March, 2026 Zagreb Belgium Corn steep liquor 1,3-Propanediol 17th March, 2026 Brussels Italy Whey ProteinsCorn residues Succinic acidBarley straw Succinic acidWheat straw PHA 25th March, 2026 Online Slovenia Wheat straw PHA 21st April, 2026 Ljubljana Austria Barley straw Succinic acid 20th May, 2026 Klagenfurt Spain Forestry residues PHA 10th June, 2026 Sevilla The focus groups were designed to raise awareness, identify friction points, and equip decisionmakers with the knowledge needed to implement industrial symbiosis. items.title: Toward Sustainable Industrial Spatial Planning: Integrating Supply Chain Management and Environmental–Economic Assessment for the Proposed Al-Kuraymat Industrial Zone, Egypt
items.venue: SVU-International Journal of Engineering Sciences and Applications
items.abstract: Industrial zones play a vital role in economic growth and regional development; however, they are increasingly challenged by inefficient resource utilization, environmental degradation, and fragmented industrial development. These challenges highlight the need for integrated planning approaches that improve industrial performance while supporting environmental sustainability. This study develops an integrated framework that combines Supply Chain Management (SCM), Material Flow Analysis (MFA), Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), and environmental–economic assessment to support sustainable industrial spatial planning. The framework is applied to the proposed Al-Kuraymat Industrial Zone in Egypt, where resource availability, material flows, industrial linkages, transportation networks, environmental conditions, and existing infrastructure are systematically assessed to identify opportunities for industrial integration and sustainable development. Based on this assessment, a spatial planning model is developed to optimize industrial zoning, strengthen logistics connectivity, promote industrial symbiosis, and enhance circular resource flows. Three alternative development scenarios are also evaluated to examine the environmental and economic implications of different levels of supply chain integration. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework identifies practical opportunities to improve resource efficiency, reduce industrial waste, enhance environmental performance, support renewable energy utilization, and strengthen spatial integration among industrial activities. By integrating supply chain principles with environmental and spatial planning, the framework provides a practical decision-support tool for sustainable industrial development and offers a planning approach that supports circular economy principles and the objectives of Egypt Vision 2030.

items.title: Developing Light Engineering Industry from Repurposing E-Waste in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Electronic waste (e-waste) refers to disposed electrical and electronic equipment. In Bangladesh, e-waste offers resource potential as well as environmental concern. The growing prominence of e-waste has the potential for contributing to resource recovery and industrial development in the context of the light engineering industry. There is still a large research gap in establishing connections among the existing literature in these aspects, which are available and relevant to the Bangladeshi context. To manage these challenges, an approach is required that links sustainability with the development of formalized, safe, and regionally appropriate industries. A qualitative approach that combines secondary statistical data analysis with spatial evaluation is adopted for this research. An indexing framework assesses existing facilities based on spatial efficiency, environmental performance, and worker safety, drawing from comparative case studies and theoretical grounding in circular economy principles and sustainable design guidelines. To bridge these gaps, the research investigates how context-responsive architectural strategies might enhance sustainability, efficiency, and safety. This will help Bangladesh to explore a potential to establish integrated light engineering industries by formally managing e-waste within a new multidisciplinary framework.

items.title: Impact of Deployment Geometry and Radio Range on Random Walk–Based SLP Protocols in WSNs
items.venue: International Journal of Wireless and Microwave Technologies
items.abstract: This research aims to understand the impact of the network area and shape on the performance metrics used in evaluating the random walk-based source location privacy (SLP) techniques developed for WSNs. In this context, the impact of circular and square network models for different network areas, node densities, and radio ranges of sensor nodes on the performance of three popular SLP techniques is investigated. The effectiveness is assessed using performance measures from the body of available literature. It has been found that square deployment performs better for sector-based SLP protocols when network area, node density, and node radio range are held constant. However, circular networks perform better for the same protocol when the radio range is varied beyond a certain threshold while holding all other parameters constant. The trend, however, changes under comparable network settings for the non-sector-based random walk protocols considered in the current work. The results reveal a strong link between deployment geometry and routing logic, demonstrating that sector-based SLP protocols are primarily geometry-sensitive, whereas non-sector-based protocols are more sensitive to radio-range variations. A radio-range threshold of approximately 100 m was identified beyond which privacy gains saturated and energy costs increased. These findings provide practical design guidelines for geometry-aware deployment of privacy-preserving WSNs. However, the conclusions are limited to simulation-based evaluation of three random walk-based SLP protocols in circular and square network topologies, and further validation in irregular and real-world deployments is required.

items.title: DIGITAL PLATFORMS AND SOCIAL MEDIA FOR WASTE MANAGEMENT: A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF CURRENT TRENDS, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE PROSPECTS
items.venue: International Journal of Entrepreneurship and Management Practices
items.abstract: Rapid urbanisation and the generation of large amounts of municipal solid waste present serious operational and ecological challenges for modern cities and require a shift toward digitally mediated circular economies. This narrative review synthesises the multidisciplinary scholarly landscape on the role of digital platforms and social media networks in promoting waste management operations, public communication, and citizen engagement. This paper analyses peer-reviewed literature indexed in the Scopus database in the period 2015-2025 to explore how emerging digital technologies and platforms, such as sensors of the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and interactive social networks, can provide a substantial shift in waste governance from a reactive disposal model to proactive data-driven resource recovery ecosystems. Although digital solutions are increasingly adopted, existing research has focused mainly on technical features, while socio-behavioural, social, and governance dimensions remain less integrated. This review synthesises the current literature to address this gap across four key domains: innovations in smart infrastructure, technology-enabled collaboration, behavioural interventions in social media, and structural barriers to implementation. Key findings reveal that digital platforms can greatly reduce communication costs, enable local civic engagement, and improve collection logistics. However, regional digital divides, organisational siloes, data privacy issues, and overreliance on short-term self-reported performance indicators (e.g., reported participation instead of long-term operational or environmental benefits) constrain the capacity to deploy at scale across municipal systems. The review therefore further develops an integrated socio-technical framework through a critical evaluation of these tensions linking technical engineering models with socio-cognitive behavioural theories and multi-level governance frameworks. items.title: Calligraphy as a Pedagogical Bridge: Reviving India’s Written Heritage through Art-Integrated Learning under NEP 2020
items.venue: Abhinavdhara International Journal of Innovation in Indic Studies
items.abstract: India possesses one of the world's richest calligraphic and scribal traditions, spanning Devanagari, Nastaliq, and dozens of regional scripts, yet calligraphy remains almost entirely absent from its formal school education.This paper argues that calligraphy deserves recognition as a living Indian Knowledge System and a high-value instrument of art-integrated pedagogy under the National Education Policy 2020.Methodologically, the paper is a conceptual and practice-informed policy analysis combining narrative literature synthesis, policy document analysis, comparative curricular analysis of Japan and China, and reflective practitioner evidence; it distinguishes throughout between published research findings, conceptual inference, practitioner observation, and proposal.The argument rests on three pillars.First, policy alignment: NEP 2020 explicitly mandates art-integrated, experiential learning and the infusion of Indian Knowledge Systems across the curriculum, and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023 and CBSE's art-integration circulars provide the operative implementation machinery, creating a natural institutional home for structured calligraphy education.Second, cognitive evidence: recent neuroscience, including high-density EEG studies of children and young adults, demonstrates that writing by hand produces far more elaborate brain connectivity patterns than typing, supporting memory, attention, and fine motor development in the developing brain; this evidence is treated here as mechanistic rationale for structured script practice rather than as demonstrated outcomes of calligraphy instruction.Third, global precedent: Japan retains shosha and shodo within its national elementary curriculum, and China's Ministry of Education made calligraphy a required course in primary and middle schools in 2013, positioning script practice as both cultural transmission and cognitive training.India, despite an older and more diverse scribal heritage, has no

items.title: Beyond Zero Waste: Who Carries the Cost of a Gathering?
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Gatherings are among a city's oldest and least accounted-for infrastructures. A festival draws on ground, materials, skills, money and people's evenings, and rarely records what it gave back. "Zero waste" and "regenerative" have become easy words for such events. Both usually count materials, and leave out who carried the cost. This paper began as a plan for a conventional report on The Soulstitch Festival, a free public evening on the winter solstice in Ahmedabad, India, and became research as the festival's own disciplines changed how its claims could be checked. It reports two prototypes, on 21 December 2024 and 2025, designed by Multopia as research instruments. The methods combine research through design, the real-world laboratory, a visual and material reading of an archive of 418 photographs and 92 video clips made by many hands, astronomical computation and material flow analysis. The contribution is Multopia's Minimum Regenerative Unit: a test that reads any gathering through three stocks of its place (culture, ecology and micro-economy) and through every person and organisation who gave to it. No gain counts if it vanishes after the night or is paid for by a loss elsewhere, and the whole is named by its weakest strand. Event standards, circular-festival accounts and multi-capital methods each do part of this; none we found lets the people who made a gathering fail it. Here the unit is specified and illustrated on its own two editions, read after the fact; the next edition is its first test fixed in advance. The strongest evidence is the material account. The 2025 edition handled about 680 kg of material (90% interval 610–830 kg). About 3% was bought new: rope and jute to shape foraged material into art, printed texts, and paper cups and bowls. About 76% stayed in use (lent and returned, kept, reused, recycled or made into art) and about 24% went back to the ecosystem: composted for a Miyawaki planting, used again on the land, or eaten by birds. items.title: Circular Modality in Construction
items.abstract: A general consensus is that conventional linear modalities guarantee no industrial sustenance in the long run for many obvious reasons. This is where the topicality of circularity has been accentuated for the last two decades or so in the socio-political arena. However, anecdotal evidence suggests that the emphasis given to circularity in the construction industry is relatively low. Tackling this issue essentially warrants a rigorous co-production of integrated know-how, preferably beyond sectoral boundaries. The present study sheds light on interdisciplinary approaches taken to deal with the slowness of transmuting circularity into the construction sector. A comprehensive literature survey was undertaken to understand this phenomenon at the policy, firm, and site levels. The analysis included 128 articles published in high-impact journals between 2003 and 2024. Eighty-seven gaps in terms of theory, knowledge, practice, method, empiricism, and policy were observed. Forty-four thematic sub-clusters have the potential for empirical research. A new framework was finally proposed to scaffold the systemic transition towards a circular construction sector. On a practical level, the study offers valuable insights and instruments for industry personnel to gauge the efficacy of their own circular approaches and initiatives.

items.title: Architectural practice and the circular built environment transition: empirical insights from Australia
items.abstract: The transition towards a Circular Economy (CE) offers a key pathway to decarbonize the built environment. However, uptake is slow and empirical research on CE adoption in the building industry remains limited, particularly in Australia, where circularity rates are below the global average.This study examines Australian architectural professionals as key actors in the transition towards a circular built environment. It investigates perceptions of CE and the barriers and enablers shaping its implementation through the lived experiences of architectural professionals in navigating CE policies, industry agendas, professional aspirations, and the realities of everyday practice.In-depth, semi-structured interviews with architectural professionals (n = 12) are thematically analysed, revealing fragmented CE perceptions and practices and systemic barriers such as regulatory misalignment, knowledge gaps, limited organizational capacity, market immaturity, and cultural inertia. The study concludes that circular built environment transition requires coordinated action across policy, markets, educational, professional and cultural domains to strengthen the agency and leadership of architectural professionals and enable them to deliver circular outcomes. Identified enablers of CE adoption include collaborative delivery, education, legal instruments, and demonstration projects. The study contributes empirical evidence on Australian architectural engagement with CE and practice-based insights into how architectural practice can accelerate the circular built environment transition.

items.title: Accelerating plastic pollution mitigation in Vietnam: A circular economy policy and implementation roadmap
items.venue: Waste Management & Research The Journal for a Sustainable Circular Economy
items.abstract: Plastic pollution poses significant environmental and public health risks in Vietnam, driven by rising consumption and inadequate waste management. As one of the leading contributors to marine plastic leakage, the country faces challenges linked to linear economic practices and weak recycling systems. This study applies a structured narrative review protocol to synthesize evidence from policy, scientific, and institutional sources in the manuscript corpus. The analysis examines circular economy strategies and evaluates them using a comparative prioritization framework based on impact potential, implementation feasibility, and time-to-effect. The article identifies high-priority interventions for Vietnam (extended producer responsibility enforcement, source segregation, and reuse systems), highlights major barriers (fragmented governance, informal-system exclusion, and weak data systems), and proposes an actionable research and policy agenda for the transition to a circular plastics economy.

items.title: Building Knowledge Infrastructure for Circular Economy: Systematic Barriers to Recycled, Reusable, and Reclaimed Material Adoption in UK Construction
items.venue: Journal of Construction Engineering and Management
items.abstract: Recycled, reusable, and reclaimed (RRR) materials comprise less than 10% of UK construction inputs despite comprehensive ISO circular economy standards and urgent postGrenfell safety reforms mandating evidence-based material selection. This research examines why knowledge infrastructure deficits—not coordination failures or organizational resistance—prevent RRR material adoption, contributing to key research priorities on knowledge production in decision making, decision-making practices, and actionable policy research. Drawing on government-funded research through the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS), we demonstrate how circular economy standards presuppose knowledge infrastructure that does not exist, creating “capability-constrained ceremonial compliance” where organizations adopt frameworks symbolically while lacking enabling infrastructure. Evidence from 474 stakeholders (242 industry professionals, of whom 222 provided complete environmental knowledge data, and 232 homeowners) reveals three systematic knowledge-policy gaps: a safety verification infrastructure gap (70.3% of homeowners demand laboratory testing versus 45.1% of suppliers currently providing it—a 25.1 percentage point gap); a coordination infrastructure deficit (50.9% experience procurement difficulties regardless of firm size or supply chain position); and an environmental knowledge gap (76.1% of industry professionals lack carbon knowledge despite 91.4% demanding government calculation tools). These gaps reflect absent information problems—knowledge infrastructure preventing environmental knowledge production and use—rather than coordination challenges. We propose capability-sequencing logic requiring government investment in verification, coordination, and environmental knowledge infrastructure before mandating RRR material compliance, reversing current policy approaches presuming enabling infrastructure exists. items.title: Comprendre les effets rebonds circulaires et innover pour les atténuer
items.abstract: Malgré des réussites locales, l’économie circulaire ne parvient pas encore à réduire significativement les consommations de matières premières vierges ou les impacts environnementaux à l’échelle planétaire. Parmi de nombreuses autres causes, la notion d’effet rebond circulaire a été mobilisée récemment pour expliquer ce constat, mais elle demeure peu connue. Cela amène deux questions : « Comment les effets rebonds se manifestent-ils en économie circulaire ? » et « Comment atténuer ces effets rebonds pour tendre vers une soutenabilité forte ? ». Cet article présente, au terme d’une revue de littérature métanarrative, une synthèse actualisée des travaux théoriques pour mieux comprendre le phénomène des effets rebonds circulaires. En croisant des études critiques sur l’économie circulaire, des travaux préconisant diverses formes d’innovation et des principes visant une soutenabilité forte, l’article propose également cinq pistes pratiques pour les atténuer à plusieurs niveaux systémiques.

items.title: An early-stage, multi-lifecycle assessment framework for sustainable material selection in automotive industry
items.abstract: The transition toward low-carbon mobility requires material-selection approaches that account for extended use cycles and cross-sector reuse pathways. However, early-stage automotive design decisions are typically informed by single-life cradle-to-grave assessments, which do not explicitly integrate reuse-induced substitution effects or multi-stage emission accounting within development timelines. This study operationalizes an integrated cradle-to-reuse-to-grave (C2R2G) assessment approach by combining established life cycle assessment (LCA), system expansion, and substitution modeling principles into an automotive-specific decision-support structure. The framework formalizes emission accounting across primary use, reuse preparation, secondary application, and end-of-life treatment, including explicit system expansion, substitution, and circular scenario modeling parameters. A bio-based laminated veneer lumber (LVL) seat-shell is evaluated as a demonstrative case within passenger vehicle applications. Scenario modeling compares single-life, recycling, and open-loop reuse pathways under varying lifetime and energy-intensity assumptions. Results indicate that reuse-driven substitution effects can significantly alter cumulative carbon footprints compared to single-life configurations, though outcomes remain highly sensitive to assumed service lifetimes, displaced material emission factors, and energy mixes in second-life sectors. Sensitivity analysis highlights key parameters influencing ranking stability and identifies boundary conditions under which reuse advantages diminish. Rather than proposing a new LCA methodology, this work demonstrates how established analytical components can be systematically integrated to support early-stage automotive material pathway evaluation. The approach enhances transparency in allocation choices and trade-off identification, contributing to more informed low-carbon design decisions in circular mobility systems.

items.title: Economía circular intercultural en comunidades agrícolas
items.abstract: This paper proposes a holistic methodology based on the concept of intercultural circular economy (ICE). It designs the autonomy index (IPa), which measures the preservation of cultural value in local and production chains, as well as the circular efficiency index (IECI). It analyzes the evolution of the CI and the opportunity offered by Latin American communities with traditional and ecological production experiences in integrating an ICE concept that interrelates economic organization, people, and nature from a perspective of balance with nature.

items.title: From Symbolic to Systemic Sustainability in Higher Education: A Readiness-Gated Framework for Governance, Monitoring, and Institutional Change
items.abstract: Universities’ sustainability commitments frequently outpace their systemic implementation. This paper addresses that gap by proposing the Sustainability Integration Framework (SIF), a mechanism-based, readiness-gated model for verifiable progression from symbolic adoption to institutionalized practice. Using a design science research approach, the study integrates institutional theory, resource-based theory, and responsible leadership to explain how external pressures, leadership interpretation, and internal capabilities shape sustainability integration. The framework is operationalized through a six-component institutional architecture, an Input–Process–Output logic model with auditable indicators, and a five-domain Readiness and Maturity Index (RMI). A six-stage mechanism—pressure, interpretation, resource reconfiguration, routinization, feedback closure, and coupling or decoupling—is supported by PDCA-gated progression, with Institutional Equity and data/AI Governance as cross-cutting levers. A dual-rater protocol, reliability thresholds, and an External Composite Readiness Index support transparent, comparable assessment across institutions. A single-rater demonstration at the American University of Beirut returns a domain profile of three defined domains (Leadership and Governance, Curriculum and Pedagogy, Operations) and two ad hoc domains (Strategy, Metrics and Data), summarized as an indicative RMI of 1.60 at the lower edge of the Intermediate stratum, indicating substantial external visibility alongside partial internal embedding. The contribution is a design proposal in the design science sense: an integrated theorized mechanism and an evidence-gated maturity model aligned with leading sustainability standards, intended to give administrators a replicable, audit-ready pathway for coordinating governance, curriculum, operations, and data systems once validated. items.title: Inside the building circularity indices - A comparative assessment of two buildings with different circular design strategies
items.abstract: The growing availability of circularity indicators in the built environment has increased the need to understand how different assessment methods evaluate circular performance. This study investigates how selected building circularity indices respond to contrasting circular design strategies by applying multiple indices to two real-life residential demonstration projects: the Upcycle House, which emphasizes reused, recycled, and upcycled materials, and the Adaptable House, which focuses on flexibility and adaptability. The analysis uses a theoretical comparison of index structures with an empirical application to both case buildings. Circularity scores were compared across indices and examined in relation to system boundaries, indicator composition, weighting principles, and underlying assumptions. The results show substantial variation in circularity scores for the same buildings depending on the selected index. Despite these differences, all indices consistently assign higher circularity scores to the Upcycle House than to the Adaptable House. For four indices, the normalized performance difference is approximately a factor of two, while one index produces a difference exceeding a factor of seven. The study demonstrates how weighting factors at indicator and sub-indicator levels are crucial to disclose and communicate clearly. The findings also demonstrate the sensitivity in assigning mass-flows to the right indicator categories, and warrants for specific attention towards the inventory scope and how fill materials are included. By empirically comparing multiple indices on two contrasting case studies, the research confirms that reuse and recycling strategies are preferred over adaptability and flexibility. The study further demonstrates that circularity assessments are strongly shaped by methodological choices and should therefore be interpreted and declared critically and transparently.

items.title: Heat-transition policy support: Policy design, material exposure, and municipal implementation capacity
items.abstract: Decarbonising residential heat requires policy packages that are technically effective, socially affordable, and democratically legitimate. Because heat is planned, financed, and contested at the scale of buildings, streets, and neighbourhoods, the decisive arena is municipal. Yet research rarely connects causal evidence on instrument design with households’ material exposure and locally grounded implementation capacities. The evidence is of three kinds and we separate them throughout. A randomised split-ballot experiment in the German Longitudinal Environmental Study (GLEN) identifies the causal effect of policy direction on stated support; linked housing and heating information supports associational and exploratory heterogeneity analyses, not causal moderation; and qualitative evidence from two German coal-transition regions identifies implementation mechanisms and carries no prevalence claim. Among 16,137 adults in the online panel, 64.8% supported public subsidies for converting heating systems to renewable energy, compared with 21.9% supporting a legal conversion mandate and 43.8% supporting repeal of conversion rules. These gaps remain nearly unchanged after covariate adjustment. Support for mandates was especially low among homeowners (16.0%) and, in an exploratory analysis using heating information measured after the experiment, among fossil-heated households (18.1%); low political trust and low climate concern strongly predicted regulatory rollback. Instrument response is also spatially and tenurially structured in ways directly usable by planners: mandate support reaches 25.3% in metropolitan regions but 16.5% in rural regions close to a city, falls to 11.9% among owner-occupiers with fossil heating and rises to 30.5% among tenants without fossil heating, and reaches 31.2% among households already connected to district heating. items.title: What can energy become? Energy-to-data and energy-to-material pathways for resource-rich economies
items.venue: Energy Sustainable Development/Energy for sustainable development
items.abstract: Resource-rich economies face competing uses of electricity, water, infrastructure and public finance. This article develops Energy-to-Value (ETV) as a bounded screening framework for Energy-to-Data (ETD) and Energy-to-Material (E2Mat) pathways. A structured narrative review distinguishes conversion outputs from development outcomes and financing conditions. Seven steps combine binding feasibility and safeguard conditions with a separate distributional dashboard. Reported data-centre efficiency, published cooling-model coefficients and ammonia-project specifications support illustrative calculations. For an assumed continuous 10 MW IT load, selected power usage effectiveness values imply 94.61–99.86 GWh of annual facility electricity. A hypothetical, location-neutral data-centre hosting candidate is defined in rack-months and assessed through all seven steps. Its baseline cooling coefficient implies 106,168 m 3 of annual onsite consumption against an assumed 100,000 m 3 cap. The water subtest fails within the declared scenario; unresolved engineering, distributional and delivery evidence makes the final action defer, with a separate redesign task. The calculated load ceiling is approximately 9.419 MW, not a verified operating limit. Three coefficients from one model provide sensitivity checks, not independent geographic validation. A 100 GWh allocation illustrates distinct opportunities in hosting, ammonia and desalinated water without asserting equivalent welfare. ETV contributes an explicit decision record with reproducible arithmetic, not a validated ranking model. Domestic capability, retained income and sustainable-development benefits require evidence beyond physical outputs and financing milestones.

items.title: SUSTAINABLE STRUCTURAL APPLICATIONS OF WASTE RUBBER, TEXTILE, AND CERAMIC MATERIALS IN THE CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW
items.venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive
items.abstract: The construction industry is one of the largest consumers of natural resources and significantly contributes to global waste generation, environmental degradation, and greenhouse gas emissions. This widespread impact primarily arises from the traditional linear "take-make-dispose" economic model, which accelerates resource depletion and creates pressing issues like overflowing landfills and ineffective waste treatment. To address these challenges, the circular economy (CE) model has gained traction by promoting the reduction, reuse, and recycling of materials as practical and sustainable alternatives. This transition is particularly crucial in construction, where early adoption of CE strategies can help reduce reliance on virgin materials and promote long-term environmental benefits. This paper examines key trends from the past decade related to the resistance of radical waste materials, specifically rubber, ceramics, and textiles, against effective recycling. It emphasizes the material characteristics and challenges these wastes present, highlighting the opportunities and barriers to integrating them into sustainable practices within the building and construction sector.

items.title: Digital pathways to circular economy adoption: the roles of digital innovation and open innovation
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores the contributions of digital capability, digital orientation and digital transformation towards digital innovation, open innovation and the circular economy adoption. Design/methodology/approach The study's framework is based on a rigorous literature review and underpinned by theories, i.e. the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capabilities theory. The study uses a quantitative design and collected data from managers, including strategic planning managers, research and development and innovation managers in the public and private energy/utilities sectors in Pakistan. The researchers used 332 useable sample size to infer the results. Findings The findings of the study demonstrate a positive effect of digital capability, digital orientation and digital transformation on digital innovation, circular economy adoption and open innovation. Digital innovation and open innovation also positively predict circular economy adoption. Finally, digital innovation and open innovation are found to be significant mediating constructs that link digital capability, digital orientation, digital transformation and circular economy adoption. Practical implications The findings provide practical guidelines for managers and policymakers by demonstrating that strengthening digital capabilities and fostering innovation can accelerate the adoption of the circular economy. These results can help organisations to prefer digital investments and innovation initiatives to enhance resource efficiency and circular operational practices. Originality/value This study extends the RBV and dynamic capabilities theory by explaining how organisational digital resources are transformed into circular economy adoption through the complementary mediating roles of digital innovation and open innovation. items.title: Do Circularity and Resource Productivity Tell the Same Story? EU-27 Evidence for Planetary Health Measurement, 2010–2024
items.abstract: Planetary health depends partly on reducing the scale and impacts of material extraction, yet headline circular-economy indicators can reward different processes. This study asks whether the circular material use rate (CMUR), which describes the share of material use supplied by recirculated materials, and resource productivity (RP), which describes economic output per unit of domestic material consumption (DMC), provide interchangeable signals across the EU-27. Official Eurostat observations for 2010 and 2024 were analysed using Pearson and Spearman correlations, Fisher-z and non-parametric bootstrap confidence intervals, exact common-component decompositions, leave-one-country-out tests, and separate analyses of endpoint-change magnitudes and directions. In 2024, CMUR and RP were positively associated (Pearson r = 0.685, 95% Fisher-z CI 0.412–0.845; Spearman ρ = 0.638). The DMC-variance term numerically equalled 63.0% of the observed transformed sample covariance, with wide bootstrap uncertainty (37.5–192.9%) but a narrower leave-one-country-out range (53.4–77.0%). By contrast, the association between 2010–2024 endpoint-change magnitudes was weak and imprecisely estimated (r = 0.163, 95% CI −0.231–0.511). Directional agreement was high descriptively: all 22 countries with higher CMURs also had higher RP, while four had lower CMURs but higher RP, and one declined on both measures. The indicators therefore illuminate complementary dimensions rather than a single transition pathway. For planetary health assessment, circularity and efficiency should be interpreted with absolute and consumption-based material pressure indicators; neither CMUR nor RP directly measures health outcomes or ecological sufficiency.

items.title: Circular economy strategies for high-rise buildings in developing countries: a review
items.abstract: Developing countries continue to progress toward more sustainable modes of operation in various sectors, particularly in the built environment. This emphasis is also prominent in high-rise buildings (HRBs), as these structures, although helpful for spatial optimisation, can be a major source of waste and environmental harm. Therefore, circular economy strategies (CESs) are becoming a primary focal point, both for researchers and professionals in practice. However, studies show that the emphasis remains on theory, as such strategies have yet to be seen in practice due to a number of factors. In response, this study conducts a semi-systematic literature review (SSLR) on this broad concept to synthesize insights from relevant papers on circular economy strategies in high-rise buildings in developing countries, highlighting its applicability, level of implementation, drivers and hindrances. After a filtering process, 67 papers met all eligibility criteria. 77.6% were published between 2022 and 2025, reflecting an increasing research interest. Only one paper out of the 67 included studies offered direct evidence on HRB-specific construction; all other included studies offered transferable evidence from the general construction sector. This suggests an under-exploration of HRB-specific CE research within built environment discourse. From the included studies, five key themes were identified: construction and demolition waste (CDW) recycling and management, the most discussed strategy; modular construction and prefabrication; Design for Disassembly (DfD) and circular design; material reuse systems; and integrated management and regenerative policy frameworks. HRB-specific empirical evidence showed an increase in waste of 29.3% in sites with weaker on-site supervision and routine discipline than in those with more controlled supervision. items.title: Show Me Your Circle! A Typology of Circular Economy Disclosure Strategies by Multinationals
items.abstract: The circular economy (CE) is featuring more prominently in emerging regulations, codes of best practice, and corporate policies. Yet, accounting research offers limited insight into how circularity is currently conceptualized and communicated in corporate reports. Consequently, this paper contributes to emergent CE accounting debates by developing and applying a framework assessing the content, mode, and integration of CE disclosures. The framework is applied to a longitudinal thematic content analysis of sustainability reports issued by 31 multinationals independently identified as CE champions. Doing so reveals substantial variation in CE reporting practices ranging from the provision of policy‐focused and generic detail to more performative and substantive reporting. Along this continuum are four CE reporting strategies: substantive implementation, targeted implementation, policy‐focused disclosure, and curtailed application. These findings add to the limited prior work on how CE is reported to investors and other stakeholders. They offer empirical insight into how new sustainability concepts are translated into corporate reporting practice with implications for standard‐setters and policymakers. The proposed framework will be a useful tool for investors, non‐government organizations and other stakeholders interested in evaluating the reporting on CE. It can also be readily modified to deal with other emerging forms of sustainability‐related reporting.

items.title: Mapping the urban policy sectors and resource circular economy landscape: Systematic literature review
items.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive systematic review of 121 scholarly publications from 2015 to 2025 to examine the development and implementation of circular economy (CE) policies in urban contexts. Using the Scopus database as the primary source, the research identifies three major policy sectors—Planning, Implementation, and Monitoring & Evaluation—supported by 10 resource management principles (10Rs: Refuse, Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Refurbish, Repurpose, Recycle, Recover/Renewable Energy, and Rot). Based on this 121-literature review, the identified cities that demonstrate strong circular economy (ES) practices through initiatives such as ES roadmaps, sustainable land use, financial and transportation planning, waste-to-energy technology, and education programs are cities in Europe and Asia. In contrast, African and South American cities show gradual but promising progress. Policies also involve private-sector regulations, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), and inclusive measures supporting informal actors such as waste pickers, highlighting the social dimension of CE. Monitoring and evaluation rely increasingly on innovative technologies and frameworks to ensure transparency and adaptability. Unlike previous studies that emphasize national or industrial levels, this research introduces novelty by framing CE strategies specifically for local and city governments, providing them with a structured overview of sectors and resources that must be integrated into urban sustainability policies. Overall, the study demonstrates that effective CE policies not only reduce waste and emissions but also foster economic opportunities, social equity, and long-term resilience, making them essential instruments for achieving sustainable urban development.

items.title: Beyond Transparency: Governing Visibility–Opacity Tensions in Circular Supply Chains
items.abstract: Circular supply chains are widely promoted as mechanisms of environmental regeneration, yet they generate a fundamental and underexplored operational tension: The same processes that require high levels of material transparency also create strong incentives for strategic information concealment. Circular supply chain research has predominantly emphasized the benefits of transparency and traceability, while adjacent research on alliances, coopetition, and knowledge protection recognizes that firms must also protect commercially sensitive information. What remains insufficiently explained is how this sharing–protection tension becomes embedded in circular supply chain operations, where the same lifecycle and recovery information can be simultaneously necessary for coordination and commercially appropriate. To address this gap, this study examines how firms manage the visibility–opacity tension through operational supply chain management (OSCM) processes. Drawing on a qualitative multiple‐case study of 32 US manufacturing firms and approximately 80 semistructured interviews, we identify three distinct tension‐management logics. Selective disclosure sequencing governs the timing and recipients of information across the partner lifecycle. Boundary‐anchored opacity recurrently reproduces comparatively stable information boundaries through institutionalized access restrictions. Adaptive transparency recalibration involves ongoing adjustment of disclosure practices in response to changing market and regulatory conditions. Collectively, these logics reveal distinct operational implications and trade‐offs that informants associate with different forms of visibility–opacity governance, particularly regarding coordination, protection of commercially sensitive knowledge, and responsiveness to changing conditions. items.title: Implementing circular manufacturing systems: A value lifecycle view on digital technology-enabled mechanisms
items.abstract: The manufacturing sector is navigating a twin transition driven by simultaneous sustainability mandates and rapid technological advancements. While digital technologies (DTs) are recognized as enablers of circular manufacturing systems (CMS), original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) lack a structured approach to systematically deploy DTs to implement CMS. Existing digitalization frameworks remain technology-centric, treating DTs in isolation rather than situating them within a lifecycle-wide view of value. Consequently, DT deployment remains fragmented rather than spanning all five phases of the value lifecycle view (value creation, value delivery, value use, value recovery, and value re-creation). This leaves the systemic value of coordinated digitalization unrealized in the context of CMS. Accordingly, this study addresses two research questions: how DTs contribute to value creation, delivery, use, recovery and re-creation in the implementation of CMS and how OEMs can systemically deploy DTs to implement CMS. This study performs a semi-systematic narrative review of 87 articles, identified through the PRISMA method from Scopus and Web of Science databases, coding them against the value lifecycle phases and DTs and applying thematic analysis to identify 13 DT enabled mechanisms to implement CMS. Their dependencies are then organized across six data transformation levels. The findings reveal that the DTs, mechanisms, and value lifecycle phases are systemically interdependent rather than related through one-to-one correspondence, with CMS guiding DT deployment. Building on these findings, this study proposes a digitalization guideline that supports OEMs in sequencing and coordinating DT deployment across the value lifecycle to implement CMS.

items.title: Evaluation of preschools in terms of sustainability: The case of Erzincan
items.abstract: This study aims to evaluate the sustainability practices of preschools in Erzincan within the 7R framework (Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Respect, Recycle). A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was adopted, with quantitative and qualitative data collected simultaneously. In nine preschools selected through purposive sampling, structured observations were conducted using the 7R Sustainability Observation and Interview Form developed by the researchers, and semi-structured interviews were conducted with administrators and teachers. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while the qualitative data were analyzed through deductive content analysis. Findings revealed that the overall level of sustainability practices in the preschools was moderate; the preschools exhibited relatively strong performance in the Recycle, Respect, and Rethink themes, whereas they displayed weak performance in the Repair, Refuse, and Reduce themes. This pattern indicates that the waste hierarchy operates in reverse and that practices are largely activity-based nature dependent on teacher initiative. Socio-cultural and environmental dimensions of sustainability were relatively strong, while the economic dimension was neglected. Preschools included in certification programs exhibited higher performance; however, certification was discussed as remaining limited in transforming the culture of consumption. Consequently, sustainability should be supported through institutional policy, green procurement strategies, and professional development

items.title: Planning for place-based circularity in mid-sized industrial cities: Accommodating industrial-scale and vernacular food waste trajectories
items.abstract: There is growing recognition of the tension between industrial/top-down and vernacular/bottom-up circular economies, as well as the need for place-based approaches to sustainable transitions policy. Yet how to reconcile place-based policy with divergent forms of circularity remains unclear. Rather than viewing such tensions as requiring resolution, we examine the place-based conditions under which industrial-scale and vernacular food waste trajectories can productively coexist, and the conditions under which they cannot. Mid-sized industrial cities (MSICs) are a favourable setting for coexisting forms of place-based circularity, yet they are often overlooked in circular economy research, despite being tasked with managing the heavy, polluting, and industrial metabolic functions upon which larger metropolitan regions depend. Drawing upon longitudinal research over a 15-year period in an exemplary MSIC – Wollongong, NSW, Australia – this article develops a framework of intersecting circularities foregrounding the co-constitution of place-based circularity and city context. Applying this framework reveals the sociomaterial qualities of circularities, the spatial reconfigurations that enable them, and the co-presence of industrial, top-down and smaller-scale vernacular approaches. From multiple qualitative research projects, we outline three drivers of place-based circularity: diverse and flexible land-use planning and zoning; logistical infrastructures that support proximity of actors; and innovative and resourced consumer engagement with food waste’s visceralities. We argue that MSICs offer distinctive sociomaterialities for hybrid circularities, that are not captured by centralised governance and planning models, nor grassroots sufficiency. Realising the potential for place-based approaches in MSICs demands acknowledgement of the regulatory, material and cultural pre-conditions that make circularity possible.

items.title: Pathways and Benefits of Industrial Green Transition from the Perspective of Circular Economy and Resource Efficiency Economics
items.abstract: Facing global resource scarcity and China’s dual‑carbon goals, this paper explores coupling mechanisms between circular economy and resource efficiency economics to identify multi‑level industrial green transition pathways. Using embedded multiple‑case study and entropy‑weight method, we analyse three Chinese cases: a chemical park, an agricultural cooperative and Haiyan Economic‑Technological Development Zone. Results indicate circular‑economy practices raise park solid‑waste utilization to 99 %, achieve 100 % straw utilization, and reduce carbon emission intensity by 22‑25 %. Theoretically, this study integrates industrial‑ecology perspectives to develop a cross‑domain coupling framework complementing prior reviews. Practically, multi‑level actionable pathways for enterprises, parks, regions and policymakers are provided. Findings are constrained by limited empirical evidence only from successful eastern‑China cases.

items.title: I nuovi spazi del planner. Come le nuove sfide ambientali, sociali e tecnologiche stanno influenzando i cambiamenti della pianificazione territoriale
items.abstract: In recent decades, reflections on planning have centred on the discipline’s fields, methods and techniques, and teaching, particularly in relation to its many dualisms (planning-urban planning, planning-design, etc.). Recognising planning’s expansive nature and the planner’s meta-technical and discursive capacity to transcend the boundaries of strictly disciplinary knowledge, this paper combines a literature review with a qualitative and quantitative exploration—including analysis of texts and textual clusters using Iramuteq—of prevailing approaches in Italian academia. The study begins with an examination of all research grants awarded in the two Scientific Disciplinary Sectors (SSD), ICAR20 Urban Planning and Techniques and ICAR21 Urban Planning, between 2023 and 2025. Reflections on the disciplinary evolution were conducted, taking into account the topics covered over the three-year period, in the SSDs, at universities, and at departments.

items.title: EPR Policy and Corporate Servitisation Transformation: Motivations, Barriers and Pathways
items.venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
items.abstract: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is increasingly seen as a policy tool to encourage businesses to adopt servitisation and support the circular economy. However, how EPR affects business model transformation remains under-researched. This paper addresses the question of whether and under what conditions EPR promotes servitisation. This study draws on institutional theory to develop an analytical framework in which EPR generates cost internalisation pressures and is influenced by product characteristics, firm capabilities, market conditions and policy design. The framework is tested through a comparative case study of Philips Lighting in the Netherlands and shared laundry services by Chinese appliance firms. The findings suggest that EPR incentivises servitisation when policies are well designed and aligned with favourable conditions, while weak EPR makes servitisation an additional cost burden. Linking institutional theory to research on circular business models, this study offers recommendations for improved policy design.

items.title: From Ad Hoc to Systemic Circular Construction: Evidence of a Legislative Bottleneck in an Emerging Economy
items.abstract: Circular economy adoption in construction is often examined through static barrier taxonomies, which offer limited explanation for fragmented implementation in emerging markets. Drawing on Institutional Theory and the Multi-Level Perspective (MLP), this exploratory study examines whether stakeholder perceived legislative and institutional barriers are associated with phase-specific circular economy (CE) adoption in Oman. A cross-sectional survey of 114 specialized construction experts was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), hierarchical regression, and multi-categorical mediation analysis across twelve circular strategies spanning design, construction, and end-of-life phases. Descriptive results indicate moderate, uneven circularity: design-for-adaptability scored highest ( M = 3.52) versus selective demolition ( M = 2.96). PLS-SEM point estimates indicate perceived regulatory and institutional barriers show a weak, non-significant association with design-phase adoption ( β = -0.12, p = 0.180), a stronger negative association with construction-phase adoption ( β = -0.29, p = 0.002), and the largest negative association with end-of-life implementation ( β = -0.47, p < 0.001), consistent with a legislative bottleneck concentrated at the end-of-life stage rather than intensifying uniformly across the project lifecycle. A supplementary mediation analysis points to a contractor-specific indirect effect through perceived legislative barriers ( β = -0.22, 95% CI [-0.42, -0.06]), suggesting a stakeholder-specific mechanism rather than a generalized effect. items.title: Circular Economy: Exploring the Adoption of Second-Hand Items on Peer-to-Peer E-Commerce Platforms in Nigeria
items.venue: Turkish Journal of Fashion Design and Management
items.abstract: The rising global emphasis on sustainability has brought the circular economy model into sharp focus, promoting reuse, recycling, and resource regeneration to reduce waste and environmental harm. This study investigates the adoption of second-hand items on peer-to-peer (P2P) e-commerce platforms in Nigeria as a means of entrenching circular economy practices. Specifically, it explores demographic influences and consumer motivations shaping recommerce, a growing trend of reselling pre-loved items online. Using a quantitative approach, data were collected from 500 respondents via structured questionnaires. Descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-square tests, were employed to analyze the relationship between demographic variables and second-hand item adoption, and to determine whether factors such as environmental awareness, perceived value, trust, and social reasons significantly influence adoption decisions. The findings offer practical insights for e-commerce platform designers, policymakers, and sustainability advocates. By targeting key demographic groups and emphasizing platform-wide values such as affordability, trust, and eco-consciousness, recommerce platforms in Nigeria can scale adoption and contribute meaningfully to circular economy goals. The study underscores the untapped potential of P2P e-commerce in Nigeria as a catalyst for sustainable consumption and waste reduction.

items.title: Nano-Enabled Circular Economy Approaches for Restoring Oil Contaminated Ecosystems
items.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
items.abstract: This study investigates the integration of nano-enabled technologies within circular economy strategies to remediate oil-contaminated ecosystems. By synthesizing current literature and empirical data from oil-impacted sites in the Absheron Peninsula, Azerbaijan, the study evaluates the efficiency, sustainability, and economic viability of nanomaterial-assisted remediation techniques. The study collated secondary data on soil contamination, application of nanomaterials, and waste management practices while comparative analysis was done for environmental and economic outcomes. The critical messages communicated are that deployment of nanotechnology with circularity such as waste valorization, resource recovery, and bio-based recycling enhances efficiency of hydrocarbon degradation by up to 85%, while the remediation cost is lower than that of conventional methods, and results in lower risks to the environment. The use of these approaches is strongly influenced by the policy and governance frameworks in place, with regulatory barriers and market readiness being cited as important. The researchers conclude that using circular strategies enabled by nanomaterials can help clean up soil contamination, as well as contribute to the goals of sustainable development. Further, it can be replicated in oil-producing regions around the world. To strengthen policy incentives, invest in nanotechnology research and incorporate circular economy indicators into environmental governance. This research contributes to knowledge by linking advanced nanomaterials with practical circular economy approaches, offering a novel framework for sustainable oil spill management.
