items.title: Integrating Circular Carbon Economy into Waste Bank Supply Chains: An Analysis of Collaborative Networks and Net-Zero Strategies in Surabaya City
items.venue: TOFEDU The Future of Education Journal
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the integration of the circular carbon economy into waste bank supply chains and to formulate an Integrated Circular Carbon Economy (ICCE) framework for net-zero strategies in Surabaya City. A descriptive qualitative research method was employed, utilizing a literature-based approach focused on 15 key journals covering waste banks, the circular economy, the circular carbon economy, circular supply chains, and social network analysis; additional publicly available references were used to provide supporting information. Data were analyzed through cross-journal comparison, thematic grouping, and synthesis into an integrative framework. The results indicate that (1) the waste bank supply chain flow comprises households, waste banks, collectors, and the recycling industry; (2) the collaborative network structure among stakeholders remains fragmented and relies heavily on collectors and the Environmental Agency; (3) the most prominent "9R" practices are R3 (Reuse) and R8 (Recycle), whereas R0–R2 (Refuse, Rethink, Reduce) practices are minimal; and (4) the circular carbon economy concept encompasses elements such as emission reduction and carbon credits, yet major obstacles persist regarding Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) mechanisms and the institutional capacity of waste management entities. Managerial and policy implications are discussed to accelerate net-zero strategies within the waste management sector.

items.title: A Risk Assessment Framework for Circular Value Chains in the Chemical Industry
items.abstract: The transition to a circular economy in the chemical industry generates not only resource efficiency gains but also new economic and criminological risks. This article adopts an analytical framework to examine the circular value chain and the windows of criminological opportunities of its stages, in conjunction with associated economic risks. This article is positioned as a conceptual study based on theoretical analysis of the literature and analytical reasoning. The analytical tool employed was conceptual modelling of a circular value chain for a chemical enterprise, utilising Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0, followed by the overlay of two distinct groups of markers onto the business process architecture: criminological windows and economic risks. The causal analysis yields findings indicating that economic risks (information asymmetry, transaction costs, quality uncertainty of secondary materials, and coordination failures) are closely intertwined with criminological risks arising from inadequate traceability, fragmented accountability, and regulatory gaps. These factors mutually reinforce one another and shape the behaviour of participants across the circular chain. This leads to the conclusion that economic and criminological risks in circular value chains ought to be analysed conjointly, as they are driven by shared institutional and behavioural determinants. For the chemical sector, effective circularity demands not only technological transformation but also risk-sensitive governance, enhanced traceability, and a clearer allocation of responsibility among actors.

Therefore, with increased production, the likelihood of inefficient resource use and waste generation is higher and has to be sustainably managed. Enterprise interviews were conducted with 53 fruit-processing Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) in the Nairobi metropolitan area (Nairobi, Kiambu, Kajiado, and Machakos counties) identified through a multistage sampling approach. On average, enterprises adopted 4.2 out of 9 possible CP practices, indicating moderate uptake. Six key factors were significantly associated with higher CP adoption (p < 0.05). Enterprises aware of CP concepts adopted significantly more practices than those unaware (4.6 vs. 0.0, p < 0.001), demonstrating that knowledge is foundational, and enterprises reporting no compliance challenges scored higher than those facing challenges (4.6 vs. 2.7, p = 0.004), indicating that barriers hinder progress. The adoption of cleaner production (CP) practices among fruit processing SMEs faces multiple barriers, including policy implementation challenges, technological and financial constraints, and capacity gaps. Transformational leadership with a clear vision and collaborative approach across the value chain was identified as a key enabler to help minimize the bureaucratic processes hindering compliance. Financial incentives by the government, such as subsidies on cleaner production technologies, would be useful in the adoption process. SMEs still require training and capacity-building opportunities to enhance their institutional capacity to adopt the cleaner production concept. items.title: Economia Circular Como Paradigma Econômico: Fundamentos, Escolas de Pensamento e Desafios Contemporâneos
items.abstract: A Economia Circular (EC) emerge como alternativa ao modelo linear de produção e consumo, que se mostra insustentável diante da escassez de recursos naturais e da crescente geração de resíduos. Este artigo apresenta revisão integrativa da literatura sobre os fundamentos da EC, destacando precedentes históricos, princípios e principais escolas de pensamento, como a Ecologia Industrial e o Cradle-to-Cradle, que moldaram as três eras (1.0, 2.0 e 3.0) de sua evolução conceitual. A partir de corpus documental definitivo de 22 obras selecionadas por critérios de inclusão e exclusão nas bases Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar e repositórios institucionais, discutem-se os modelos de negócio circulares (servitização, compartilhamento, recuperação de recursos, prolongamento da durabilidade e suprimentos circulares), os “Rs” da circularidade e o impacto das recentes diretrizes internacionais da série ISO 59000 lançadas em 2024, que consolidam diretrizes globais alinhadas à Agenda 2030 da ONU. A análise evidencia tanto as oportunidades, como ecoinovação, competitividade e impacto social, quanto os desafios, incluindo ambiguidades conceituais, barreiras institucionais e resistências culturais. O estudo ressalta a relevância da EC como paradigma econômico capaz de alinhar crescimento, inovação e sustentabilidade diante dos desafios contemporâneos.

items.title: Sustainable Cities and Plastic Waste: Innovation and Organizational Model of an Applied Case in Brazil
items.abstract: This article analyzes partnerships among the public sector, private companies, and waste pickers/cooperatives in urban plastic waste management, in light of the sustainable cities concept, assessing the economic, social, and environmental impacts of a reverse logistics arrangement involving schools and associations in southern Brazil and questioning its replicability and effectiveness. The methodology consisted of action research, with five years of data collection (2019–2024), combining document analysis, quantitative impact indicators, and qualitative discussion in light of theories of sustainable cities, circular economy, and associative models. The arrangement links a packaging industry, social collection entities, schools, and an independent technical verifier. Between 2019 and 2024, the model recycled 4.2 million PET bottles, benefited more than 60 schools and entities, reached more than 50,000 people, and transferred more than R$200,000 (≈US$40,000) to schools and recyclers, generating estimated savings of R$600,000 (≈US$120,000), with reductions of 152,000 kg CO2eq, 90,440 L of petroleum, 229,694 kWh, and 600,000 L of water, and up to a 100% reduction in waste compared with regular selective collection. The results indicate that this traceable model, anchored in environmental education and independent verification, can boost the local economy; whether and how it can be replicated in other cities remains a question for future comparative research rather than a claim established by this single case.

items.title: СУТНІСТЬ ТА РОЛЬ ТРАНСПОРТНО-ЦИРКУЛЯРНОГО ХАБУ В ПАРАДИГМІ СТАЛОГО РОЗВИТКУ
items.abstract: У статті розкрито сутність транспортно-циркулярного хабу як самостійної економічної категорії, що виникає на перетині теорії транспортних вузлів і концепції циркулярної економіки. Систематизовано наукові підходи до трактування категорії «хаб», зокрема просторово-мережевий, локаційно-математичний, портово-економічний, нормативно-інституційний, логістично-функціональний, інфраструктурний, комерційний та економіко-логістичний. Еволюція зазначених підходів у поєднанні з поширенням принципів сталого розвитку зумовила формування нового бачення функціонування хабів, орієнтованого не лише на ефективність переміщення та концентрації матеріальних потоків, а й на ресурсозбереження, мінімізацію відходів, повторне використання ресурсів і зниження негативного впливу на довкілля. Розвиток такого сталого підходу до функціонування хабів створює передумови для виникнення нової економічної категорії − «транспортно-циркулярний хаб», що поєднує транспортно-логістичні функції з принципами циркулярної економіки. Обґрунтовано якісну відмінність транспортно-циркулярного хабу від традиційного транспортного хабу, що полягає в інтеграції функції відновлення вартості матеріальних потоків до основного циклу діяльності вузла, забезпечуючи зниження ресурсоємності транспортної діяльності та підвищення конкурентоспроможності транспортного комплексу. Сформульовано авторське визначення категорії «транспортно-циркулярний хаб», а також виокремлено сукупність сутнісних ознак останнього: поліфункціональність, зворотність матеріальних потоків, інституційну вбудованість, мережеву відкритість, ресурсну ефективність та екосистемний характер взаємодії учасників. Визначено роль транспортно-циркулярного хабу у формуванні стійких ланцюгів постачання та забезпеченні ефективного використання ресурсів. items.title: Circular economy and macroeconomic performance: a comparison of Central and Western European EU countries
items.venue: Journal of Business Economics and Management
items.abstract: In the context of the growing importance of sustainable development and efficient resource utilization, the circular economy (CE) is becoming a key component of economic policy in EU countries. In the present study, the dependencies of selected CE indicators on three key macroeconomic variables were modelled across two distinct groups of European countries, specifically the Central European bloc (Slovakia, Poland, Czechia) and the Western European bloc (Austria, Switzerland, Germany). Agility captures the responsiveness of CE performance to macroeconomic conditions. To quantify these relationships, multiple linear regression was applied, enabling the assessment of the sensitivity of CE performance to macroeconomic dynamics characterized by GDP per capita, population size, and employment rate. The results provide comparative insights into how structural economic conditions influence progress toward a CE, defined by the recycling rate and the development of domestic material consumption within the examined country blocs. The findings highlight clear structural differences between the two blocs, with Western Europe demonstrating more mature and efficiency driven environmental performance, while Central Europe exhibits features of an economy in transition. The findings advance the understanding of the macroeconomic determinants of CE performance and underscore the need for policies that translate economic growth into measurable environmental efficiency gains.

items.title: Design Strategies and Solutions for Circularity Across the Building Lifecycle
items.venue: SpringerBriefs in applied sciences and technology
items.abstract: The built environment is one of the most resource-intensive sectors globally, yet progress towards circularity remains constrained by fragmented implementation, limited lifecycle integration, and insufficient governance frameworks. This chapter examines design strategies and solutions for circularity across the entire building lifecycle, drawing on a systematic comparative analysis of 45 international case studies. Using a matrix-based analytical framework, circular strategies are mapped across six dimensions: design for circularity, materials and products, construction practices, building operations and maintenance, end-of-life and deconstruction, and business models and policy support, and aligned with the 10R circular economy hierarchy. The findings reveal a clear concentration of circular maturity at the design and material levels, with strategies such as adaptability, flexibility, design for disassembly, and low-carbon material selection widely present across the dataset. In contrast, operational circularity, advanced end-of-life planning, digital traceability, and enabling business models remain significantly underdeveloped in mainstream practice. Cross-case analysis identifies five building clusters and six transferable circular design patterns, ranging from reuse-first approaches and design for disassembly as a system, to procurement-driven circularity and use-based strategies. The evidence consistently demonstrates that high circular performance is achieved through integrated, multi-lifecycle-stage approaches rather than isolated interventions. Policy and practice recommendations are derived directly from the pattern analysis, targeting design regulation, public procurement, operational management, and end-of-life governance. items.title: Scanvas: Discovering and Developing Synergistic Opportunities in Generative Design Spaces
items.abstract: Good design is often synergistic, creating super-additive value by linking goals so that existing resources produce greater outcomes. However, finding these synergistic opportunities in sparse design spaces is difficult, and current LLM-supported ideation tools largely default to additive paradigms such as feature blending, variant generation, or local patching. We present Scanvas, an AI-supported system for systematically discovering and developing synergistic design opportunities. Scanvas operationalizes synergy through a two-step computational process: first, it decomposes seed ideas into explicit properties (components, behaviors, surpluses, and issues) to enrich the design space; second, it systematically searches across enriched ideas using three theory-grounded strategy operators: unlocking or strengthening goals, turning weaknesses into resources, and sharing components across functions. We instantiate Scanvas as an auto-generation pipeline and an interactive system. Pipeline ablations and a user study with 12 professional designers demonstrate that Scanvas enables users to surface and develop significantly higher-quality, synergistic concepts compared to LLM ideation baselines.

items.title: An Integrated Conceptual Model of Recommerce in the Circular Economy
items.abstract: This study explores recommerce as a key mechanism within the circular economy (CE) supporting sustainable development. Although the exchange of second-hand goods (SHG) has existed for centuries, its business processes, market structure, and principal components remain insufficiently systematized. Designed as a conceptual paper, the research employs a literature analysis to identify the defining characteristics of SHG, examine the role of product re-use within the CE, analyse the principal actors, business processes, market channels, and implementation challenges, and develop an integrated model of recommerce. The findings demonstrate that recommerce creates economic, environmental, and social value by extending product life, improving resource efficiency, reducing consumer expenditure, generating new business opportunities, and promoting sustainable consumption. The proposed integrated conceptual model brings together the definition, process, market structure, implementation challenges, and key interrelationships of recommerce into a unified framework, explaining the relationships among its principal drivers, inputs, business processes, market channels, and long-term outcomes. The proposed model provides practical implications for retailers, policymakers, and researchers, establishes a theoretical foundation for future empirical research supporting circularity and sustainable development, and requires further validation across different industries and national contexts.

items.title: How do the different levels of governance appropriate the circular economy? A topic modelling analysis of French public policy discourse
items.venue: Journal of Environmental Planning and Management
items.abstract: Over the past decade, the circular economy (CE) has become a central reference in environmental and industrial policy. Yet despite its institutional ubiquity, global circularity rates continue to decline. This article argues that public policy discourse itself contributes to this paradox. Using topic modelling on approximately 2,500 institutional documents from four governance levels in France between 2015 and 2025, we identify three interlocking disconnects. A discursive gap stems from structured thematic differentiation across European, national, regional, and metropolitan levels, where institutions mobilise distinct, and sometimes incompatible, visions of circularity. An operational disconnect follows, as coherent policy coordination becomes structurally difficult. A metrological gap emerges as the foundational 4 R framing declines sharply after 2017, giving way to innovation and strategic governance themes, while thematic diversity increases consistently across all levels. This discursive shift is not incidental but constitutive of the paradox itself.

A integração das premissas da sustentabilidade nas dimensões econômica, social e ambiental é fundamental para a obtenção de vantagens competitivas e impactos positivos na sociedade. Contribuições teóricas: Proposição de um framework de Modelos de Negócios Sustentáveis que evidencia, de forma integrada, as premissas da sustentabilidade na criação, entrega e reprodução de valor sustentável. Contribuições sociais e de gestão: A aplicação empírica do framework pode contribuir para a identificação e análise de modelos de negócios regionais e seus impactos e benefícios nas organizações e na sociedade. items.title: Intelligent Governance of Complex Social Systems: A Hybrid AI–System Dynamics Model for the Simulation and Projection of Sustainable Energy Transition
items.abstract: Amidst growing uncertainty regarding global sustainable development goals and the increasing complexity of social systems, accurately characterizing long-term transition processes driven by the interactions of multiple agents and factors remains a critical challenge. Using China’s energy transition toward carbon neutrality as a proof-of-concept case, this paper constructs a bidirectional coupling framework based on a hybrid Artificial Intelligence–System Dynamics (AI-SD) approach. Within this framework, an axiomatic SD formal system imposes hard constraints on the nonlinear learning processes of the AI, while the nonlinear corrections generated by the AI feed back to modify the system dynamics structure, thereby establishing an iterative cycle of structural constraints, data-driven corrections, and re-imposed structural constraints. Simulation results demonstrate that the hybrid AI-SD model exhibits good comprehensive adaptability in historical fitting and long-term scenario extrapolation, preserving the system feedback structure while characterizing certain nonlinear and time-delay features. The multi-policy synergy scenario, under the conditions set in this paper, shows a high cumulative emission reduction level and exhibits a relatively coordinated characteristic between emission reduction effects and comprehensive social costs. Model-based sensitivity and attribution analyses indicate that, within the defined parameter space, cumulative technology investment and energy cost conditions are associated with higher model output sensitivity; the contribution of carbon pricing shows a certain scenario dependence. This study provides a computable axiomatic framework for the deep integration of mechanistic models and data-driven approaches, and offers theoretical reference for long-term energy governance and complex system decision optimization under deep uncertainty.

items.title: Portfolio-Level Material and Carbon Hotspot Screening for Circular-Economy Prioritisation in Flood-Risk Infrastructure
items.abstract: Infrastructure organisations must reduce carbon emissions, improve resource efficiency, and maintain service performance across large ageing asset portfolios. However, circular-economy interventions in infrastructure are often organised around individual projects, limiting understanding of where material and carbon impacts accumulate at portfolio level. This paper develops a top-down portfolio-level modelling approach to support circular-economy prioritisation in flood-risk management infrastructure. The study integrates public asset-register data with organisational carbon and material-flow datasets to identify lifecycle, asset, and material hotspots across a distributed infrastructure portfolio. Using 415 asset-level carbon records and 5486 material-level records, the analysis estimates whole-life carbon distribution across asset classes and maps material inflows across material–asset combinations. The findings reveal a strong concentration effect: a small number of lifecycle stages, asset types, and materials account for a disproportionate share of portfolio-level impacts. Replacement carbon emerges as a major whole-life contributor, while walls, embankments, and channels dominate asset-level emissions, given the organization context. At the material level, soil/clay, steel, concrete, and stone represent key hotspots, showing that circular-economy strategies should address both high-carbon materials and high-material mass earthworks. The paper contributes a portfolio-level screening approach that shifts circular-economy analysis from project-level optimisation to portfolio-level prioritisation.

items.title: Raising Awareness of the Circular Economy Among SMEs in Emerging Economies: Evidence from an Experiential Learning Activity in Brazil
items.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are central to any meaningful circular economy (CE) transition, yet they remain the segment least served by CE education and engagement initiatives. Lack of awareness, rather than lack of incentives, is increasingly recognized as the binding constraint on SME uptake of circular practices. This paper examines the Circular Experience, an experiential learning activity developed by Movimento Circular in partnership with SEBRAE, the Brazilian national SME support agency. Drawing on mixed-method data from three activity editions held in 2025, this research analyses the effects of the immersive sessions on 108 participants' self-reported CE knowledge and interest. Pre- and post-session survey data document a 64 percentage-point gain in participants reporting high or very high self-assessed CE knowledge and a 33 percentage-point increase in high or very high CE interest. Qualitative evidence, including spontaneous word-association responses and participant testimonials, documents a concurrent shift in how participants conceptualise CE, from recycling-centered framings toward opportunity and business-model-centered ones. Because all outcome measures are self-reported and were collected immediately after a self-selected activity, the gains are interpreted as changes in perceived knowledge and interest rather than in objectively tested competence. The activity achieved a Net Promoter Score of 91, and all respondents across the three geographic contexts reported that their expectations had been met. These results bear on the assumption that meaningful cognitive change requires prolonged intervention, and they offer an applied model of scalable public-private CE education applicable to other emerging economy settings.

items.abstract: У статті досліджено еволюцію та якісну трансформацію сучасної транспортно-логістичної інфраструктури в умовах цифровізації та поширення концепції сталого розвитку. Обґрунтовано періодизацію розвитку транспортно-логістичних хабів, що комплексно охоплює п’ять послідовних поколінь. Перше покоління представлене традиційними локальними вузлами перевалки вантажів; друге − базується на логістичній інтеграції, комерціалізації та мультимодальності; третє − характеризується глобальною мережевою моделлю та високою вбудованістю в міжнародні транспортні коридори; четверте − безпосередньо пов’язане з масштабною цифровою трансформацією. П’яте покоління постає як синтетична багатофункціональна циркулярна екосистема, яка гармонійно об’єднує екологічні, економічні та соціальні цілі із замкненими регенеративними циклами ресурсокористування. Обґрунтовано концепт транспортно-циркулярного хабу як якісно нового утворення п’ятого покоління, що володіє унікальними адаптивними властивостями. Зроблено висновок, що еволюція хабів відбувається не шляхом лінійної заміни застарілих технологій, а через нелінійне послідовне розширення функціонального призначення вузла на основі конвергенції процесів діджиталізації та сталого розвитку. Розкрито зміну функціонального застосування цифрових технологій при переході від класичного цифрового до транспортно-циркулярного хабу: якщо на четвертому етапі діджитал-інструменти застосовуються переважно для автоматизації й оптимізації прямих вантажопотоків, то на п’ятому − вони трансформуються у ключовий каталізатор управління зворотними матеріальними потоками, повторним використанням, відновленням та регенерацією ресурсів у межах економіки замкненого циклу. Визначено, що складні умови повоєнної відбудови національного транспортного комплексу України створюють передумови для реалізації еволюційного стрибка через проміжні фази розвитку. Це стає можливим за рахунок синергетичного впровадження інноваційних цифрових і циркулярних рішень безпосередньо на початковому ет

items.title: Implementation Effectiveness of Circular Economy Practices on Medical Devices Industry of Indonesia: A Case Study of PT Kimia Farma Tbk and PT Kalbe Farma Tbk (2020-2022)
items.abstract: Indonesia medical device industry experienced significant acceleration during COVID-19 pandemic era (2020-2022), marked by significant increased of demand that challenging conventional manufacturing best practices. This period also witnessed heightened motivation from both government and industry to reduce national dependence on imports. This situation has spurred industry participants to adopt circular economy practices as a more efficient and effective alternative approach. This research employed qualitative analysis of official sustainability reports of PT Kimia Farma Tbk and PT Kalbe Farma Tbk for the period 2020 to 2022. The objective was to examine implementation of circular economy principles into national medical device industry as a regenerative approach that maximizes value of manufacturing resources. This research identified variety of positive outcomes following the implementation of circular economy practices. These outcomes demonstrate significant transformative change, evidenced by waste reduction, material recycling and resource efficiency. These changes are indicative of positive impact of circular economy practices on both the company's performance specifically and medical device industry in general. The significant contribution of circular economy practices has enhanced the resilience of national medical device industry, improved resource efficiency, reduced negative environmental impact of industrial activities, supporting both economic and ecological sustainability. This research offers new insights into strategic decision-making and can serve as reference for future empirical studies on how to maximize the sustainable productivity of national medical device industry.

items.title: The circular economy, explained by AI
items.abstract: Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the circular economy (CE) has largely examined how AI can improve circular operations. Much less attention has been paid to AI tools widely used to understand and reason about the CE, particularly large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Yet researchers, practitioners, students, and decision-makers use these tools to seek explanations and support reasoning about circularity. This paper examines what is at stake when LLM-generated accounts enter CE inquiry. As a conceptual contribution, it develops a framework for analysing how AI-supported CE knowledge is formed, how it may influence action, and what ethical implications follow. The Content dimension concerns the construction and credibility of CE knowledge, focusing on pattern-based generation, opaque and heterogeneous sources, and fragmentation within CE scholarship. The Transformative dimension considers how such knowledge may influence innovation and entrepreneurship, including whether familiar, optimisation-oriented approaches overshadow systemic alternatives. The Moral dimension addresses the risks of relying on LLM outputs, including operational indifference to truth, AI assertiveness, the absence of moral agency, and the need for human judgement and accountability. The paper argues that LLMs can widen access to CE knowledge and support inquiry, but cannot independently determine which interpretations are better supported, exercise the judgement required to challenge linear assumptions, or decide how environmental, social, and economic values should be balanced. It identifies governance priorities concerning transparency, expert scrutiny, human agency, and epistemic humility. The framework can also guide future empirical research on how LLM-generated accounts vary across models, prompts, languages, and user contexts.

items.title: Sustainability knowledge capability in infrastructure projects: linking sustainable operations, leadership innovation and operational transformation
items.abstract: Construction organisations increasingly adopt sustainable technologies, process controls and formal policies, yet temporary project arrangements can fragment what teams learn. This study examines sustainability knowledge capability (SKC) as an organisational capability associated with sustainable leadership innovation capability (SLIC) and sustainability transformation ability (STA), while testing digital readiness (DR) as a boundary condition. We analysed survey data from 355 infrastructure-project professionals in Indonesia using PLS-SEM, bootstrapped indirect-effect and interaction tests, predictive assessment, common-method diagnostics and endogeneity sensitivity checks. Technical practices, operational processes and organisational structures each showed positive associations with SKC. SKC showed strong positive associations with SLIC and STA, and the tests supported all six specific indirect effects through SKC. DR showed substantial lower-order associations with both outcomes, while its incremental interaction effects remained small. These cross-sectional findings support a capability-conversion interpretation but do not establish temporal ordering or causation. They indicate that organisations benefit when they retain, retrieve and reuse sustainability experience, while digital readiness complements rather than substitutes for those knowledge routines.

items.title: What is the upper-bound circularity performance of wind turbine blade recycling? A comparative assessment of mechanical, thermal, and chemical routes under current and optimised conditions
items.abstract: The rapid deployment of wind energy is creating an end-of-life challenge for wind turbine blades (WTBs), whose large size and composite structure constrain recycling and material recovery. Existing studies compare WTB recycling technologies but rarely estimate upper-bound circularity performance under explicit technological, material-quality and substitution conditions. This study evaluates the upper-bound circularity performance of mechanical, thermal and chemical recycling and examines whether approaching these conditions yields environmental and economic benefits. Environmental Footprint-based life cycle assessment is combined with the Product Circularity Indicator (PCI), Total Substitution Potential (TSP) and Economic Value (EV) for a 53-tonne WTB under current, improved and technologically optimised configurations. Mechanical recycling reaches PCI 0.79 and TSP 36 %, shifting from a net climate burden of 14.7 t CO2-eq to a net credit of 13.1 t CO2-eq, although EV remains negative because of the low value of downcycled outputs. Thermal recycling reaches PCI 0.94 and TSP 31 %, delivers a net climate credit and achieves the highest EV (€31,415) under technologically optimised conditions. Chemical recycling achieves the highest PCI (0.98) and a TSP of 30.6 %, but solvent production dominates its environmental burdens; solvent recirculation reduces climate impacts by 42 % relative to the improved configuration. The results show that higher circularity does not necessarily reduce environmental impacts or improve economic performance and support more realistic recycling targets and technology-development priorities for WTB and composite waste management.

items.title: Conceptualizing a building passport: defining its scope and requirements through a Delphi study
items.abstract: The construction industry is among the most resource-intensive sectors, contributing substantially to global resource consumption. In light of the escalating scarcity of natural resources, the circular economy (CE) paradigm offers a promising avenue for the recovery and reuse of raw materials. In order to achieve this objective, it is essential to establish a reliable information base that encompasses both semantic and geometric building data throughout the entire life cycle of a building. Presently, there is an absence of both a standardized information structure and a uniform definition in the form of a Building Passport that systematically integrates this content. The objective of this paper is to identify the relevant information requirements across the entire life cycle of a building, thereby establishing a foundation for defining a uniform Building Passport. The requirements were derived deductively based on a literature review and then evaluated through a two-stage Delphi survey involving construction industry experts. The results are then prioritized using comparative metrics and pairwise comparisons and documented in a structured requirements catalog. The findings suggest that a Building Passport is defined as a comprehensive and reliable compilation of building-related information intended to be maintained continuously. The primary focus of the Building Passport is on the deconstruction phase. This includes information on separability, dismantlability, and the potential for recycling and reuse. Additionally, indicators pertaining to materials, products, hazardous substances, and buildings are deemed pertinent. Furthermore, location-related information, general building data, and data concerning the circularity as well as timeliness of the stored information are considered relevant.

items.title: Institutional Architecture and Formal Coordination in an Entrepreneurial Ecosystem: The Case of Gliwice, Poland
items.abstract: Entrepreneurial ecosystems can support innovation-driven and sustainable regional development, yet less is known about how local institutions coordinate support across successive stages of firm development. This study examines the entrepreneurial ecosystem associated with Gliwice, Poland, focusing on its institutional architecture, formally available support instruments, institutional roles, and potential coordination issues. A qualitative single-case study was conducted using structured document analysis of 59 sources, institutional mapping, classification of support instruments across three firm-development stages, and an exploratory adaptation of the RACI framework. The analysis distinguishes a locally embedded ecosystem core from an external regional and national support environment. The documentary evidence indicates broad formal support across R&D and innovation, commercialization, expansion, scaling, and internationalization. However, several financing, investment, and internationalization functions are provided primarily by regional and national institutions, while formal mechanisms connecting organizations and support instruments across successive stages are less clearly documented. The study contributes by distinguishing the availability of institutional support from documented formal coherence, understood as documentary evidence of support continuity, complementarity, clarity of institutional roles, and formal coordination mechanisms.

items.title: Embracing Circularity: How Indian Small Businesses Are Redefining Sustainability
items.abstract: On account of resource insufficiency and polluted environmental situations, companies in India have adopted the principles of circular economy to gain sustainable development. In the present study, an attempt has been made to investigate the practice of circular economy principles by small companies in India by emphasizing more on the pros and cons of the concept. For the purpose of this chapter, case studies of the companies that have adopted circular economy practices were considered. The outcome of this study provides guidelines about the integration of the principles of circular economy model into their business operations. This research also gives suggestions about the support required from change agents in order to make this framework a sustainable economic model.

items.title: Transparency-Oriented Management Control in the Digitalized Circular Economy Context: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: The transition to a circular economy increases the need for information sharing, accountability, and coordination across organizational boundaries. While transparency is widely recognized as a prerequisite for circular economy implementation, existing research has primarily treated it as a reporting outcome rather than a managerial objective. This paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding how organizations can systematically manage and enhance transparency in the digitalized circular economy context. The study adopts a conceptual approach and synthesizes literature on circular economy, organizational transparency, management control, and organizational capabilities. Insights from these literature streams are integrated into a transparency-oriented management control framework. The paper proposes a framework in which transparency emerges from the interaction of three complementary dimensions: organizational transparency capabilities, transparency-oriented management control, and controller competence and activity. The framework conceptualizes transparency as a managed organizational capability and identifies controllers as key actors who transform digital data into meaningful transparency information and practices. The study shifts transparency from a disclosure outcome to a strategic management objective and offers a novel framework linking digitalization, management control, and circular economy implementation. It provides a foundation for future empirical research on transparency maturity and management control in circular economy ecosystems.

items.title: Transitioning to a circular economy for plastics in India: what role for grassroots innovation?
items.abstract: Plastic has become a ubiquitous material in our societies and plastic pollution is an issue of significant concern due to its environmental and health impacts. The circular economy (CE) is increasingly considered an important approach to improve plastic management. Until recently, the focus of academic research has been primarily on actions taken by businesses and policymakers to facilitate the emergence of the CE, with civil society mainly considered in its role as a consumer. As such, actions undertaken by civil society to address plastic management issues are under-researched. This paper draws on the concept of ‘grassroots innovation’ to examine initiatives targeting plastic issues in India to characterise factors of success and challenges. We conducted 13 semi-structured interviews with stakeholders involved in 15 initiatives. Using a composite framework, we characterised initiatives using six categories: context, appropriateness, governance and management, innovation, diffusion, outcomes and impacts. Our findings show that initiatives focus on three areas of innovation: alternative socio-economic settings, alternative material arrangements, and individual competences. Contextual factors (e.g. infrastructure, regulations) were often found to constrain the emergence and success of initiatives, while various forms of collaboration, stakeholder engagement and financial sustainability emerged as determining aspects of governance and management. Initiative diffusion, when it occurred, followed strategic, demand-led and participant-led scaling up patterns, as well as government-led or citizen-led replication. We conclude by identifying areas for improvement of the framework and reflecting on whether/how the initiatives studied progress the CE for plastics in India.

items.title: Business environmental innovation and circular economy practices: global evidence from corporate waste recycling
items.abstract: This study examines the role of business environmental innovation in advancing circular economy practices, with a particular focus on corporate waste recycling. Using a large sample of publicly listed firms from 41 countries over the period of 2007–2024, we provide robust empirical evidence that firms’ engagement in environmental innovation has a positive impact on their waste recycling performance. This relationship is significantly stronger in countries with lower levels of circular economy capability accumulation, suggesting that firms’ strategic decisions play a more critical role in the presence of institutional voids. Further analysis shows that although firms with greater environmental innovation engagement achieve lower waste intensities and higher waste recycling, they also generate larger absolute volumes of waste, pointing to the presence of a potential circular economy rebound effect. This study contributes to the rapidly growing interdisciplinary literature on the circular economy transition and offers important implications for policy design and corporate sustainability strategies.

items.title: CircuPuncture in Action: A Comparative Policy Analysis of Circular Economy Transitions in Wroclaw and Lódz
items.abstract: This article conducts a comparative policy analysis of circular economy (CE) transitions in Wroclaw and Lódz, through the theoretical lens of the CircuPuncture model. This adaptive governance framework proposes a step-by-step, project-based approach to CE implementation via circular clusters. The study moves from theory to empirical assessment, aiming to evaluate the alignment and effectiveness of urban CE strategies. Employing a qualitative case study design based on desk research, the methodology involves systematic document analysis of strategic plans, thematic coding within the CircuPuncture framework, and mapping of key performance indicators. The analysis contrasts the two cities’ pathways, revealing differing degrees of model implementation. It validates CircuPuncture as a diagnostic tool for urban CE governance, identifying specific “acupuncture points” for intervention, particularly in waste management. The article provides an evidence-based critique of Polish urban CE strategies, offering refined theoretical insights and practical, transferable lessons for fostering economic sustainability through adaptive local action. items.title: From Urban Growth to Material Accumulation: Reconstructing Building Stock Dynamics in Gothenburg, from 1960 to 2015
items.abstract: Urban building stocks accumulate large quantities of materials, but their long-term development is difficult to reconstruct at the building level because historical inventories often lack consistent information on building attributes and turnover. This study develops a spatially and temporally explicit framework for reconstructing building-stock dynamics and associated material flows by integrating historical GIS, building morphology, street-network characteristics, and machine-learning-based attribute enrichment. The framework is applied to Gothenburg, Sweden, from 1960 to 2015. Successive historical building layers are compared to identify construction and demolition, while missing information on building function and residential structural typology is inferred using machine-learning models. The reconstructed attributes are combined with gross floor area and material-intensity coefficients to quantify residential material stocks, construction inflows, and demolition outflows. Over the study period, Gothenburg’s population increased by 29%, while residential gross floor area increased by 102% and the estimated residential material stock by 39%. Approximately 10.9 Mt of residential materials entered the stock through new construction, while 1.14 Mt were released through identified demolition, resulting in approximately 9.75 Mt of net material accumulation. Construction and material inflows were concentrated in the late 1960s and early 1970s and were distributed unevenly across the city. Contemporary population density was positively associated with cumulative material-inflow density but explained only part of its spatial variation. The study demonstrates how historical spatial data and machine learning can support building-level reconstruction of long-term stock dynamics, providing an empirical basis for analysing the spatial formation, persistence, and turnover of urban material stocks.

items.title: Circular Economy and Climate Resilience: Implications for Governance, Adaptation Strategies, and Economic Inclusion of Smallholder Farmers in Nigeria
items.abstract: Climate change, environmental degradation, and global supply chain disruptions highlight the urgency of advancing circular economy (CE) practices for sustainable agricultural transformation. However, in fragile governance contexts such as Nigeria, CE adoption among smallholder farmers remains uneven. This study investigates the role of governance quality, socioeconomic conditions, and climate variability in shaping CE implementation in Southwest Nigeria. Using survey data from smallholder farmers, we applied an instrumental-variable multivariate probit regression model to account for interdependencies across multiple CE practices, residue recycling, composting, and waste-to-energy. Governance quality was assessed through five indices: transparency, participation, enforcement, coordination, and service delivery. Socioeconomic (education, income, farm size) and climatic variables (rainfall, drought shocks) were included to capture enabling and constraining conditions. The results show that governance quality significantly affects CE adoption patterns: transparency strongly drives residue recycling, participation fosters composting, and enforcement enables capital-intensive waste-to-energy. Coordination and service delivery exert broad positive effects across multiple practices. Education, income, and farm size were positively associated with adoption, whereas climatic variability significantly influenced adoption decisions, reflecting farmers’ sensitivity to ecological shocks. The findings imply that scaling CE in Nigeria requires more than technical innovation; it demands transparent, participatory, and credible governance alongside inclusive socioeconomic support. Policy interventions should prioritize the strengthening of advisory systems, farmer cooperatives, regulatory enforcement, and integrated service delivery while embedding the CE within broader climate adaptation strategies. items.title: Identifying and Prioritizing the Components of Circular Accounting: A Qualitative Study Based on Systematic Content Analysis
items.abstract: The expansion of the circular economy has increased the need to transform accounting systems and identify the components required to support decision-making and reporting related to efficient resource utilization, waste reduction, and environmental performance. Despite the growing body of research on circular accounting, its constituent components and dimensions have been addressed in a fragmented manner across different studies, highlighting the need to identify and integrate these components. The present study aimed to identify, categorize, and prioritize the components of circular accounting. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of methodology, it employed a qualitative, descriptive–analytical approach. To collect the data, scientific publications and texts related to circular accounting, the circular economy, sustainability, environmental accounting, and material flow management were systematically reviewed. During the analytical stage, conventional qualitative content analysis was used to extract relevant concepts from the texts, code them, and organize them into categories and subcomponents based on conceptual similarity. Through the process of analyzing and integrating the codes, three main categories were identified: dynamic capabilities of circular accounting, material flows in the circular economy, and institutional–environmental drivers and barriers. Subsequently, 12 subcomponents were extracted and classified: flexibility and reconfiguration; innovation and technology; learning and knowledge development; interaction and accountability; efficient material management and consumption; life cycle and environmental traceability; supply chain and resource optimization; policymakers and regulations; infrastructure and information technology; culture, education, and media; economic incentives and market pressure; and organizational and coordination barriers. items.title: ARISE: an urban political economy-informed resilience indicator framework for south asian metropolitan cities
items.abstract: Introduction Existing urban resilience indicator frameworks combine literature-derived pooling, expert validation, and multi-criteria weighting independently of any explicit theory of why some urban conditions, rather than others, are politically constituted as resilience priorities. Methods This paper’s contribution is methodological: it demonstrates how Urban Political Economy (UPE) theory can condition an indicator-development pipeline, from category structure through to how weighting outcomes are interpreted against theoretical commitments. ARISE, the Adaptive Resilience Indicator System for Equity, operationalises this UPE-conditioned approach through five stages: identification, categorisation, reduction, validation, and prioritisation. Drawing on 75 studies and 193 indicators, ARISE applies Pareto analysis and Staticized Group Technique consultation to produce 32 Resilience Indicators across seven dimensions, weighted via the Analytic Hierarchy Process by 18 experts. Results Urban Design and Spatial Planning carries the highest weight (36.04%); sensitivity analysis confirms stability for four dimensions, with Ecosystem and Resources (5.96%) the most panel-sensitive. Discussion The contribution is theory-conditioned indicator-development methodology: a UPE-derived categorisation structure, a two-track mechanism protecting under-cited indicators from elimination, and an explicit interrogation of the divergence between theoretical commitments and empirical outcomes, rather than a claim that the underlying AHP, Pareto, and SGT instruments are themselves novel. The indicator set illustrates what this conditioning produces, transferable in logic to other theory-grounded efforts. ARISE is not a validated scoring instrument at this stage; it is an expert-prioritised indicator-development framework whose empirical application to real cities constitutes the next research phase.

items.title: A systematic review of foresight methods used in the formulation of futures scenarios: evidence from articles indexed in scopus and web of science (2014–2023)
items.abstract: This study presents a systematic literature review of the foresight methods used in the formulation of futures scenarios, analyzing 115 articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science between 2014 and 2023. Applying the PRISMA methodology, the review identifies a plural methodological ecosystem in which—although qualitative approaches predominate—there are patterns of combination toward methodological triangulation aimed at strengthening plausibility and reducing bias in complex environments. The analysis shows that the most frequently used methods are environmental scanning (PESTEL), participatory workshops, the Delphi method, structural analysis (MICMAC), and Causal Layered Analysis (CLA). A significant expansion of these practices is observed beyond the traditional corporate sphere into sectors such as public health, higher education, governance, and environmental sustainability. The study further highlights an incipient presence of methods that incorporate artificial intelligence, text mining, and computational models, which complement qualitative narratives with quantitative rigor. The article proposes the concept of methodological aggregation capacity to describe the ability of scenario methodologies to coherently incorporate techniques of different epistemic natures. In conclusion, the maturity of the field rests on the systemic convergence between data-driven rigor and narrative depth, consolidating scenarios as instruments for social learning and strategic decision-making.

items.title: Evolution of waste management concepts: From recycling to resource economy in the context of Industry 4.0 and 5.0
items.abstract: The relevance of the study is conditioned by the aggravation of the global problem of waste management against the background of accelerating digital transformation of production systems. More than 2 billion tonnes of solid household waste are generated annually in the world, and by 2050 this figure, according to various estimates, will grow to 3.4-3.8 billion tonnes, while the share of processed products remains critically low even in developed countries. The purpose of the study was to systematise the evolution of conceptual approaches to waste management from its disposal to the development of a resource economy, to assess the role of institutional and regulatory mechanisms in this transition, and to substantiate the impact of Industry 4.0 technologies and human-centred Industry 5.0 principles on the transformation of the resource management system. The methodological basis was a systematic review of the literature, comparative and analytical and institutional analysis of scientific publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science for 2016-2024, analysis of corporate practice cases, and a secondary analysis of official reports and EU regulations. Six conceptual stages of waste management evolution have been identified, a threshold relationship between the rate of the landfill tax and the level of recycling in the EU countries has been established depending on regulatory instruments, the role of AI, IoT, blockchain, and digital product passports as catalysts for a closed material cycle in Industry 4.0 logic has been determined, and the concept of “Circular Economy 5.0”, which integrates human-centredness, resilience, and resource efficiency, has been substantiated. The practical significance of the study lies in the development of the author’s conceptual model of transition to a resource economy in the context of Industry 5.0, which can serve as a basis for developing strategies for the “green” restoration of Ukraine in the context of post-war reconstruction

items.title: Linking Circular Economy Practices to Sustainability Performance: The Roles of Extended Producer Responsibility and Institutional Support in Ethiopian Manufacturing
items.abstract: Translating circular economy practices (CEP) into sustainability performance requires understanding the organizational mechanisms and institutional conditions through which circularity is implemented. This study examines Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) as an intervening product-stewardship mechanism linking CEP with sustainability performance (SP) and Institutional Support (IS) as a boundary condition of the CEP–EPR and CEP–SP relationships in Ethiopian manufacturing. Data from 98 professionals with relevant manufacturing and sustainability-related experience were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). CEP was positively associated with EPR (β = 0.558, p < 0.001) and SP (β = 0.289, p = 0.022), while EPR was positively associated with SP (β = 0.358, p = 0.004). EPR partially mediated the CEP–SP relationship (β = 0.200, p = 0.017). IS significantly strengthened the CEP–EPR relationship (β = 0.196, p = 0.010), whereas its moderation of the direct CEP–SP relationship was not statistically significant. The findings position EPR as an intervening product-stewardship mechanism through which broader circular practices are associated with sustainability performance and show that institutional support is particularly relevant to translating circular practices into EPR implementation. By integrating the Natural Resource-Based View and Institutional Theory, the study clarifies how organizational circular practices, product stewardship, and institutional conditions interact within an emerging circular-economy context.

items.title: Biomass-integrated hybrid renewable energy for agri-food decarbonisation
items.abstract: Decarbonising energy-intensive agri-food facilities requires hybrid renewable systems that pair variable solar generation with dispatchable, locally sourced biomass. Hybrid sizing, gasification of agri-food residues and multi-criteria ranking are each well established. This study integrates them, optimising a biomass-photovoltaic hybrid against a measured industrial load across three candidate feedstocks, one a host-process by-product, and testing the ranking against alternative weightings. Fifteen grid-connected scenarios for a Greek slaughterhouse and feed plant drawing 404 MWh/yr are simulated in HOMER Pro from measured 2021 hourly load data and decadal NASA POWER meteorology, ranked by a distance-to-ideal multi-criteria method and stress-tested across six parameters. The selected configuration pairs 215 kW of photovoltaics with a 30 kW syngas generator on a 9:1 olive-pomace and feather blend, consuming 179 t/yr of a contracted 237 t/yr. Under the stated assumptions the model estimates a levelised cost of 0.135 EUR/kWh, 57 per cent below the 0.316 EUR/kWh baseline, and a 5.07-year discounted payback on an initial investment of 0.36 M EUR. Carbon intensity falls by 87 per cent on both accounting bases, and annual emissions from 190 to 24 tonnes CO₂eq, an avoided 166 tonnes a year. The generator is dispatched at a tariff of 0.221 EUR/kWh and not at 0.158 EUR/kWh, which brackets the threshold below which biomass dispatch ceases to be viable.

items.title: Circular Economy and Supply Chain Performance Under Geopolitical Tensions: The Roles of Recycling Efficiency and Logistics Infrastructure Capability
items.abstract: This study analyzed the effects of circular economy practices, resource self‐sufficiency capability, and organizational resilience capability on supply chain distribution performance in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region amid geopolitical tensions. The escalating geopolitical uncertainty, trade restrictions, and disrupted supply chains have illustrated the vulnerability of global supply chains, compelling organizations to implement measures that improve resource efficiency, resiliency, and sustainability over the long term. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was used in manufacturing and logistics firms, and data were collected from 320 manufacturing experts, supply chain managers, logistics experts, policy advisors, and sustainability officers across all six GCC countries. Smart PLS used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) to analyze the data, including measurement model evaluation to assess reliability and validity and structural model evaluation to assess the effects of direct, mediating, and moderating variables. Moreover, logistics infrastructure capability is studied as a moderating factor reinforcing the relationship between recycling efficiency and distribution performance by making it able to revive efficient product returns, recovery, and reintegration processes. items.title: Reversing the role of the customer: the new ‘customer-as-a-supplier’ supply chain principle for the circular context
items.abstract: This paper evaluates the relevance and sufficiency of a suite of six established supply chain principles for uncertainty reduction in circular supply chains, focusing on plastics in the construction sector. Using a structured intervention-based research approach, two trials with industry consortia designed and implemented closed-loop models for mortar tubs and aggregate packaging, incorporating higher recycled content and new reverse logistics arrangements. Findings confirm that original principles remain relevant but insufficient in circular contexts. We propose an additional principle ‘Customer-as-a-Supplier (CaaS)’ to address uncertainties in quality, timing, and volume of returned materials, and the changing role of customers in closed loop supply chains. CaaS emphasises communication, incentives, convenient return logistics, contamination control, and retailer engagement to enable high-quality material recovery. This extends the existing framework and highlights the active, and changing, role of customers. Future research should test the generality of CaaS and existing principles across diverse closed-loop supply chains.

items.title: The lifespan problem: Why EU circular economy indicators understate progress
items.abstract: The European Union circularity rate increased by only 1 %age point between 2013 and 2024 despite sustained regulatory effort. Aggregate circularity indicators combine sectors with fundamentally different material lifespans into a single metric, systematically understating progress in sectors dominated by long-lived material stocks. A stock-flow framework formalizes the mechanism: recovered material flows within any observation window are determined by the lifespan distribution of accumulated stock rather than by current recovery effort alone. The framework is illustrated using nineteen European industries spanning packaging, textiles, electronics, vehicles, construction, and energy infrastructure. The analysis develops three reform options within the existing EU statistical architecture. Class-disaggregated reporting could be piloted within the Circular Economy Monitoring Framework, a quality-adjusted construction and demolition waste indicator would require revised Eurostat reporting, and forward-looking credits depend on mandatory digital product passport infrastructure. Improving circularity measurement is necessary for directing policy attention and investment toward sectors that dominate future material use.

items.title: Circular City in the Smart City: Interactions Between Urban Typologies in Curitiba
items.venue: Encontro Nacional de Tecnologia do Ambiente Construído
items.abstract: This study investigates the convergence between Smart City and Circular City concepts through the case of Curitiba, analyzing how digital urban strategies interact with circular economy practices. The research adopts an exploratory qualitative approach, based on a systematic literature review (PRISMA protocol) and thematic analysis, resulting in the development of an analytical matrix structured into four dimensions: technological infrastructure, resource management, urban governance, and urban impacts. The matrix was applied to municipal programs to assess levels of integration between the analyzed paradigms. The findings indicate that Curitiba presents significant advances in digital infrastructure and governance; however, the incorporation of circularity remains fragmented and sectoral. The study concludes that the transition toward a circular-smart city depends on the systemic integration of digital technologies and resource flows, as well as the strengthening of institutional arrangements and public policies oriented toward urban sustainability.

items.title: Assurance and Accountability in Circular Economy Transitions for Sustainable Development
items.abstract: This study examines how disclosed circular implementation, reported circular accountability and circular‐specific assurance coverage are associated with sustainable development. Drawing on accountability theory, it distinguishes circular economy transition (CET), circular economy accountability (CEA) and circular economy assurance (CEAU) as analytically distinct disclosure‐based constructs. Using 79,260 firm‐year observations from 13,211 listed firms during 2020–2025, panel regressions with industry, year and country fixed effects show that greater disclosed circular implementation and circular‐specific assurance coverage are positively associated with reported circular accountability. The CET–CEA association is also stronger at higher levels of CEAU, a pattern consistent with an accountability demand–difficulty mechanism in which verification becomes more consequential as circular implementation creates dispersed evidential requirements. Results remain broadly consistent across lagged, alternative‐measurement and continental analyses. CET, CEA and CEAU are also positively associated with the retained broad sustainable‐development performance (SDP) composite, while the CET–SDP association is stronger at higher levels of reported accountability and assurance coverage. These findings are between‐firm conditional associations rather than causal or within‐firm effects. The study conceptualises circular‐specific assurance as boundary‐spanning verification infrastructure.

items.title: Green transition as selective (im)mobilities: towards a political economy of mobility justice
items.abstract: Green transition policies increasingly reshape how people, goods, workers and communities move, adapt and remain in place. This article argues that the green transition should be understood as a reorganisation of the social conditions under which mobility and immobility are produced, governed and distributed, extending analysis beyond decarbonisation targets and technological substitution. Existing debates on sustainable mobility and mobility justice do not fully capture how transition selectively enables some forms of movement while constraining, delaying or devaluing others. The article introduces selective (im)mobilities as an analytical framework for examining how green transition redistributes capacities for movement, adaptation and staying. The framework brings together five theoretical strands: the mobilities paradigm, the politics of mobility, mobility justice, motility, and political economy approaches to uneven development, spatial restructuring, labour and work. It develops a four-dimensional typology of infrastructural, economic, spatial and labour selectivity, showing how these dimensions interact to shape uneven mobility futures across places, households and workers. By reframing mobility justice around structured capabilities rather than formal access alone, the article conceptualises green transition as a political economy of differentiated mobility futures and provides a framework for tracing how transition burdens and opportunities are distributed across social and spatial positions.

items.title: GRIDS: An integrated sustainability framework for the net-zero transition
items.abstract: Net zero is not a single-sector decarbonisation problem: it spans energy, resource circularity, biodiversity, climate-aligned finance and supply-chain governance, and interventions in one domain register on the others. The review responds to a specific gap: these determinants are examined in separate literatures whose interactions are asserted rather than modelled. Following PRISMA 2020 conventions, this review consolidates twenty-four determinants into the GRIDS framework, comprising Governance and capital allocation, Resource circularity, Infrastructure and energy transition, Digitally enabled integration, and Stewardship of natural capital; nests them in eight validated clusters; and models their interdependence rather than asserting it. Fifty-three studies anchor the digital domain in oil and gas. A directed cross-impact matrix over the clusters is examined through MICMAC, interpretive structural modelling and perturbation simulation, as complementary lenses on one model rather than independent tests. Digital measurement and traceability are the only cluster whose independent classification survives boundary perturbation: it sits alone at the hierarchy's base, emitting strong links to six of the seven other clusters and receiving none, inverting the conventional treatment of digital tools as a service function. Ecological state and energy infrastructure jointly absorb perturbation from across the system, reported as a pair rather than ranked. The implication is a sequence: measurement layer first, energy build-out screened hardest, supply-chain and municipal outcomes last. The matrix is author-coded under a stated admissibility rule, not independently elicited, so these results are offered as falsifiable propositions released for re-elicitation. Priority gaps concern cross-domain metrics harmonisation, developing-economy applicability and AI governance.

items.title: Co‐Creating Circular Pathways in the Fashion Industry: A Participatory System Dynamics Perspective
items.abstract: Circular economy transitions in the fashion industry are frequently constrained not by a lack of reinforcing drivers but by endogenous feedback structures that limit growth as systems expand. Focusing on the Brazil context, this study identifies the dominant feedback archetypes governing circular transitions across four distinct socio‐technical contexts, namely, fashion brands, consumers, micro‐businesses, and digital circular platforms and offers an explanation, grounded in a participatory system dynamics approach, for why circular initiatives stall or progress. A participatory approach was adopted, combining co‐created causal loop diagrams, group model building, and backcasting workshops targeting a shared 2030 circular economy scenario, actively engaging 20 heterogeneous stakeholders including fashion brands, waste picker cooperatives, local government officials, and academics. Four causal loop diagrams were developed and validated through recorded and transcribed stakeholder interviews. The results identify a dominant limits to growth archetype across all four contexts, each driven by a distinct limiting mechanism: margin erosion in fashion brands, price‐mediated adoption constraints in consumer markets, infrastructure and workforce deficits in micro‐business recycling systems, and a dual operational and financial constraint in digital circular platforms. By structurally mapping reinforcing drivers, limiting feedbacks, and generic solutions onto four empirically grounded causal loop diagrams, this study contributes to the understanding of circular economy transitions as feedback‐driven processes and offers context‐specific leverage points for firms, cooperatives, and policymakers seeking to design more durable and coordinated circular strategies in comparable settings.

items.title: Consumer Engagement in SME-Based Circular Economy Practices: Evidence from a Plastic Upcycling Enterprise in Indonesia
items.venue: Journal of Environmental and Development Studies
items.abstract: Circular economy practices depend not only on waste-processing technologies but also on consumer participation in sustaining material circulation and value creation. This study examines how consumers engage in circular economy practices and contribute to economic, social, and environmental value creation in Paste Lab Yogyakarta, a community-embedded plastic upcycling SME in Indonesia. Using a qualitative single-case design, the study collected data through seven semi-structured interviews with six consumer informants and one internal informant for triangulation, complemented by observation and documentation. The study analyzed the data thematically, guided by stakeholder theory and perspectives on value co-creation. The findings identify three recurring consumer roles: material contributors who supply post-consumer plastic, co-design collaborators who support product and application development, and advocates who extend sustainability narratives and stakeholder networks. These roles contribute to resource circulation, commercial opportunities, social legitimacy, and environmental value, although participation is constrained by limited consumer literacy, durability concerns, price sensitivity, and restricted design options. The study concludes that consumer engagement can support distributed value co-creation in SME-based circular economy practices by linking material recovery, application, and network diffusion within a local circular value chain.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF INDUSTRIAL PARKS ON THE IMPLEMENTATION OF REGIONAL SMART SPECIALISATION
items.abstract: The article examines how industrial parks influence the implementation of regional smart specialisation. The relevance of the study stems from the need to convert strategic regional priorities into specific production projects, value chains and employment while accounting for resource, energy and security constraints that are particularly significant for Ukrainian regions. The purpose of the article is to substantiate the mechanism through which an industrial park can support the implementation of a region’s production profile based on smart specialisation. The methodological framework combines analysis and synthesis of scientific literature, comparison of universal and profile-based approaches to industrial park development, structural and logical modelling, and systematisation of Ukrainian regulatory and analytical data. The study shows that the sectoral profile of an industrial park should derive from the competitive advantages of the territory, including existing enterprises, labour skills, logistics, energy conditions, educational and research capacity, raw materials and confirmed investment demand. Particular attention is paid to the selection of mutually complementary residents. Their production and resource links can create industrial symbiosis in which by-products, waste, heat, water or services of one enterprise become inputs for another. This approach reduces operating costs, limits environmental pressure and strengthens local value chains. A conceptual model of regional smart specialisation implementation through an industrial park is proposed. The model links the resource profile of the region, smart priority, park profile, resident selection, production and resource cooperation, and regional effects. A matrix of criteria for assessing the correspondence of an industrial park to the regional smart specialisation profile is developed. items.title: Time Management in Circular Construction: A Systematic Review of Secondary Materials Integration
items.abstract: The transition of the building and construction industry towards a circular economy (CE) increasingly relies on the integration of secondary materials. This integration can disrupt the traditional cost, time and quality metrics of project success. While research has extensively examined the technical feasibility (quality) and economic viability (cost) of secondary materials, time implications remain underexplored. This study employs a systematic literature review approach to identify key time‐intensive activities associated with the use of secondary materials in construction, their underlying causes and potential mitigation strategies. Through a review of 41 relevant publications, the study found that time‐intensive activities occur across the project life cycle, including planning, design, predemolition, demolition, waste collection and processing, procurement and construction. These time demands largely arise from misalignments between conventional construction workflows and the requirements of circular practices, coupled with a lack of enabling digital, regulatory, logistical and contractual infrastructures, which increase uncertainty. Accordingly, this study provides recommendations for seven key stakeholder groups, namely, clients, architects and design consultants, builders, demolishers, project managers, procurement managers and policymakers, to help reduce or strategically invest time in ways that better support the integration of secondary materials in construction.

items.title: Advancing Industrial Symbiosis: The Dynamic Role of Public Organisations
items.abstract: Industrial symbiosis is a key circular economy strategy that relies on collaboration among diverse actors to turn residual streams into new value. Although prior research acknowledges supportive public‐sector involvement, there is a lack of understanding of how public organisations' roles evolve over time as industrial symbiosis initiatives develop. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative case study of a regional industrial ecosystem in northern Sweden. Drawing on 25 interviews with public organisations, support actors and producers, five distinct public‐sector roles are identified (policymaker, facilitator, knowledge broker/data provider, participant and financier). The study shows that roles shift across industrial symbiosis development phases, and a framework is developed that links role configurations to phase‐specific barriers. The study contributes by conceptualising public organisations as dynamic ecosystem actors and by offering a practical framework that helps public organisations to align roles with evolving ecosystem needs to support long‐term circular economy transformation.
